Fida M Kamal, Advocate ------ For Petitioners 
No one appears ------ For Opposite Parties.
parties:
Rezia Sultan & another ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Md Haroon Malik and another ------ Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule by the plaintiffs directed against Order dated 19-2-1987 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 114 of 2983 affirming order No. 35 dated 4-9-1982 passed by the learned Munsif, 6th Court, Dhaka allowing Miscellaneous Case No. 65 of 1982 under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure arising out of Title Suit No. 211 of 1978 of the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka renumbered as Title Suit No. 933 of 1982 of the Court of Munsif, 6th Court, Dhaka.

2. Plaintiffs instituted the aforesaid suit for ejectment of ordinary ejectable monthly tenants at will stating that plaintiffs are the sole 16 annas owner of Municipal Holding No. 64, Purana Paltan, within PS Lalbagh now Motijheel, Dhaka. The defendants have been inducted by the plaintiffs as monthly tenants-at-will at a rent of Taka 320 per month payable according to English Calendar in respect of one pucca ground floor room No.3 of the building lying and situated at Rezia Manzil, 64, Purana Paltan in which defendants are carrying on business therein under the name and style 'Continental Motors'. As per agreement of tenancy dated 15-4-69 the rent of the month concerned of the suit room shall be paid within 7 days of following next  month. Defendants are always irregular in making payment of monthly rent and stopped payment of rent for the period of January, 1975 to December, 1977 totaling Taka 11,520. In further case of the plaintiffs that without the knowledge and consent of the plaintiffs the defendants have allowed others to display their sign board over the tenanted suit room. The suit room is now bonafide required by the plain- tiff for personal use and occupation to accommodate their family members. Plaintiffs through their Advocate issued notice dated 4-1-77 under section 106 of the Transfer of property Act under registered post with A/D to the defendants asking them to quit and vacate the suit room with the expiry of 31st day of January, 1977. But the defendants did not pay any heed to the aforesaid notice and did not vacate the suit room within the time fixed in the notice. The defendants with malafide motive did not receive the aforesaid notice dated 4-1-77 which was returned to the plaintiffs with the remark 'refused' as per postal endorsement dated 6-1-77, thereafter plaintiffs filed the suit.

3. In the suit, as it appears from the order sheets that defendant did not appear and the suit was posted for exparte disposal and the suit was decreed exparte on 12-9-78. After exparte decree, plaintiff put the decree into execution and Court issued writ of delivery of possession on 30-9-80; defendants were evicted from the suit premises on 5-10-80. Thereafter, defendants filed application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka, which is registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 192 of 1980. In the said miscellaneous case plaintiff entered appearance after service return. On 30-10-1981 said miscellaneous case as per notification No. 26-J-IV /50C-9/78 dated 14-1-81 was transferred to the Court of Munsif 6th Court, Dhaka. learned Munsif received the case record on 22-4-1982 and registered the miscellaneous case as Miscellaneous Case No. 65 of 1982. Learned Munsif on 4-9-82 allowed the miscellaneous case exparte and after vacating the order of exparte decree, registered the suit to its original file and number as Title Suit No. 9333 of 1982. The petitioners thereafter moved before the learned Munsif as well as revisional Court for setting aside the ex parte order registering the suit to its file and number. Thereafter, petitioners moved this Court and obtained this rule. Defendant opposite parties appeared in the rule, filed counter affidavit but at any point of time defendant-opposite parties did not appear before this Court. In the counter-affidavit defendant-opposite parties denied the plaint case of the petitioners.

4. Mr Fida M Kamal, learned Advocate, appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners, submits that, learned judges of both the Courts below did not consider that the miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed long after 2 years 1 month 21 days after the exparte decree and allowed miscellaneous case exparte without considering the delay is liable to be set aside. Learned Advocate on reference to section 24A (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure submits that, as per section 24A (2) of the Code, Court is bound to inform the parties as to transfer of the case and in absence of any notice to the parties informing the transfer, Court has no jurisdiction to pass any order on the case/suit. Learned advocate cited the decision of Abdul Khaleque vs Abdul Barek Howlader, 2 BLC 276 and also the Appellate Division of this case of Abdul Khaleque vs Abdul Barek Howlader, reported in 3 BLC (AD) 174 and another decision i.e. the case of Muhammad lshaque vs Abdul Haque, reported in PLD (Karachi) 899. In these decisions the question arises whether transfer Court without satisfying as to service of notice upon the parties can pass the decree exparte. It is admitted position that defendants are out of possession, as such, whether defendants can maintain the application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the suit after setting aside the said decree passed exparte without any prayer for recovery of possession.

5. Section 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure restricted power of Small Cause Courts constituted under the Small Cause Courts Act, 1887 or to Court exercising the jurisdiction of a Court of Small Causes under the said Act, that is to say,

(a) so much of the body of the Code as relates to-

(i) 	suits excepted from the cognizance of a Court of Small Causes;

(ii) the execution of decrees in such suits;

(iii) The execution of decrees against immovable property; and

(b) the following sections, that is to say,- Section 9. Section 91 and 92, Sections 94 and 95 so far as they authorize or relate to,-

(i) 	orders for the attachment of immovable property,

(ii) 	injunction

(iii) 	the appointment of a receiver of immovable property, or

(iv) the interlocutory orders referred to in clause (e) of section 94 and sections 96 to 112 and 115.

6. Small Cause Courts constituted under section 5 of Small Causes Courts Act; section 15 of the Act gives jurisdiction of Courts of Small Causes i.e. the Court has jurisdiction in the case of eviction of the tenant and Small Causes Courts cannot decide title of any party, it has no jurisdiction to pass the decree for recovery of possession if the tenant thrown out of possession of the premises. It can settle only the rightly of the tenant as regard possession over the suit premises i.e. whether he landlord acted in accordance with law or in accordance of the terms of the agreement, that is, if the rents illegally enhanced, if the land lord curtail the facilities provided under tenancy agreement of the tenant or if the landlord disturbed the tenant in any manner, then Small Causes Court has jurisdiction to look into the matter but Small Causes Courts cannot restored to possession of any tenant dispossessed or thrown out of suit premises by execution of decree. In the instant case as I find by execution of decree defendants were thrown out of the suit premises and when the Miscellaneous case was filed, tenants were out of possession that means, decree of the suit or for the purpose the suit was filed has been satisfied and jurisdiction of Small Causes Courts has been totally ousted as a tenant cannot fight any legal battle if he she is out of possession as Court cannot compelled the land lord to restore possession of an unwanted tenant. And in that case, defendants can seek for damage not for restoration of possession or restoration of the suit.

7. Next point raised by the learned Advocate i.e. what is effect of transfer of the suit from one Court to another. Section 24A (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure is the governing law on this subject. Let me quote section 24A (2) of the Code:-

(2) Where any suit, appeal or other proceeding is transferred from one Court to another, otherwise that on the application of a party, the parties thereto shall appear before the Court from which the suit, appeal or other proceedings is to be transferred, on the day already fixed for their appearance before the Court, and such Court shall than communicate the order of transfer to such parties and direct them to appear before the Court to which the suit, appeal or other proceeding is to be transferred, either on the same day, or on such earliest day as may be reasonable having regard to the distance at which the other Court is located.

8. Learned Advocate relied on the decisions of Abdul Khaleque vs Abdul Barek Howlader, 3 BLC (AD) 174 wherein it is held that the High Court Division on the ground of following the provision of law as required under section 24A(2) of the Code sent back the case on remand after setting aside the decree of the appellate Court. Leave to appeal was sought from the said judgment on the ground of maintainability of the suit which having not been raised before the revisional Court, it is not open to him now to argue on the merit of the case.

<u>9. As per section 24A (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure transfer Court is required to pass order of transfer on a date fixed for the appearance of the parties, and such Court shall communicate the order to such parties direct them to appear before the Court to which the proceeding is transferred. As per provision of section 24A(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure I do not find from the order sheets that order of transfer was made on a Date when the case was fixed for appearance. Such requirement of law would have been duly complied with if the transferee Court would informed the parties of the transfer. But on record there is nothing to show that petitioners were informed about the transfer of the case either by the transferor Court or by the transferee Court. Further, the transferee Court did not pass any order indicating or showing that the petitioners were duly informed about the transfer.</u>

10. As per provision of section 24A(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure I do not find from the order sheets transferee Court after receiving the record informed the parties to the case. So these orders passed by the Courts below are bad on this count.

11. On the question of limitation, it appears from the record that application filed by the defendants under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure after the period of limitation. I personally checked the application filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and find no explanation as to delay caused in filing the application, which is required to be filed within 30 days and if it is not within that period then there must by some satisfactory explanation explaining the delay in filing the application, present in the application. Learned Judges of the Courts below must have to go through the case record between lines but I find that they did not. Moreover, it appears that the suit was filed in 1987 and also from record it appears that defendants were evicted from the suit premises on 5-11-1980 and it is now more than 31 years, defendants are out of possession, as such, in no imagination defendants can be restored to possession as by this time much water flows in the river Buriganga and such position as I see accepted by plaintiffs and defendants by their conduct.

12. In the meantime it appears that plaintiff No.2 died and application for substitution of the heirs of plaintiffs No.2 have been filed and plaintiff No.1 is wife of the deceased and other heirs of plaintiffs executed Vokalatnama to prosecuted the rule. The application for substitution is allowed. Office is directed to cause substitution of the heirs of the deceased plaintiff No. 2 in his place.

13. On an overall consideration of the entire matter I find substance in this rule.

14. In the result, this rule is made absolute. No costs.

15. The judgment and order dated 19-2- 1987 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 114 of 1983 dismissing the Civil Revision against Order No. 35 dated 4-9-1982 passed by the learned Munsif, 6th Court, Dhaka allowing the Miscellaneous Case No. 65 of 982, original Miscellaneous case No. 192 of 1980 are set aside.

16. Send down the lower Court records at once.

Communicate this order at once.

End.

lawyer:
Lutfor Rahman Mondal, Advocate ------ For the Petitioner 
No one appears ------ For Opposite-parties.
parties:
Johura Khatun and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Sajed Ali Khan & others  ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
The certified copy of the plaint of Title Suit No. 309 of 2004 and the Order dated 13-8-2005 passed by the Joint District Judge, First Court Dhaka be kept with the record.

2. In an application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure leave was granted to examine the legality and propriety of the impugned judgment and Order passed by the revisional Court dated 5-2-2008 in Civil Revision No. 191 of 2007 reversing the judgment and Order: dated 31-5-2007 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, 6th Court Dhaka in Title Suit No. 17 of 2006 in rejecting the application for rejection of plaint.

3. The predecessor in interest of the present opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 7 of 1956 for partition which was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 49 of 1957 and lastly Title Suit No. 68 of 2003 now pending before the Joint District Judge, Dhaka wherein the predecessor in interest of the petitioners are different. The defendants contested the suit and ultimately the trial Court after hearing the parties, considering the facts and circumstances, provision of law, evidence both oral and documentary decreed the suit in preliminary form vide judgment and decree dated 20-2-1959. Being aggrieved the predecessor in interest of the present petitioners i.e. the defendants of the aforesaid suit preferred Appeal being First Appeal No. 179 of 1959. However, the appellate Court affirmed the decree with some modification. Thereafter, the trial Court proceeded with the suit and the same is now pending. The present petitioner as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 17 of 2006 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka for a declaration that the judgment and decree in preliminary form passed in Title Suit No. 49 of 1957 is obtained by practicing fraud upon the Court as well as the defendants. The defendants opposite party entered appearance and filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejecting of the plaint. The trial Court after hearing the parties, considering the facts and circumstances and the plaint vide judgment and Order dated 31-5-2007 rejected the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and directed the defendants to file written statement. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and Order passed by the trial Court the opposite party as petitioner invoked section 115 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure before the District Judge, Dhaka being Civil Revision No. 191 of 2007 and the same was heard and disposed of by the District Judge who vide the impugned judgment and Order allowed the said revision and thereby allowed the application for rejection of plaint by setting aside the judgment and Order passed by the trial Court.

4. Being aggrieved the petitioner moved before this Court under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure resulting granting of leave.

5. The matter is being fixed for hearing by this Court on 10-5-2009 and since then the same is appearing in the cause list. The hearing of the case was concluded on 20-7-2009 and today the matter has been fixed for pronouncement of judgment and the matter has been appearing in the list with the name of the learned Advocate for the contesting parties. Though the learned Mr Serajul Islam Bhuiyan filed power but no one appear on behalf of the opposite party to oppose the Rule.

6. Mr Lutfor Rahman Mondal, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the revisional Court without applying its judicial mind and without considering the facts arid circumstances and the provisions of law specially by misinterpreting the provision relates to rejection of plaint, limitation etc, most illegally and in an unlawful manner passed the impugned judgment and Order and thereby the revisional Court committed an error of an important question of law occasioning failure of justice. He submits that the revisional Court on misconception and by misinterpretation of the law and relevant provisions relates to rejection of plaint most illegally and in an arbitrary manner passed the impugned judgment and Order which is liable to be set aside for ends of justice. The learned Advocate frankly submits that the petitioners contesting the original suit and also filed an Appeal unsuccessfully. He also submits that the petitioner preferred Title Suit No. 309 of2004, plaint of which has been rejected but in the present case in hand the petitioner raises the practice of fraud only in such circumstances the suit is not barred under any law of limitation. Referring the decision reported in 13 BLD (AD) 217 and 11 MLR (AD) 58 he submits that the question of res judicata is to be considered by the Court below very carefully. Referring the decision reported in 32 DLR (AD) 167 as well as 19 DLR (SC) 433 he submits that in the case of practice of fraud the limitation shall run from date of actual knowledge of such practice of fraud. He submits that the revisional Court ought to have considered the complicated question of fraud raised by the petitioner in the present suit thus the Courts below committed an error of an important question of law occasioning failure of justice.

7. I have perused the impugned judgment and Order, Order passed by the trial Court, supplementary affidavit annexures, and the plaint of Title Suit No. 309 of 2004 as well as the Order dated 13-8- 2005.

8. On perusal of the same it appears that a partition suit was initiated in the year 1956 being Title Suit No.7 of 1956 and the same is still pending for final disposal. In the said suit the trial Court passed the preliminary decree in the year 1956 and the same challenged by the present petitioner by way of Appeal and the appellate Court however affirmed the same. The trial Court proceeded with the same and the same is now pending being Title Suit No. 68 of 2003.

9. Admittedly the petitioner filed a suit challenging the aforesaid decree being Title Suit No. 309 of 2004 wherein the ground pressed by the petitioner is the ground of adverse possession. Raising the question of adverse possession the petitioner in that suit challenged the legality and property of the original decree and the Trial Court rejected the plaint.

10. The petitioner thereafter preferred the present suit namely Title Suit No. 17 of 2006 raising the question of fraud. The defendants opposite party filed an application for rejection of plaint before the trial Court unsuccessfully but ultimately the plaint was rejected by the revisional Court.

11. On perusal of the impugned judgment and Order passed by the revisional Court it appears that the revisional Court rejected the plaint mainly on the ground of limitation, rejection of Title Suit No. 309 of2004 in earlier occasion as well as preferring First Appeal being No. 179 of 1956 by the present petitioner.

12. Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure deals with the provision relates to rejection of plaint which runs as follows;

"The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:

(a) 	Where it does not disclose a cause of action;

(b) 	Where the relief claimed is undervalued and the plaintiff on being required by the Court to correct the valuable within a time- to be fixed by the Court fails to do so;

(c) 	Where the relief claimed is properly valued but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped and the plaintiff on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the court, fails to do so;

(d) Where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law:

Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not exceed twenty one days."

13. So it appears that the plaint may be rejected on the aforesaid grounds. In the present case in hand the Courts below invoked Rule 11(a) and (d).

14. It is admitted position, that the present petitioner contested the original suit, preferred appear as well as preferred Title Suit No. 309 of 2004 i.e. the present petitioners are aware of the proceeding.

15. On perusal of the judgment passed by this Court in Civil Order No. 1465 of 2007 it appears that the petitioner also filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the trial Court in Title Suit No. 68 of 2003 for setting aside the preliminary decree in the original on the allegation of fraud. The trial Court however rejected the application and the first revisional Court affirmed the same. Being aggrieved the petitioner preferred revision before this Court under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure which was rejected summarily. In the said Order the High Court Division held as follows:

16. The trial Court though found-

১ম আপীলে বিাদীপক্ষ প্রতারনার কোন যুক্তি নেয় নাই। কিন্তু আরজী, জবাব, তপসীল, প্রদর্শনী ও পেপার বুক পর্যালোচনা করিয়া কিছু প্রতারনার বিষয় প্রতীয়মান হয়। অত্র প্রাথমিক রায় ও ডিক্রী মহামান্য উচ্চ আদালত কর্তৃক কিছু পরিবর্তন সহ বহাল রাখা হয়। মহামান্য উচ্চ আদালত উক্ত ক্রটিগুলি লক্ষ্য করে নাই বলিয়া দরখাস্তে উল্লেখ করা হয়।বিবাদী ১ম সাব জজ আদালতে আরজী দায়ের করিলে তাহা প্রত্যায়ন হয়। সহকারী জজ ৬ষ্ট আদালতে দেঃ ১৭/০৬ মালমা একই বিচারাধীন আছে। মহামান্য উচ্চ আদালতের ক্রটি অত্র আদালত সংশোধন অধিকার রাখে না।

According by Order dated 4-6-2006 the trial Court rejected the application filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and fixed 4-7- 2006 for commissioners' reports."

17. The Court further held;

"When the remedy available to the defendants has been availed of by filing Title Suit No. 17 of 2006 for setting the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 7 of 1956 on the ground of fraud in obtaining the said decree the revisional Court accordingly not allow such prayer and by the impugned Order dated 4-3-2007 - rejected Civil Revision No. 277 of 2006."

18. The Court further held;

"If any error or fraud was committed in obtaining the contesting decree in the partition suit that may be brought on record by the defendants by producing all relevant evidence and the said Court will be free to decide the suit on merit."

19. So it is apparent from the record that the trial Court in Title Suit No. 68 of2003 found prima facie case of fraud.

<u>20. Since the present petitioner filed the suit for setting aside of the preliminary decree absolutely on different ground of fraud at this stage it cannot be said that the plaint is barred by Order VII, rule 11 (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Regarding the limitation it is now a well settled proposition of law is that the limitation shall run from the date of actual knowledge and in the case in hand the period of' limitation is very much in favour of the petitioner. The question of fraud is being raised in the suit and the same question was neither raised by the petitioner in Appeal or in Title Suit No. 309 of 2004. In such circumstances it cannot be said outright that the present suit is hit by doctrine of resiudicata. Obviously the trial Court by framing issues regarding res judicata and limitation can dispose of the suit after taking evidence after commending the facts and circumstances. The decisions as referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner lend support to above contention.</u>

21. Considering the facts and' circumstances, provisions of law, decisions as referred to I am of the view that the revisional Court by the impugned judgment and Order committed an error of an important question of law rejecting the plaint and thereby occasioning failure of justice. Accordingly I find sufficient reason to interfere. The application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure is allowed without any Order as to cost. The impugned judgment and Order dated 5-2-2008 passed by the revisional Court rejecting the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure is hereby set aside. The trial Court is directed to dispose of the suit expeditiously as possible not later than 6 (six) months from the date of received of the judgment without fail.

Communicate this Order at once.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Shahadat Tanvir Amin, Advocate, with Mr. Abul Quashem, Advocate------ For the Petitioner, Iqbal Hossain, Assistant Attorney General------ For the Opposite Party No.1. 
Mr. ARM Hasanuzzaman Advocate------ For the Opposite Party Nos. 2 (a)-2(m).
parties:
Rakibuddin Talukder  ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and another  ------ Opposite- Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule calls in question the legality and propriety of the Judgment and decree dated 09-03-1989 passed by the learned Subordinate Jude, Sirajganj, allowing Other Class Appeal No. 47 of 1984 and dismissing the suit by reversing those of dated 11- 03-1984 passed by the learned Munsif, Sirajganj, Decreeing the Other Class Suit No. 259 of 1980.

2. Short facts leading to this Rule are that on 04- 07-1980, the petitioner as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No. 259 of 1980 in the Court of Munsif, Sirajganj, pleading opposite parties as defendants for declaration of title in respect of 1.83 acres of land out of 9.80 acres described in the schedules ক and খ of the plaint.

3. The plaintiff's case put in a nutshell are that the suit land of Mouza Chak Bahuka, Police Station Sirajganj, District Pabna (now Sirajganj) appertaining to CS plot no 8415 measuring an area of 9.80 acres was recorded in abstract khatian as Ichchamair river in the names of Dinesh Chandra Chowdhury, and Mutwalli and Akfar Ali Talukder of Amiruddin Wakf Estate during CS operation. Thereafter the said land became cultivable whereupon the plaintiff got ক schedule land measuring an area 1.28 acres from three sons of Dinesh Chandra Roy and Bhupendra Chandra Roy by way of pattan on 15th Aswin, 1348 BS and on 15th Ashar, 1350 BS got খ schedule land measuring an area of 0.55 acres from Akfar Ali Talukder by way of Pattan. The plaintiff executed a kabuliyat in favour of Zamindar for the ক schedule land on 1st Kartik, 1348 BS. Since then the plaintiff has been exercising right, title and possession over the suit land. But during S.A. settlement operation, the land was recorded in abstract khatian of the Government for which the title of the plaintiff was clouded. Hence the suit.

4. The defendant No. I (Government of Bangladesh) and added defendant No.2 contested the suit by filing separate written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint.

5. The case of the defendant No.1 are that the suit land was the khas land of Ex-landlords which by operation of law vested with the Government. The Government is now exercising its right of possession in the suit land.

6. The case of the defendant No.2 are that the suit land measuring an area of 9.80 acres was originally belonged to Zamindar Amiruddin Talukder and Dinesh Chandra Roy. On the basis of amicable settlement Amiruddin Talukder got the entire land who died leaving behind one son Akfar Ali Talukder as his heir. He got 2.00 acres of land including the suit land claimed by the plaintiff by way of pattan in 1350 BS and during S. A. operation the land was duly recorded in his favour in S.A. khatian No.985. During Liberation War, his all documents were lost. The plaintiff has been claiming the suit land by way of some fictitious documents and he has no right, title and possession in the suit land. Therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

7. On the pleadings following issues were settled by the trial Court.

a)	Whether the suit was maintainable in the present form?

b)	Whether the suit was barred by detect parties?

c)	Whether the plaintiff has right, title and possession in the suit land?

d) Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree as prayed for?

e)	To what relief, if any, the plaintiff was entitled to?

8. In course of trial the plaintiff examined three witnesses, of them PW 1 Md Rakibuddin Talukder (Plaintiff) proved his documents which were exhibited and marked as exhibits 1-6, PW 2, PW Md. Wahejuddin and PW 3 Md. Wabiruddin Talukder are the local witnesses who were examined to corroborate evidence of PW 1 in respect of possession.

9. The defendants examined six witness, of them, Md. Abdul Quddus, the local Talisilder who deposed on behalf of defendant No.1, PW 2 Md. Matiur Rahman (added defendant No.2). DW 3, Md. Jahurul Haq Talukder, DW 4 Md. Delwar Hossain Talukder, DW 5 Joynal Abedin and DW 6 MA Gafur were examined to corroborate the evidence of DW2 regarding possession. They proved their documents which were exhibited and marked as exhibits A-1.

10. After trial the learned Judge of the trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 11-03-1984 decreed plaintiff were found suspicious but he could prove his adverse possession in the suit land. Against which the added defendant No.2 as appellant preferred Other Class Appeal No. 47 of 1984 in the Court of District Judge, Sirajganj, which was ultimately heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, Sirajganj, who by judgment and decree dated allowed appeal and dismissed the suit by reversing those of the trial Court.

11. Feeling aggrieved, the plaintiff as petitioner preferred the instant application and obtained the present Rule.

12. Mr. Md. Shahadat Tanvir Amin, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr. Abdul Quashem, Advocate, and the petitioner seeks to impeach the impugned judgment and decree on the threefold arguments. Firstly, the possession even under mistaken or invalid title for sufficient length of time and continuity gives the holder a good title. In support of his contentions the learned Counsel refers the case of Amirunnessa vs Abdul Mannan Howlader reported in 17 BLD 251 = 1 BLC 183 wherein it has been held:-

"Acquisition of title on imperfect document

The plaintiff basic title deed is an unregistered deed of gift. But since the plaintiffs have been successful in proving that they exclusively possessed the suit property for over 12 years on the basis of this imperfect document and kept the defendants out of possession for the said period the plaintiffs have acquired a valid title by adverse possession even on the basis of the defective deed of gift.

13. He next refer the case of Hriday Ranjan Dey vs Niranjan Dey being dead his heirs- Probate Dey reported in 6 MLR (AD) 267 = 54 DLR (AD) 16 wherein it has been held:

“Section 28-Acquisation of title by adverse possession-

Person entering into possession of land on the basis of defective title document and having been in continuous possession thereof for more than, 12 years acquires title perfected by adverse possession as contemplated under section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908 and, as such, he is entitled to get decree for declaration of his title."

14. Secondly, the learned Judge of the trial Court after considering the consistent oral evidence of the plaintiff decreed the suit. There is no illegality in such decree. In support of his contentions the learned Counsel refers the case of Dudu Mia being dead his heirs: 1(a) Md. Moyezuddin vs Ekram Mia Chowdhury reported in 7 MLR (AD) 7 = 54 DLR (AD) 7 wherein it has been held:

"Appellate Court has the jurisdiction to decide the issues of fact and law in under perspective than that of the trial Court. Appellate Court can reverse of finding of possession of the trial Court upon re-assessment of the evidence on record. But it cannot reverse the finding of possession of the trial Court merely on assumption or any other hypothesis contrary to the evidence on record. The learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in law in reversing the finding of possession of the trial Court, based on proper appreciation of evidence merely on assumption contrary to the evidence on record."

15. He next refers the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) vs Abdur Rashid reported in 5 BLC (AD) 76 wherein it has been held,

"The trial Court had considered the material evidence in detail in coming to its finding of title and possession in favour of the plaintiffs, but the appellant Court, without discussing they evidence had abruptly reversed the finding of facts arrived at by the trial Court which is not a proper judgment of reversal as has been correctly found by the High Court Division.

16. He also refers the case of Narayan Chandra Dey vs Ali Azam Sarder (minor) reported in 1 BLC (AD) 185 wherein it has been held:

"Judgment of reversal the trial Court considered the oral evidence of both the parties in dismissing the suit, but the lower appellate Court, being the final Court of fact, did not at all consider the oral evidence of the parties in reversing the decree. The lower appellate Court did not at all arrive at any finding on possession, far less reversing the trial Court's finding thereon, but the High Court Division wrongly held that the lower appellate Court had found possession of the plaintiff in the disputed land, as such, judgment of High Court Division is not sustainable. The Judgment and order of the High Court Division as well as the judgment and decree of the tower appellate Court are set-aside and the appeal is sent back to the lower appellate Court for rehearing the case in accordance with law."

17. The learned Counsel lastly submits that without reversing the finding of facts arrived at by the trial Court, the Court of appeal below allowed the appeal thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

18. Mr. Iqbal Hossain, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the opposite party No. arid Mr. ARM Hasanuzzaman, Advocate appearing the opposite party Nos. 2(a)-2(m) oppose the Rule. The common contrition's are that the plaintiff failed to prove his title and continuous possession in the suit land more than sixty years so he is not entitled to get a decree on consideration of the adverse possession against the Government in view of the provisions laid down in section 26(2) of the Limitation Act, 1908. In support of their contentions the learned Counsels refer the case of Niropoma Ritchel vs Md Abdul Jalil Mea reported in 41 DLR 467 wherein it has been held:-

" It is really surprising to note that a decree has been passed on basis of adverse possession alone without framing any issue on such vital question of law and fact. On our query Mr. Khondker Mahhubuddin Ahmed, the warned Advocate could not lay his hand on any material piece of evidence and the averment in the plaint on which such, a decree could be passed in the present case. Thus we find the trial Court was not justified in raising the plea of adverse possession suo-motu by not framing any issue on this point and this is not a defect in the proceeding itself but material defect in substance and, as such, the second point of the learned Advocate for the appellant must succeed."

19. They lastly submit that the learned Judges of the Courts below concurrently found that the kabuliyat and other relevant documents of the plaintiff were forged and fictitious and the Court of appeal below after reversing the finding of facts regarding adverse possession allowed the appeal which calls for no interference by this Court.

20. In order to appreciate the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels I have gone through the provisional application, pleadings, evidences, all exhibits, other materials on record, impugned judgment and decree of the Court below, and given my anxious consideration to their submissions.

21. Now the question calls for the consideration whether the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment and decree.

22. Ongoing to the materials on record it transpires that the suit land measuring an area of 9.80 acres appertaining to CS plot no 8415 as described in the schedules ক-খ of the plaint was recorded Ichehamai river in the names of Dinesh Chandra Roy Chowdhury and Mutawalli Akfar Ali Talukder of Amiruddin Wakf Estate. The plaintiffs claimed that they got pattan on 1.28 acres of land described in K schedule from the sons of Dinesh Chandra Roy Chowdhury on 15th Aswin, 1348 BS and 0.55 acres of land described in খ schedule from Akfar Ali Talukder on 15th Ashar, 1350 BS by way of Pattans exhibits (1 and lA), Consequently, the plaintiff executed a kabuliyat of the খ schedule land in favour of the Zamindar on 1st Kartik, 1348 BS Since then he is in possession. The defendant No.1 (Government of Bangladesh) claimed that the suit land was the khas land of the Zamindar and subsequently by operation of law the same was vested to the Government as khas land and recorded in abstruck khatian. The added defendant No.2 claimed that he got 2-00 acres of land including the suit land from Mutwalli Akfar Ali Talukder by way of pattan in 1350BS.

23. It transpires that the plaintiff instituted the suit for declaration of the title and in support of the title he proved his different as exhibits 1-6, of which exhibits 1-1 (A) are the documents of patans. P.W 1 the plaintiff stated that he executed the kabuliyat being No. 2968 in respect ক schedule land in favour of the Zamindar on 1st Kartik, 1348 BS At the time of trial the respective volume from the concerned registry office was called by the trial Court and on examination of the volume it was detected that the deed No. 2968 is not kabuliyat but a different deed (Exht. B). In view of such facts both the Courts below came to a definite findings that the alleged kabuliyat No. 2968 (exhibit-3) was forged. On appraisal of the materials on record I am also in full agreement with the aforesaid views.

<u>24. It is evident from the evidence on record that die plaintiff by adducing evidence measurably failed to prove his title. It is pertinent to mention that the plaintiff took pattans of the suit land in 1348 BS and 1350 BS corresponding to 1941 and 1943 respectively and the instant suit was instituted on 04-07-1980. So it transpires that the plaintiff is not in continuous possession in the suit land more than sixty years, as required by law as laid down in section 26(2) of the Limitation Act, 1908. The acquisition of right to a property claimed against the Government a continuous possession of sixty years is required. The plaintiff failed measurably failed to prove his title and also failed to make out a case of adverse possession. The learned Judge, of trial Court declared the title of the plaintiff on the basis of adverse possession, but there is no ascertain either in the plaint or in the deposition before the Court that the plaintiff has acquired title by adverse possession. It is really surprising to note that a decree has been passed on the basis of adverse possession alone without framing any issue on such vital question of law and fact. Thus, I hold that the trial Court was not justified in raising the plea of adverse possession suo-motu by not framing any issue on this point and this is not a defect in the proceeding itself but materially affected the merit of the case.</u>

25. It further transpires to me that the findings arrived at by the Court of appeal below having been rested upon considerations and discussions of legal evidences and materials on record and also on a correct and proper analysis of the legal aspect involved in the suit and the findings being a finding of facts are not liable to be disturbed by the High Court Division in exercising of the power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

26. In the case of Akrab Ali vs Zahiruddin Kari reported in 30 DLR (SC) 81 wherein it has been held: "High Court Division not competent to interfere with finding of facts arrived at by the lower appellate Court which is based on appreciation of evidence however wrong the same may appear, in the absence of error of law or procedure affecting merit of the case". his view receives support in the cases reported in 43 DLR (AD) 82, 51 DLR (AD) 57, 19 BLD (AD) 156 and 38 DLR (AD) 201.

27. Moreover, the impugned judgment and decree. of the Court of appeal bellow in its entirety are well founded in the facts and circumstances of the case. Therefore, grounds urged and the contentions advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioner are not the correct exposition of law, however, I have gone through the decisions reported in 17 BLD 251 = 1 BLC 183, 6 MLR (AD) 261=54 DLR (AD) 16, 7 MLR (AD) 7=54 DLR (AD) 7, 5 BLC (AD) 76, 1 BLC (AD) 185 as referred by him . I am in respectful agreement with the principles enunciated therein, but the facts leading to those cases are quite distinguishable to that of the instant case inasmuch as, in all those cases the litigations erupted between the private parties, but in the instant case the entire claim of  the plaintiff is against the Government. Therefore, to that effect I am also unable to accept his submissions. On the contrary the legal pleas taken by the learned Counsel for the opposite parties prevail and appear to have a good deal of force.

28. In view of discussions made above, and the preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above I am of the view that the impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below suffers from no legal infirmity which calls for no interference by this Court. Thus the Rule having no merit fails.

29. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 09-03-1989 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Sirajganj, in Other Class Appeal No. 47 of 1984 is hereby affirmed.

Office is directed to send down the records of this case at once with a copy of judgment for information and necessary action.

End.

lawyer:
Md Asrarul Hoque, Advocate -------- For the Petitioner. 
Akram H Chowdhury, Advocate -------- For Added Respondent No.3.
parties:
FR Garment (Pvt) Ltd -------- Petitioner.
Vs.
Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka -------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal, J : In this Rule Nisi the respondents have been called upon to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 1-10-2006 (Annexure-E) passed by respondent No. 1 rejecting the application for dismissing the Money Execution Case No. 658 of 2005 arising out of judgment and decree dated 3-3-2005 passed by the Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Dhaka in Artha Rin Suit No. 914 of 2004 should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2.  Material facts leading to this Rule are that the respondent No.2. Agrani Bank as plaintiff instituted Artha Rin Suit No. 914 of 2004 in the Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Dhaka impleading the petitioner and others for realisation of its outstanding dues amounting to Taka 2,20,33,779 as stood on 31-7- 2004. The defendant did not turn to contest the suit in which the suit was decreed ex parte vide judgment and decree dated 3-3-2005 (preliminary decree was signed on 9-3-2005).

3. In usual course the decree-holder Bank (respondent No. 2) put the decree into execution by filing Artha-Jari Case No. 658 of 2005.

4. The defendant-petitioner (judgment- debtor) entered appearance in the said Artha-Jari case by filing power and on 17-9-2006 filed an application for dismissal of the Money Execution Case on the ground that the execution case is barred by limitation as per provision of sections 28( 1) and 29 of the Ain, 2003 and also on the ground the decree is hit by section 47 of the Ain, 2003. The Adalat on considering the materials on record rejected the said application by his order dated 1-10-2006.

5. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order dated 1-10-2006 (Annexure-E to the writ petition) the petitioner approached this Court and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr Md Asrarul Hoque, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that execution case is barred by limitation, inasmuch as in view of the provision of sub-section (1) of section 28 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (hereinafter called the Ain, 2003) the execution case has to be filed within 180 days but in the present case the ex parte judgment and decree was passed on 3-3-2005 (decree signed on 9-3-2005) and the Money Execution case was filed on 9-11-2005 which is beyond 180 days. He next submits that the Artha Rin Suit No. 914 of 2004 was also barred by limitation, in as- much as the respondent Bank filed the same beyond the limitation period of 3 years as laid down in section 47 of the Ain, 2003 although, the learned Judge of Artha Rin Adalat under misconception of law and facts most illegally and mechanically rejected the application for dismissal of the execution case in a summery manner by the impugned order dated 1-10-2006 and, as such, the same should be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

<u>7. On the other hand, Mr Akram H Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the added respondent No. 3, Bangladesh Shilpa Bank (BSB), supports the impugned judgment and decree and order dated 1-10-2006 passed by the Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka which were, according to him correct, just and proper. He submits that the instant writ petition has filed by the petitioner challenging the impugned judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat which is misconceived and not maintainable in law, inasmuch as by now it has been well settled that no writ petition lies against the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat since there is a specific provision in the Ain for seeking remedy against the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat. The learned Advocate next, on referring the provisions of sub-section 1 to sections 28 and 48 of the Ain, 2003 submits that the execution case is not barred by limitation which was filed well within 180 working days and, as such, the rule is liable to be discharged, Mr Akram H Chowdhury in support of his submissions relied on the decisions reported in 46 DLR (AD) 191, 54 DLR (AD) 6 and 59 DLR (AD) 6.</u>

8. These are the points which were argued by the learned Advocates for the respective parties.

9. We have perused the writ petition, affidavit-in-opposition, supplementary affidavit and other materials on record. In order to appreciate the submissions of the learned Advocates for the respective parties from a correct angle, it would be convenient for us to decide first of all as to the question of maintainability of the writ petition.

<u>10. In the case of Zahirul Islam vs National Bank Ltd reported in 46 DLR (AD) 191, where it has been decided as follows:</u>

<u>"The petitioner, without filing any appeal, filed an application under Article 102 of the Constitution, namely, Writ Petition No. 892 of 1991 which was dismissed summarily by a Division Bench of the High Court Division on 30-6-91 on the ground that the petitioner has an alternative and efficacious remedy by way of appeal... ... .The petition is dismissed."</u>

<u>11. In the case of Gazi M Towfic vs Agrani Bank reported in 54 DLR (AD) 6, where the principles has been laid down in the following terms:</u>

<u>"The law is now settled that since specific provision for appeal has been made against the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat no application under Article 102 lies against such judgment and decree."</u>

<u>12. In the case of Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) vs Artha Rin Adalat reported in 59 DLR (AD) 6, it has been decided:</u>

<u>"In view of the decisions quoted above we are led to irresistible conclusion that there being specific remedy in the statute for filing appeal against the judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat in the present case the defendant not availing of the aforesaid remedy cannot maintain the writ petition."</u>

13. From a reading of the above quoted uniform decisions of our Apex Court, we find a clear view of the law as it stands today that an application under Article 102 of the Constitution does not lie against the judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat since there being specific provision in the statute for filing appeal against the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat. Therefore, we find substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the respondent-bank that the instant writ petition is a misconceived one and not maintainable.

14. To meet the contention of Mr Md Asrarul Hoque that the Execution Case No. 658 of 2005 arising out of judgment and decree dated 3-3-2005 passed by the Artha Rin Adalar No. 1, Dhaka in Artha Rin Suit No. 914 of2004 is barred by 11 days from the judgment and 5 days from the date of signing decree. We have examined the execution case as well as the provisions of sections 28, 29 and 48 of the Ain, 2003. Section 28(1) of the Ain, 2003 provides the execution case shall be filed within 180 days. Admittedly, ex parte judgment and decree was passed on 3-3-2005 (preliminary decree signed on 9- 3-2005) with a direction for payment of money to the defendant within 60 days and the execution case was filed by the respondent Bank on 9-11-2005 in order to execute the decree. Section 48 of the Ain, 2003 provides that in order to counting the days under the provision of this Ain, only the working days of the Court shall be counted. Although, in this case we find from the chart for calculation of time as given in the writ petition that the petitioner did not minus so far it relates to non working days of the Court. So, on this point, we are of the view that the execution case is not barred by limitation.

15. Mr Md Asrarul Hoque, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, at the end of the day, submits that in this case the decree-holder bank started the execution proceeding on the basis of the preliminary decree which is ex facie illegal.

16. In deciding this question, we feel it necessary to reproduce the provision of section 5(3) of the Artha Rin Ain, 2003.

17. Section 5(3) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 reads as follows:

“(৩) উপধারা (২) এর অধীন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক দায়েরকৃত মামলা নিস্ক্রিয় সমাপ্তির (Foreclosure) উদ্দেশ্যে একটি বন্ধকী মামলা (Mortgage suit) হইলে, কেবলমাত্র সেই ক্ষেত্রে আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত ডিক্রি প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি (Preliminary decree) হইবে এবং অন্যান্য সকল ক্ষেত্রে ঋন আদায়ার্থ দায়েরকৃত মামলার আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত ডিক্রি চুড়ান্ত ডিক্রি (Final decree) হইবে।”

<u>18. From a reading of the above quoted provision, it manifests that if a suit is a mortgage suit and brought for foreclosure, in that case, the decree pronounced by the Adalat shall be a preliminary decree and the decrees of the Adalat for recovery of loans in other cases are to be treated final decrees. Therefore, we find no merit in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner on this point.</u>

19. As to the question that the Artha Rin Suit No. 914 of 2004 was barred by limitation, we have already indicated that Artha Rin Suit No. 914 of 2004 was decreed by the Artha Rin Adalat by judgment and decree dated 3-3-2005 against which there being specific provision in the statute for seeking remedy by way of appeal. This venture under the writ jurisdiction is not permissible.

20. In view of our discussions made in the foregoing paragraphs vis-a-vis the uniform decisions of our Apex Court as cited above by now it is clear that the instant Rule must fail.

21. In the result, the Rule is discharged with a cost of Taka 5,000 (five thousand). The order of stay granted by this Court stands vacated.

22. The Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka is directed to proceed with the Execution Case No. 658 of 2005 expeditiously.

Communicate the judgment at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mustafa Niaz Muhammad, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Records -----For the Appellants.
Md Khurshid Alam Khan, Advocate, instructed by ASM Khalequzzaman, Advocate-on-Record -----For the Respondents.
parties:
Shafiqul Islam Chowdhury (Md) and ors ----- Appellants 
vs
Mustafizur Rahman and ors ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 5-12-2001 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No, 4631 of 2000).
full_judgment:
Md Joynul Abedin J: This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 5-12- 2001 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4631 of 2000 discharging the Rule and thereby refusing amendment of the plaint.

<u>2. The appellants as plaintiffs filed Other Suit No. 184 of 1994 for declaration of title and Khas possession by evicting the defendants on removing obstructions. The defendants appeared and filed written statement opposing the claim of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs thereafter filed an application under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the plaint by incorporating a prayer for partition as an alternative to the prayer for eviction and also for addition of two persons as defendants.</u>

<u>The trial Court on consideration of the application for amendment rejected the same on contest by order dated 3-9-2000 on the ground that the amendment sought, if allowed, would totally change the nature and character of the suit. The plaintiffs then challenged the aforesaid order dated 3-9-2000 in revision and a Division Bench of the High Court Division initially issued Rule but finally discharged the same on affirmance of the said order of the trial Court on the ground that the amendment in question would not help settle the real "controversy in issue whether the plaintiff was in possession and then, was dispossessed from the schedule Kha land".</u>

<u>3. Against this backdrop, the plaintiffs, who are appellants before us, filed the civil petition for leave to appeal. Leave was granted in the following terms:</u>

<u>"Whether the proposed amendment does change the nature and character of the suit or it is an additional/ alternative prayer for doing the complete justice in the matter, requires investigation."</u>

4. We have heard Mr Mustafa Niaz Muhammad, the learned Advocate for the appellant and Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan, the learned Advocate for respondents and perused the judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers.

<u>5. The learned Advocate for the appellants submits that the amendment in question in effect seeks to incorporate an alternative prayer for partition if the defendants are found to be co-sharer in the suit holding and such amendment will not change the nature and character of the suit, rather such alternative prayer should be considered necessary for the purpose of effective adjudication of the matter in dispute and for doing the complete justice in the matter avoiding multiplicity of suits and proceedings and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge as well as the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in law in rejecting the prayer for amendment of the plaint.</u>

6. In order for correct understanding of the question at issue and the dispute between the parties it is necessary to be apprised of the respective contentions of the parties. The plaintiffs purchased the suit land on 15-8-1975 from one Mrs Anwarul Islam, wife of one Sirajul Islam, in RS Dag Nos. 2632, 2633 and 2637 from the western portion of the said Dags. Defendant Nos. 1 and 5 and one Abul Kalam Azad purchased 1 Kani 4 gonda 3 kara 1 danti land from the eastern portion of the said Dags by kabala dated 13-2-1986 from Anwarul Islam Boby, son of said Sirajul Islam. Defendant Nos. 2- 4 exchanged some of their purchased land with defendant No.1. But the defendants forcibly dispossessed the plaintiffs from a portion of their purchased land as shown in the Kha schedule to the plaint on 16-6-1993. The defendants do not dispute the purchase of the suit land by the plaintiffs from the wife of Sirajul Islam but they only denied the allegation of dispossession of the plaintiffs from the suit land mentioned in the Kha schedule to the plaint. In this context of the dispute the plaintiffs prayed for the amendment in the plaint.

7. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff- appellants submits that since the defendants admit that the plaintiffs purchased the suit land from the suit holding the plaintiffs are therefore co-sharer in the suit holding with the defendants. Hence the amendment for partition of the suit land is permissible in law as an alternative prayer in case the dispossession of the plaintiffs by the defendants, is not proved. The learned Advocate for the defendants on the other hand, contends that the real question in controversy is, whether the plaintiffs had possession and they were subsequently dispossessed by the defendants. But the amendment to the plaint seeking incorporation by way of an alternative prayer for partition is not considered necessary to resolve the dispute between the parties. The amendment has therefore, been rightly disallowed.

8. From the pleadings of the parties, it is clearly discernible that both the parties are co-sharers to the disputed holding by purchase and exchange. The only question that is raised and calls for determination is, whether the plaintiffs are owners having title to the land described in the Kha schedule to the plaint and whether they have been dispossessed therefrom by the defendants and are entitled to recovery of possession thereof from the defendants. It is therefore, clear that the instant case is not a case for mere recovery of possession by the plaintiffs under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act regardless of whether the plaintiffs have title to the suit land. But regrettably both the trial Court as well as the High Court Division in erratic and perfunctory exercise of their judicial function rejected the aforesaid prayer for partition of the suit land by way of amendment to the plaint after declaration of title thereto by the plaintiffs. Both the Courts below mistook the present suit as a suit for recovery of possession under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act regardless of whether the plaintiffs have title to the suit land. But regrettably both the trial Court as well as the High Court Division in erratic and perfunctory exercise of their judicial function rejected the aforesaid prayer for partition of the suit land by way of amendment to the plaint after declaration of title thereto by the plaintiffs. Both the Courts below mistook the present suit as a suit for recovery of possession under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act and rejected the prayer for amendment of the plaint. This is a glaring example of non-application of mind to the facts of the case by the learned Judges of the High Court Division.

<u>9. Amendment of a plaint can be allowed in the discretionary power of the Court and such discretion is required to be exercised judicially and not in an arbitrary or perfunctory manner amounting to an illegal exercise of jurisdiction. An amendment to the plaint must not be allowed if it tends to change the character of the plaint or the character of the suit. In the instant case, the amendment sought for will not change the character of the suit or the plaint; rather such amendment is capable of determining the real question in controversy by allowing partition and giving possession of the respective share of the parties to the suit land by dividing the suit land between the parties by metes and bounds on measurement if necessary. Both the Courts below therefore committed an error in law in rejecting the prayer for amendment of the plaint for partition as an alternative prayer.</u>

<u>The appeal is accordingly, allowed without any order as to cots.</u>

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Order No.5 of 1971
lawyer:
M.H. Khondaker, with Mozammel Hoq Khan, Mr. B. K. Das ------ For the Appellants. 
No one ------ For Respondent.
parties:
Md. Abdur Rahim & others  ------ Appellants 
Vs. 
Sree Sree Gredhari Jeo  ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
K. Hossain, J.: The short point involved in the appeal though a very important question of law, is whether the execution petition is barred by limitation. On this point the trial Court held that it is so, whereas the appellate Court held that it is not so and is within time. Facts are not in dispute and may set out as follows :

<u>2. The decree-holder respondent got a decree and started title execution case against judgment debtor appellants being Title Execution Case No. 29 of 1955 on 15-3-55. It was struck off on 17-5-55. The second Execution Case No.15 of 1958 was filed on 17-5-58 and it was struck off on the same date. Execution Case No.10 of 1961 was struck off on 29-5-61. The next Execution Case No.10 of 1964 was filed on 3-7-64 and it was struck off on 27-7-64 and the last Execution Case No.19 of 1965 was filed on 4-12-65. The question is whether this was filed within the period of limitation. It is to be noted that from the dismissal of the last execution case this Execution case is within 3 years but the question is whether the Execution Case which was filed on 4-12-65 was within 12 years from the date of decree sought to be executed. The original decree was passed on 18-12-49. It appears that an appeal was taken by the judgment-debtors to the Dacca High Court being Appeal from Original Decree No.40 of 1949, but it is dismissed for non-prosecution on 4th December, 1953 and it appears that a formal decree was drawn up on 13-1-54 on that. The facts are not in dispute The only question is whether the appeal which was dismissed for non-prosecution by the High Court is the starting point of limitation or the date of the decree of the trial Court.</u>

3. Mr. Khondkar has submitted that the languages of article 182 of the Limitation Act and section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure are different and meant for different purpose and as such the language of article 182 shall not govern the period of limitation prescribed under section 48 C.P.C. He further submits that section 48 is independent of the Limitation Act and if an application is barred by limitation under section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure the execution is to fail. On the question of interpretation that the languages of the two Statutes are different and should be considered differently, he has referred to some decisions: They are A.I R 1940 Madras 127 (F.B.) (Paladuga Veers Ramchandra Rao Vs. Paladugu Parasuramayyal; P.L.D. 1954 Lahore 388 (Hakim Ghulam Jilani Vs. Hakim Muhammad Abdullah), and A.I.R. 1970 (S.C.) 1525. There is much substance what the learned Advocate submits on this ground. After comparing the language of the two Statutes, one of Article 182 of the Limitation Act and the other of section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure no doubt an anomaly arises. In Article 182 of the Limitation Act there are 7 different categories giving different dates as the starting point for taking out execution by the decree-holder. The second part of 3rd column of Article 182 speaks that where there has been an appeal the date of final decree or order of the Appellate Court or the withdrawal of the appeal. Then again Article 182 clearly excludes the operation of section 48 from being affected by this Article.

4. Turning to section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure we find that the governing part of section 48 clause (1) says that no fresh application for execution shall be presented after expiration of 12 years from the date of the decree sought to be executed. The obvious difference of language cannot be ignored.

<u>5. On consideration of the provisions of the two enactments, we find that the language of section 48 the Code is different from that of the limitation Act but neither nullifies the language of the other. Of course of the language employed creates an anomaly. The removal of the anomaly is the function of the Parliament and not the court. The court is to interpret them. Both prescribes the period of limitation for the execution of the decree. The Civil Procedure Code fixes the longest period, whereas the Limitation Act the earliest period to take the first step in execution and the subsequent step known as steps-in-aid. Each will have to be given full effect within its language. Read in this manner we think that we can get some reasonable meaning.</u>

6. The Limitation Act prescribes the period of limitation which the decree-holder must take earliest in point of time for execution, whereas section 48 of the Code, fixes the maximum limit, but it does not prescribe the time for filing the first application or the subsequent applications for execution. Limitation Act prescribes that an application for execution is to be made within 3 years from the cases mentioned in third column or Article 182. An application for execution has, therefore, to satisfy first Article 182 of the Limitation Act the earliest period prescribed and then also section 48 of the Code which prescribed the maximum period of limitation. If the execution petition is hit by any of the two provisions it is to fail.

6. In the Court below a large number of decisions were cited and Mr. Khandkar has also cited a good number. All of them are not material for our discussion. We shall mention those material for our purpose. They are : 18 C.W N. 963 (Chaudhri Abdul Majid Vs., Jawahir Lal)- I.L.R. 36 Allahabad 350: 1914 (P.C.) 65 (Batuk Nath Vs. Munni Dei) I.L.R. 36 Allahabad 284; A.I.R.1933 (P.C.) 68 (Abdullah Asghar Ali Vs. Ganesh Das Vig); 36 C.W.N. 803 (P.C.) Negendra Nath Dey Vs. Suresh Chandra Dey. These decisions are mostly related to the dismissal for non-prosecution of leave to appeal to the Privy Council. Since the matters relate to leave to appeal to the Privy Council and the matter before us is for non-prosecution of an appeal, we do not want to dilate on them any further.

There is a line of decisions on the point that dismissal of an appeal for non-prosecution is an appellate order and is the starting point of limitation under article 182 (2) of the Limitation Act, whereas another line of decisions holds otherwise. The few in favour are: I L R. 30 Allahabad 499 (Mujibullah Vs. Umed Bibi); and A.I.R. 1938 Patna 401 (Ram Ranbijaya Prasad Vs. Kesho Prasad Singh). The others holding contrary view are: A. I. R. 1943 Patna 371 (Jagannath Sal); and A.I.R. 1960 Allahabad 515 (F.B.) (Smt. Rabia Bibi Vs. Smt. Mohammadi Bibi). We are not called upon to enter and deal with them as we have already held that the languages of the two Statutes are widely variant and each operates in its own field and they are not to overlap. We also refrain from referring to the other decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the appellants inasmuch as they are not material to the point at issue.

7. The question is whether the appeal taken by the judgment-debtor to the High Court, and dismissed for non-prosecution is a decree of the Appellate Court. With some difference, we fail to hold that it is so.

8. Turning to the Code we find that section 48 provides the maximum period of 12 years limitation for the execution from the date of decree sought to be executed. It is now well-settled that a decree means an appellate decree if an appeal is taken. In this particular case there was an appeal to the High Court but was dismissed for non-prosecution and a formal decree was drawn. Could it be said a decree in terms of section 2 (2) of the Code ? In the plain language of the Code it is not  it says that any order of dismissal for default shall not be counted a decree.

<u>9. That the dismissal of a suit or an appeal for non-prosecution is not a decree is a proposition that requires no authority. However, some of them may be cited. They are: 47 I C. (Oudh) 125 (Ram Adhin Vs. Ram Lot); 21 C.W N. 776 (Syam Mandal Vs. Sitanath Banerjee); and A.I R. 1963 Allahabad 398 (Maharaja Pateshwari Prasad Singh Vs. Aditry Prasad). In these authorities we find that it has been held that dismissal for non-prosecution is dismissal for default and the order does not amount to a decree. And in ascertaining its nature it is substance and not from which is the determining factor.</u>

10. On the question before us we have of course very few authorities to cite. A very old one from the Judicial Commissioner of Oudh reported in the case of Ram Adhin Vs. Ram Lot (47 I.C. 125) has been cited by Mr. Khandkar. There is another decision reported in A.I.R. 1963 Allahabad 398 (Maharaja Pateswari Prasad Singh Vs. Aditya Prasad). In those decisions it has been held that for the purpose of limitation under section 48 of the Code an appeal dismissed for non-prosecution is not a decree. In Ram Adhin's case 47 I.C. (Oudh) 125 it was further held that the period of limitation under section 48 of the Code is to be counted from the date of the original decree not from the date of the order dismissing the appeal for default.

<u>11. Upon the authorities, we find that in the execution of a decree where an appeal has been taken and dismissed for default or for non-prosecution, the period of limitation under section 48 of the Code is to run from the date of the decree of the Trial Court and not from such appellate order.</u>

<u>12. Turning to the facts of the present case we get that the original decree was passed on 18-12-49. The judgment debtor preferred an appeal to the Dacca High Court but was dismissed for non-prosecution on 4-12-53. The appeal in the High Court ended in an order which is not a decree and so the decree-holder cannot count this appellate order as the starting point of limitation under section 48 of the Code. The decree-holder after several unsuccessful attempts last sought to execute the decree on 4-12-65. Calculating from this date the execution petition was filed manifestly beyond 12 years and hence barred under section 48 of the Code. No doubt, from the last infructuous execution proceeding taken by decree-holder, which, was struck off on 27-7-64, the present execution petition is within three years, but then the bar of section 48 of the Code proves fatal to it.</u>

<u>For the reasons we set aside the order of the learned First Additional District Judges Sylhet, and restore that of the original executing Court.</u>

<u>The appeal is allowed, but as there is no appearance on the other side we make no order as to costs.</u>

Amirul Islam Chowdhury, J.— I agree.

End.
