full_judgment:
S.M. Mohsen Ali J. - This rule arises out of an order passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court at Patiya in Miscellaneous Case No. 46 of 1967 started on an application filed by the defendant opposite party Maniruzzaman under Order 9 rule 4 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure restoring his Misc. Case No. 2 of 1967 filed by him under Order 9 rule 13, Civil Procedure Code, for setting aside the ex parte decree which was obtained by the plaintiff petitioner before me.

2. Circumstances giving rise to this rule are as follows:

The plaintiff petitioners instituted Money Suit No. 1 of 1967 in the Second Court of Munsif at Patiya for realizing Rs. 535/- as the price of a barga paddy on the basis of a barga kabuliat executed by the defendant on 18. 4. 65 corresponding to 5th Baisakh, 1372 B. S. in favor of the plaintiffs for one year. It has been alleged that the notice of the suit was duly served on the defendant but he did not appear and the suit was decreed ex parte on 20. 2. 67. Thereafter the defendant opposite party filed an application under Order 9 rule 13 C. P. C. for setting aside the aforesaid ex parte decree and a Misc. Case No. 21 of 1967 was started. The plaintiff appeared in that Misc. Case and submitted their written objection and the date of hearing was fixed on written objection and the date of hearing was fixed on 10. 6. 67 but on that date the defendant did not take any step, but it appears that the plaintiff filed an application for one month's time enabling him to produce witnesses and the Court recorded the following order:

“Petitioners filed no hazira. Opposite party files a petition for adjournment of the hearing on the ground stated therein. Copy served. Heard the learned Advocate. The prayer is rejected. Hence ordered that the Misc. Case be dismissed for default.”

3. Thereafter on 8. 7. 67 the defendant opposite party filed an application under Order 9 rule 4 and under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoring the aforesaid Misc. Case and his application was restored as Misc. Case No. 46 of 1967. In his application for restoration the defense stated inter alia that the Mohrar of the pleader, who is an old man, wrongly gave him 20. 6. 67 as the date of hearing of Misc. Case No.21 of 1967 although the actual date was fixed on 10. 6. 67 and it was due to this mistake of the lawyer's clerk the defendant did not come and hence the Misc. Case was dismissed for default. The defendant came to know of the dismissal of the Misc. Case on 20.6.67 when he came to the Court to take steps in the case. The plaintiff filed written objection against the application. It appears, that subsequently on 21. 8. 67 defendant filed a petition praying for amendment of his application for restoration by deleting section 151 C.P.C. from the heading of the application which was allowed by the Court and the defendant was directed to file an affidavit in support of his case by 31. 8. 67 and this affidavit was filed by the defendant on 30. 8. 67, and on 31. 8. 67 the Court recorded the following order:

“Petitioner files an affidavit in support of his Misc. application under Order 9 rule 4 C. P. C. filed earlier. Hence ordered that the Misc. Case be allowed and the ex parte order of dismissal of the Misc. Case No.21 of 1967 passed on 10.6.67 be hereby set aside and the Misc. case No. 21 of 1976 be registered of file.”

The present rule is against this order of restoration which has been obtained, by plaintiffs-petitioners.

4. Mr. Md. Yahya, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, has contended that the learned Munsif has acted illegally and with material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction in allowing the petition of defendant opposite party under section 151 and under Order 9 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the Misc. Case No. 21 of 1961-67 under Order 9 rule 13 C. P. C. dismissed for default. According to him, the defendant could file an appeal against the order of dismissal for default under Order 43 Rule 1(d) C. P. C. and, as he did not avail himself of that remedy provided under the statutory provision of law, he cannot invoke the aid of section 151 C. P. C. which can be only invoked when there is no other specific remedy. He has in this connection referred to 1952 PLR 2 Dac. 87, Abdur Rahman Miji and ors. Vs. Abdul Wadud Mea and ors. and  AIR 1959 Pat. 121 (Full Bench), Doma Chowdhury and ors. Vs. Ram Naresh Lal and ors. In PLR 2 Dacca 87, defendant's application under Order 9 rule 13 C. P. C. for setting aside an ex parte Money Decree obtained by plaintiff was dismissed for default as the defendants were absent on the date of pre-emptory hearing. Thereafter the defendant filed an application for restoration under Order 47 Rule 1 and under section 151, C. P. C. which was rejected by the learned Munsif and subsequently on revision this was also affirmed by the High Court.

5. It was held that an order dismissing an application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code for default comes within the language of Order 43 Rule 1(d) of the Code and is appealable. It was further held that section 151 of the Code does not provide any alternative remedy. It is based on the principle that no one should suffer for absence of a rule of procedure. His Lordship Ibrahim, J., relying on the case of Thakur Prasad Vs. Fakirullah, ILR 17 All. 106 Privy Council and Sarat Krishna Bose and Biseshawar Mitra and others, 31 CWN 576, also held that an application to set aside an order of dismissal for default of an application under Order 9 rule 13 C. P. C. is not an original matter and does not come within the scope of section 141 C. P. C. and as such Order 9 rule 9, C. P. C., cannot be invoked to set aside the dismissal for default of an application under Order 9 rule 13 C. P. C.

6. In  AIR 1959 Pat. 121 (Full Bench), Doma Chowdhury & ors Vs. Ram Naresh Lal & ors. in which the principle point was whether Court can in exercise of its inherent power under section 141 C. P. C. set aside an order of dismissal for default of an application under Order 9 Rule 9 C. P. C. and it was held:

On a plain reading of Cls. (c) and (d) of rule 1 of Or. 43 that there is no ground for discriminating between rejection of an application on merits and its rejection for default. The order which gives rise to an appeal is one whereby an application of the kinds mentioned in the clauses is rejected. Even if the application is dismissed for default it is an order of rejecting and hence appealable under either of the two clauses which may be applicable.

There is no reason at all to give a restricted meaning to the word "rejecting" in the clauses by saying that it refers only to rejection on merits. If it is argued that there is no specific provision in the clauses regarding dismissal of an application for default, that argument can be countered by saying that there is no specific expression in them even relating to the rejection on merit.

Mr. A. Hamid, the learned Advocate for the defendant opposite party on the other hand, has contended that in the facts and circumstances of the case the learned Munsif acted rightly in allowing the application under section 151 C P. C. and has cited 4 DLR 621, 14 DLR 256, 31 DWN 576,  AIR 1929 ALL. 906 and PLD 1959 (W.P.) Quetta 1. He has further argued that there was no appearance of plaintiffs on 10. 10. 67 the application under Order 9 rule 4 was maintainable.

7. In 4 DLR 621, Saferaddi Munshi Vs. Farman Ali Mridha & anr. an application under section 26F of the B. T. Act was allowed ex parte when an application under Order 9 rule 13 C. P. C., for setting aside the ex parte decree was filed and which was dismissed on contest but on appeal it was allowed. It was held that no appeal lay against an order dismissing an application under Order 9, Rule 13, C. P. C. filed for setting an order passed under section 26F of the B. T. Act, because Order 9, rule 13 contemplated an application for an order to set aside an ex parte decree (underlining is mine). If it is an application to set aside an ex parte order (underlining is mine), as in the case under section 26F of the B. T. Act, an order rejecting the application does not become appealable as the right of appeal allowed under Order 43, Rule 1, clause (d) C. P. C. is limited only to an order rejecting an application to set aside a decree passed ex parte and in that view the lower appellate Court's order allowing the application under Order 9 Rule 13 was set aside. This case is obviously not applicable to the present case.

In 14 DLR 256, Sarbeswar Mandal & ors. Vs. Fakur Chand Sarker & ors. plaintiff's suit was decreed on contest against defendant No. 1 and ex parte against defendant No. 2 and 3 whereupon defendant No. 3 filed an application under Order 9, rule 13, C. P. C. to set it aside which was subsequently allowed ex parte. Thereafter the plaintiff filed an application under Order 47, rule 1, read, with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte order passed under Order 9 rule 13 which was rejected by the learned Munsif as not maintainable. It was observed by his Lordship Asir, J.

“No authority has been placed before me to support the proposition that where a party was free to move this Court under section 115, Civil Procedure Code should be deemed to have precluded himself from seeking justice under section 151, Civil Procedure Code. I am therefore of the opinion, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the present case, that the application as made under section 151, Civil Procedure Code could not be thrown in limine on the ground of maintainability. The learned Munsif ought to have treated it as a proper application under section 151, Civil Procedure Code and heard and disposed of the same on merits.”

This case is also not applicable and has no direct bearing on the point at issue in this case.

In 31 CWN 576, Sarat Krishna Bose Vs. Bisweshwar Mitra & ors., plaintiff applied under Order 9 rule 9 C. P. C. to set aside the order dismissing his previous application under order 9 rule 9 for the restoration of his suit dismissed for default for not filing talabaan and process. It was observed as follows:

“I entirely agree with the learned Judges of the Allahabad High Court in the view expressed in the case of Pitamber Lal Vs. Dadhi Singh, ILR 46 All. 319, that if the fresh application is treated as an application to restore the suit itself and not to restore the first application and is within time there can be no bar to its being dealt with as an application under Order 9 C. P. C.”

It was further observed:

“The application which he presented on 28th October, 1925 (the second application under Order 9 rule 9 C. P. C.) cannot by reason of the bar of limitation be entertained as a second application for setting aside the ex parte decree. To meet cases such this section 151 of the Code was enacted, and where there is no provision in the Code expressly providing for a remedy and none which prohibits a remedy being administered and as such remedy is called for in order to do that real and substantial justice for the administration of which it exists, the provision of section 151 may and should be resorted to.”

8. In this connection it may be noted that this case was also referred to in the Full Bench case in AIR 1959 Pat. 121 (Supra) wherein it was observed as follows:

“In that case also their lordships did not consider whether an appeal lay from the order of dismissal for default of the first application. It they had held that an appeal lay they could not take the view that there was no provision in the Code expressly providing for a remedy.”

I, therefore, respectfully differ from their decision."

9. Similarly in PLD 1959 (West Pakistan) Quetta 1, Muhammad Hashim Khan Vs. Major Fazal Elahi Khan, the order of dismissal for default of proceeding for setting aside of an ex parte decree was restored under section 151 C. P. C. and the learned Judge proceeded on the footing that there was a distinction between dismissal on merits and dismissal for default as in the latter case there can be no evidence for the appellate Court to decide whether the appellant had a sufficient cause for his non attendance. The learned Single Judge who decided the case observed:

“If the contention of the learned council that appeal lies under Order 43 Rule 1(d), whether the matter is decided on merits or is dismissed in default, were to prevail, the position will be that in the latter case there will be no evidence before the appellate Court for its scrutiny. On what basis then, can it be decided whether the order of dismissal is corrector not. There is no provision in C. P. C. excepting Order 41 Rule 27, empowering the Appellate Court to record evidence. Order 41 Rule27 empowers them in certain limited case, to record additional evidence, i.e. evidence in addition what is already on record and then too only in that case, where the evidence already on record is found to be either insufficient or not clear enough to enable them to give judgment. In a case where a matter is dismissed for default, there could be no evidence. The question that an Appellate Court will be called upon to decide will be whether or not, the appellant had sufficient cause for his non attendance, and the law does not permit him to lead evidence before me. It is this obstacle which comes in the way of accepting a proposition that an appeal lies whether the decision is on merits or it is on account of non attendance of a party. The proposition, if accepted, will lead to absurd results, and there is always a presumption again absurdity. It cannot, therefore, be said that the respondent had a remedy under Order 43 Rule 1(d).”

10. Mr. Hamid has further submitted that even if an application for restoration under section 151 C. P. C. is not maintainable but regard being had to the fact that on the date when the application under Order 9 rule 13 was dismissed for default, the plaintiff prayed for time and that the defendant failed to appear on the date of hearing and it will not be just and proper in the circumstances of the case to interfered under section 115 C. P. C. In this connection he has cited 10 DLR  521 and 969  DLC  590.

In 10 DLR 521 in the case of Sreenibash Mukhupaddya and ors. Vs. Elahi Haider and ors. an application under Order 21 rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside a sale on the ground of material irregularity and fraud in publishing and conducting the sale was dismissed. On appeal it was allowed on the ground that the decree was a nullity in view of section 35 sub-clause (iii) of the Bengal Agricultural and Debtors Act. On revision against it the High Court held that the lower Appellate Court acted without jurisdiction because that was not relevant question for determination under Order 21 rule 19, but the High Court did not interfere under section 151 C. P. C. for the ends of justice. It was observed:

“Thus although I am satisfied that in the present case the learned Subordinate Judge, sitting it appeal, acted without jurisdiction in taking into consideration matters not relevant for the purpose of an application under Order 21 rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure, yet I do not think that it is a fit case in which I should interfere. It is patent upon the face that the award was still subsisting, and, therefore, clearly hit by the provisions of section 35, sub-clause (iii) of the Bengal Agricultural Debtors Act.”

11. In 1969 D.LC 590 Nur Md. Babar Ali & ors. Vs. Shah Md. Ali and ors. where an application under section 151 C. P. C. was filed for restoration of the application under Order 9, Rule 13, dismissed for default. The learned Judge similarly was of the opinion that an appeal was a proper remedy but did not exercise its discretion under section 115 C. P. C. in this case, observation of a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court in Civil Order No. 14 of 1966, in the case of Lutfar Rahman Vs. Montashemuddin & ors. arising in a similar situation was quoted as follows:

“It has been rightly contended that there can be no question of any inherent jurisdiction of the Court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure when the statutes provides for a specific remedy, namely, an appeal against the order of dismissal of the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code. This contention of the petitioners must be upheld. However, we feel that there were good grounds for restoration of the said Misc. Case under Order 9 rule 13 as backed by the affidavits made by the lawyer appearing on behalf of the defendants.

From the facts and circumstances of the case, we feel that if an appeal had been taken from the order of dismissal of an application, the Appellate Court would have been fully justified in allowing the appeal. We refrain from exercising the power vested in us under section 115 the Code of Civil Procedure because we feel that we would otherwise set aside an order which was just and proper and which acts the ends of justice.”

<u>12. In the instant case the application for restoration is under Order 9, rule 4 and under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The application is undoubtedly misconceived. Order 9 rule 4 of Civil Procedure Code provides for the plaintiff to bring a fresh suit which is dismissed either for non-service of summons in consequence of plaintiff failure to pay cost or for non-appearance of both the plaintiffs and defendant. An application under section 151 C. P. C., from the decisions cited and discussed above, I am of the view, is not maintainable. It may be mentioned, as already noted above, prayer under section 151 C. P. C. was deleted on the application filed by Moniruzzaman, the defendant himself. It is thus not clear under what provisions of law the Court has granted the prayer of the defendant restoring the application. From the circumstances it may be presumed that the Court purported to act under section 151 C. P. C. and that is also the tenor of the argument advanced by the learned Advocates. However, I feel, that there were good grounds for restoration of the case under Order 9, rule 13 as evidenced by the affidavit of the defendant if an appeal had been taken from the order of dismissal, and it cannot be said that substantial justice has not been done by such restoration. I do not think that I should exercise the power vested in this Court under section 115 C. P. C.</u>

<u>The result, therefore, is that this Rule is discharged but I direct the defendant opposite party to pay cost of Rs. 100/- to the plaintiff which is to be deposited in the Trial Court within one month from the arrival of the record, failing which his application for restoration in Misc. Case No. 46 of 1967 will stand dismissed. The Misc. Case No. 21 of 1967 should be disposed of as early as possible.</u>

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 13-8-1995 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1222 of 1981 with Second Appeal No. 116 of 1979).
full_judgment:
MM Ruhul Amin J: These two appeals by leave are directed against the judgment and order dated 13-8-1995 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1222 of 1981 (heard with Second Appeal No. 116 of 1979) discharging the Rule issued in the Civil Revision No. 1222 of 1981 and allowing the Second Appeal No. 116 of 1979 and thereby decreeing both the Title Suit Nos. 984 of 1962 and 134 of 1964.

2. Title Suit Nos. 134 of 1964 and 984 of 1962 were filed by the plaintiff respondents in the 1st  Court of Assistant Judge, Khulna for ejectment of the defendant-appellants as monthly tenants from Municipal holding Nos. 13 and 12 respectively. Admittedly the suit land measuring 0.17 acres being CS Plot No. 3871 appertaining to CS Khatian No.1865 of Mouza Baniakhamar originally belonged to one Rakhal Das Bose and his wife. The case of the plaintiff is that their predecessor in interest, Baidyanath Chatterjee purchased the suit land from the original owners in the benami of his relative Srish Chandra Bhattacharjee by a registered kabala dated 28-7-1927. Subsequently he divided the suit land into two equal parts and created two separate Municipal holding being holding No. 12 (new 23) and holding No. 13 (new 24). Baidyanath Chatterjee filed a suit being Title Suit No. 102 of 1958 in the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Khulna for a declaration that he purchased the suit land from the original owners in the benami of Srish Chandra Bhattacharjee who was his benamdar. On the basis of a solenama, a compromise decree was passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) on 22-8-1958 declaring that Srish Chandra Bhattacharjee was benamdar of Baidyanath Chatterjee. Baidyanath subsequently transferred the suit property comprising holding Nos. 12 and 13 to the plaintiffs by a registered kabala dated 4-11-1961. The plaintiffs brought two suits, one 984 in 1962 another 134 in 1964 for ejectment of the defendants as monthly tenants from holding Nos. 13 and 12 respectively on the ground of default in payment of rent and bonafide requirement of the owner.

3. The defendants contested the suits by filing written statements denying the material allegations made in the plaint. Their case, in short, is that the defendants were never the monthly tenants of the plaintiffs or of Baidyanath; that no landlord and tenant relationship existed between them and Srish Chandra Battacharjee was not a benamdar of Baidyanath Srish Chandra Bhattacharjee died leaving two sons Dhirendra Bhattacharjee and Birendra Bhattacharjee, Baidyanath Chatterjee was the karmachary (employee) of Dhiren Bhattacharjee and Biren Bhattacharjee who migrated to India immediately after partition of India. Dhiren and Biren Bhattacharjee settled the suit properties along with other lands of the suit plot to defendants' predecessor in interest, Khondaker Abdus Salam on 17-5-1950 at a rental of Taka 30 on receipt of a salami of Taka 4001 by executing an amalnama (amaldari) and that the defendants have been possessing the suit holding since then on the basis of the aforesaid settlement. Their further case is that Dhiren and Biren Bhattacharjee agreed to complete the transaction by executing registered documents in favour of the defendants predecessor in interest but they did not do so. They also asserted that the solenama filed in Title Suit No. 102 of 1958 was fraudulent and the plaintiffs did not acqire any interest in the suit property by virtue of the kabala dated 4-11-1961.

4. The learned Assistant Judge found that Baidyanath Chatterjee was the real owner of the suit premises and Srish Chandra, was benamder of Baidyanath of the suit premises and the plaintiff respondents acquired title to the same by purchase by kabala dated 4-11-1961 from Baidyanath Chatterjee. The trial Court also disbelieved the case of settlement of the suit premises to defendant appellants by Dhirendra Bhattacharjee and Birendra Bhattacharjee, two sons of Srish Chandra Bhattacharjee. The trial Court accordingly, decreed the plaintiffs suit for ejectment. The defendants filed Title Appeal No. 295 of 1963 against the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 984 of 1962 and Title Appeal No. 145 of 1965 against those passed in Title Suit No. 134 of 1964. Title Appeal No. 295 of 1963 was allowed by the appellate Court on the findings, inter alia, that the relationship of landlord and tenant was not established between the parties. The other appeal being Title Appeal No. 145 of 1965 arising out of Title Suit No. 134 of 1964 was dismissed by the appellate Court upon findings, inter alia, that the plaintiffs having prima facie title to the suit property the defendants are monthly tenants in respect thereof under the plaintiffs.

5. Being aggrieved by the decision in Title Appeal No. 145 of 1965, the defendants filed Civil Revision No. 1222 of 1981 while the plaintiff respondents being aggrieved by the decision in Title Appeal No. 295 of 1963 filed Second Appeal No. 116 of 1979.

6. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division heard both the matters together and disposed of them by the impugned judgment. The High Court Division upon hearing passed the impugned judgment and order for which the defendants-appellants are aggrieved and obtained leave from this Division.

7. Leave was granted to consider the submission that the High Court Division erred in affirming the decree for ejectment of the defendants from the suit premises as monthly tenants when there is no proof of landlord-tenant relationship between the parties and section 109 of the Transfer of Property is also not applicable in the facts of the case and the submission that the High Court Division upon a misconstruction of Exhibits 7, 8(a), 9 and 12(b) and the decree passed in Title Suit No. 102 of 1958 wrongly held that the defendants appellants were tenants under the plaintiff-respondents and their predecessor in interest, Baidyanath Chatterjee and the further submission that the High Court Division was clearly wrong in not adverting to the reasonings and findings given by the appellate Court in Title Appeal No. 295 of 1963 in which it was held that there was no relationship of landlord and the tenant between the plaintiffs and the defendants and accordingly, Title Suit No. 984 of 1962 was dismissed.

8. We have heard Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel for the appellants and Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Counsel for the respondents and perused the judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers.

9. It is not disputed that the suit property originally belonged to Rakhal Das Bose and his wife. The plaintiffs' case is that Baidynath Chatterjee purchased the suit property in benami of his relative, Srish Chandra Bhattacharjee by kabala dated 28-7-1927 and Baidyanath Chatterjee possessed the said land and constructed huts. He let out the suit premises to the defendants who are monthly tenants. The further case of the plaintiffs is that Baidynath instituted Title Suit No. 102 of 1958 for a declaration that he purchased the suit property in the benami of his relative Srish Bhattacharjee who was his benamder. Dhiren and Biren, sons of Srish, filed solenama in the suit and a compromise decree was passed declaring Srish as benamder of Baidyanath. The further case is that by a registered kabala dated 4-11-1961 the plaintiffs purchased the suit properties at a consideration of Taka 8,000 from Baidyanath and late Khondaker Abdus Salam, predecessor of defendant Nos. 1-4, was a monthly tenant in the premises at a monthly rent of Taka 15 under Baidyanath Chatterjee and thereafter under the plaintiffs and notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was duly served upon the defendarit-appellants.

10. The case of the respondents, on the other hand, is that Srish Bhattacharjee was not a benamder of Baidyanath and he purchased the suit properties with his own money for his own benefit. On the death of Srish Bhattacharjee that property devolved upon his two sons, Dhiren Bhattacharjee and Biren Bhattacharjee who settled the same by executing an unregistered amalnama (amaldari) in favour of defendants' predecessor in interest on receipt of a salami of Taka 4001 and a rental of Taka 30 on 17-5-1950. Since then they are in possession and they were never tenants under Baidyanath or the plaintiffs.

11. The learned Advocate for the appellant submits that the compromise decree obtained in Title Suit No.102 of 1958 by Baidyanath against Dhiren Bhattacharjee, and Biren Bhattacharjee, sons of Srish Bhattacharjee is not a transfer document and after the decree Dhiren and Biren did not execute any transfer deed in favour of Baidyanath and hence by such sole decree Baidyanath did not acquire any title to the suit property, We are unable to accept this argument of the learned Counsel as it is the definite case of Baidyanath that he purchased the suit land with his own money and for his benefit in the benamio"f his relation Srish Bhattacharjee and he himself was in possession initially by residing in the suit land and thereafter he left out the same to Khandaker Abdus Salam, predecessor in interest of the defendants as monthly tenant. Since the sons of alleged benamder Shrish Bhattacharjee filed solenama in Title Suit No. 102 of 1958 brought by Baidyanath for a declaration that Srish Bhattacharjee is benamder and the suit having been decreed on compromise on the basis of solenama filed by Dhiren and Biren, sons of Srish Bhattacharjee, in our view, no transfer document is necessary in favour of Baidyanath by Dhiren and Biren.

12. The learned Counsel then argued that since the defendants or their predecessor were/was not parties in Title Suit No. 102 of 1958 brought by Baidyanath against Dhiren and Biren, sons of Srish Bhattacharjee, they are not bound by the sole decree passed in Suit No. 102 of 1958. It is true that the defendants or their predecessor were not parties in the suit. In our view, they were not necessary parties in the suit and, as such, they were not rightly made parties in the suit. He next submits that Exhibits 7, 8(a), 9 and 12(b) were not properly considered by the High Court Division and upon misconstruction of those documents the High Court Division wrongly held that the defendants are tenants under the plaintiffs and their 'predecessor in interest Baidyanath. Exhibit 7 is the copy of the order dated 31-5-1950 passed by the House Rent Controller on a petition filed by the defendants predecessors, Khandaker Ansar Ahmed praying for fixation of rent of house No. 12. The House Rent Controller fixed the rent at Taka 15. Exhibit. 8(a) is the copy of an order dated 9-1-1963 passed by the Assistant Settlement Officer, Khulna in Objection Case No. 808 under section 19(1) filed by the defendant Khandakar Ansar Ahmed against the preparation of record of rights. It shows that record of rights was not prepared in the name of defendants' predecessor but order was passed to record his possession in Col. 13 of the Khatian Exhibit. 9 is the copy of reply to the show cause filed by the second party Abdus Salam in a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before Mr SA Hamid, Magistrate 1st Class, Khulna on 21-3-1958. In this petition he clearly stated that he came to the then East Pakistan in 1950 as a refugee and has been residing in holding Nos. 12 and 13 of Ward No.4 of Khulna Municipality (now City Corporation) as monthly tenant. Exhibit 12(b) is the copy of deposition of Khandakar Ansar Ahmed, in the above noted proceeding under section 145,Code of Criminal Procedure as second party. In his deposition he categorically stated "In 1950 we migrated to Pakistan and occupied the disputed house in holding No. 12 of Ward No. IV. We also occupied holding No. 13. Dhirendra Bhattacharjee is the owner of both the holdings. He lived in Calcutta. We are tenants of holding No. 12 and paid rent. Exhibit. A series are rent receipts granted by Bidhu Bhusan who was the karmachari of Dhiren, Exhibit. B is the certified copy of the suit register of the House Rent Control Case for the disputed house." In his evidence he also stated "We occupied the house after settling rent Taka 15 was fixed as rent for holding No. 12 from House Rent Controller in 1950. I have no paper to show the fixation of rent. Previous to the rent control case, we used to pay Taka 18 per month as house rent for holding No. 12 I have rent receipt for holding No. 13 which I will not file." In his evidence he further stated that he would deposit the rent of the suit premises before the House Rent Controller after disposal of the pending case.

13. Thus it is clear that the predecessor in interest of defendants and defendant Kh Ansar Ahmed himself admitted that he was a monthly tenant in the suit premises. Therefore, in our view, the High Court Division properly considered these document viz Exhibits 7, 8(a), 9 & 12(b) and there is no misconstruction of the documents.

14. Mr Ahmed then argued that there was no proof of attornment of the defendants either in favour of Baidyanath or the plaintiffs. Attornment is absolutely necessary in absence of a transfer by lessor. There being no transfer by Dhiren and Biren in favour of Baidyanath or plaintiffs, section 109 of the Transfer of Property Act cannot come into operation and the plaintiffs' remedy lies in a regular suit for declaration of title. In reply, the learned Counsel for the respondents submits that this point was not raised before the High Court Division or before the courts below. Let us quote below.

15. Section 109 of the Transfer of Property Act:-

"109. Rights of lessor's transferee-If the lessor transfers the property leased, or any part thereof, or any part of his interest therein, the transferee, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, shall possess all the rights, and, if the lessee so elects, be subject to all the liabilities of the lessor as to the property or part transferred so long as he is the owner of it; but the lessor shall not, by reason only of such transfer, cease to be subject to any of the liabilities imposed upon him by the lease, unless the lessee elects to treat the transferee as the person liable to him:

Provided that the transferee is not entitled to arrears of rent due before the transfer, and that, if the lessee, not having reason to believe that such transfer has been made, pays rent to the lessor, the lessee shall not be liable to pay such rent over again to the transferee.

The lessor, the transferee and the lessee, may determine what proportion of the premium of rent reserved by the lease is payable in respect of the part so transferred, and, in case they disagree, such determination may be made by any Court having jurisdiction to entertain a suit for the possession of the property leased."

16. This section provides that if the lessor transfers the property leased, the transferee acquires the right of the lessor and if the lessee so elects, the transferee shall be subject to all the liabilities of the lessor as to the property transferred. Since the plaintiffs acquired right, title and interest in the suit property through Baidyanath whose title was confirmed by sole decree passed in Title Suit No. 102 of 1958, it cannot be said that the defendants are not tenants under the plaintiffs in the face of Exhibits 7, 8(a), 9 & 12(b) and in view of our discussion made above. Hence the argument of Mr Ahmed does not stand.

<u>17. Admittedly the suit property was Non-Agricultural Property from before 1947 and the same is situated within Khulna Municipal Corporation. The defendants once claimed that they were monthly tenants under Srish Bhattacharjee and thereafter under his sons, Dhirendra and Birendra. They again claimed that they took settlement of the suit property by unregistered Amaldari from Dhirendra and Birendra on 17-5-1950. It is the settled principle of law that settlement of Non-Agricultural land within Municipality cannot be effected by unregistered document. The same must be effected by bilateral registered document executed by both the lessor and the lessee. Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 came into force on 28th October, 1949 and according to defendants' case they took settlement by unregistered amaldari on 17-5-1950 and, as such, the same is hit by section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act.</u>

18. Both the courts below concurrently held that notices under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act were duly served upon the defendants of the suit. The defendants did not set out in their pleading that they have been paying rent for the suit premises.

19. Mr Ahmed lastly argued that Title Suit No. 134 of 1964 is barred under the provisions of Order II, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He submits that the cause of action of both the suits arose at the same time and, as such, the subsequent suit namely Title Suit No. 134 of 1964 is barred under the aforesaid Rules. In reply the learned Counsel for the respondent submits that the suit holdings being different, the provisions of Order 2 rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure are not applicable in the present case. The contention so made by the learned Counsel of the respondent appears to be of merit.

20. Therefore, in view of the discussions made above, we are of the view that the High Court Division upon correct assessment of the materials on record arrived at a correct decision. There is no cogent reason to interfere with the same.

Both the appeals are, therefore, dismissed with costs at all stages.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 95-97 of 2007.
lawyer:
Abdus Salam Khan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record -----For the Petitioners (In all the cases). 
Abdul Quayum, Senior Advocate, instructed by Syed Mahbubur Rahman, Advocate-on-Record -----For the Respondents (In all the cases)
parties:
Ramesh Chandra Barman and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Iswar Kalachan Jieu Thakur and another ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 19-7-2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4243, 4244 of 2005 and 4654 of 1998)
full_judgment:
Md Tafazzul Islam J: The Civil Petition Nos. 95 and 96 of 2007 are directed against the common judgment and order dated 19-7-2006 of the High Court Division passed in Civil Revision Nos. 4243 and 4244 of 2005 and the Civil Petition No. 97 of 2007 is directed against the judgment and order dated 19-7-2006 passed in Civil Revision No. 4654 of 1998. In all the civil revisions the Rules were discharged.

2. In respect of the above Civil Petition Nos. 95 and 96 of 2007 facts, in short, are that Biswajit Dutta (Bhula), as plaintiff No.2, instituted the above Title Suit No. 227 of 1998 in the Court of Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka seeking declaration that the power of attorney dated 9-7-1998 executed by Benode Behari Dutta in favour of Ramesh Chandra Barman, the defendant in the above suit, is illegal, fraudulent, void, without jurisdiction and not binding upon him and also praying for an order of permanent injunction restraining the defendant/petitioner from making any obstacle to his functioning as the shebait of the deity Sree Iswar Kalachan Jieu Thakur, the plaintiff No.1, on the averments that Janaki Ballov Dutta, by deed dated 17-1-1931, bequested the suit property in favour of the above deity on the terms and conditions that he will become the shebait of the deity to perform the daily worship, etc and after his death, his wife, Mollika Sundari Dutta, will become the next shebait and after her death, the shebaitship would devolve upon his sons and heirs who are to act as joint shebaits to perform worship, etc.  jointly and if the numbers of the shebaits become numerous and if they cannot agree to joint management they will constitute a committee, not exceeding six in number representing the line of his Six sons, and such committee be given the power to entrust the management of the deity to one of the shebaits.  After the creation of the above endowment Janaki became the first shebait and after his death on 12-9-1943, Mallika Sundari Dutta, his wife, became the next shebait-and she died on 4th Ashar, 1363 BS. Out of six sons of the Janaki, Kali Kinkore Dutta died in the then East Pakistan and four others i.e. Kali Kishore Dutta, Kali Prosanna Dutra, Kali Sankar Dutta, Kali Bhusan Dutta left for India long ago and became Indian citizens and dispute having arisen among the sons of lanaki regarding appointment of shebait, Kali Pad a Dutta the remaining son of lanaki who alone remained in the country, filed Title Suit No. 39 of 1959 in the Court of the then Munsir, 1st Court, Dhaka against his aforesaid four brothers and then, among them, Kali Kishore Dutta, Kali Prosanna Dutta and Kali Sankar Dutta appointed Md Nasiruddin of Sawgat as their attorney to manage the property of the deity in East Pakistan; Sreemanta Kumar Dutta, son of Kali Kishore Dutta, who remained in the then East Pakistan alone, also gave similar power of attorney in favour of the above Md Nasiruddin; the above appointment of Md Nasiruddin as attorney was not in accordance to the terms of the deed of bequest dated 17-1-1931; Md. Nasiruddin, as attorney holder of Kali Kishore Dutta, kali Prasanna Dutta and Kali Sankar Dutta, compromised the above suit by filing solehnarna dated 17-7-1965; then Sreemanta Kumar Dutta, the attorney of Kali Kishore Dutta, filed Title Appeal No, 305 of 1965 challenging the above solehnama decree dated 17-7-1965 but on 1-4-93 the same was dismissed and as against that Sreemanta Kumar Dutta moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No, 9 of 1994 which is pending; in the mentime on 21-5-1994 Md Nasiruddin died and thereafter Sreemanto Kumar Dutta also died on 28-2-95 leaving behind Biswajit Kumar Dutta, the plaintiff No, 2; thereafter Kali Pad a Dutta having fallen ill, his son Binode Behari Dutta, an Indian citizen, came to Bangladesh on 26-3-97 and took his father Kali Padaputta to India for treatment but Kali PadaDutta died in India on 31-12-97; the plaintiff No 2 is the only heir of Janaki in Bangladesh; since Binode Behari Datta, an Indian citizen, had been living in Bangladesh illegally after the expiry of his visa, on the basis of the complaint filed by the plaintiff No 1, the Ministry of Home, after inquiry, made him blacklisted and drove him out of Bangladesh but however before leaving Bangladesh Binode Behair Dutta, by power of attorney dated 9-7-98, appointed Ramesh Chandra Bannan, the defendant, as his attorney but then the above defendant was also blacklisted; Binode Behari Dutta having left for India had no right to appoint Ramesh Chandra Bannan, the defendant, who was not an heir of Janaki, as attorney to look after the deity.

3. The defendant contested the suit by filing written statement contending that four sons of Janaki, who on obtaining citizenship had been living in India permanently, having refused to conduct sheba puja of the deity, Kali Pada Dutta, after the death of Mallika Sandari Dutta conducted the sheba puja and requested his remaining four brothers to constitute a committee comprising of six members and the above four brothers having refused the said request, Kali Pada Dutta filed the above Title Suit No 39 of 1959 seeking declaration that his above four brothers, who were made defendants in the above suit, ceased to be the shebait of the deity and also praying for removal of the above four brothers from the shebaitship of the said deity and also prayed for a scheme for the management of the properties of the deity and for worship of the deity in conformity with the terms and conditions of the deed of endowment and the then learned Munsif after hearing, decreed the above suit in terms of the solenama dated 17-7-1965 by which Kali Pada Dutta became shebait and Md Nasiruddin became the manager of the deity; then Sremanta Kumar Dutta, an Indian citizen and one of the sons of Kali Kishore Dutta, who died in India on 29-9-65, came to Bangladesh and filed Title Appeal No 305 of 1965 against the above compromise decree and the above appeal: being dismissed after hearing, he moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No 9 of 1994; after the death of Sreemanta Kumar Dutta his son Biswajit Dutta alias Bhulu, the plaintiff  No. 2, came to Bangladesh from India in the year 1972 and was living in Bangladesh illegally; Binode Behari Dutta went to India for study with Bangladeshi passport and student visa and when his father Kali Pada Dutta fell ill he came back to Bangladesh to look after his father and then took his father to India and then Kali Pada having died in India on 31-12-97, Binode Behari Dutta became the shebait in place of Kali Pada Dutta and then he by power of attorney dated 9-7-98 appointed Ramesh Chandra Barman, the defendant, to look after the property of the deity and so the plaintiff No. 2 has no right to file this suit. The learned Joint District Judge, after hearing, by judgment and decree dated 8-1-2005 decree the suit in part i.e. only declaring that the power of attorney executed by Binode Behari Dutta on 9-7-98 in favour of Ramesh Chandra Barman, the defendant, is illegal and not binding upon the plaintiffs and rejected the prayer of permanent injunction. As against that the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 104 of 2005 on the ground that the suit should have been decreed in full by passing the decree of permanent injunction as well and the defendant preferred Title Appeal No.108 of 2005 on the ground that the suit ought to have been dismissed. The learned Additional District Judge, who heard both the appeals analogously, by judgment and decree dated 13-9-2005 allowed Title Appeal No. 104 of 2005 decreeing the suit in full i.e. granting decree of permanent injunction as well and dismissed Title Appeal No. 108 of 2005. Then both the parties moved the High Court Division and obtained Rules in Civil Revision Nos. 4243 and 4244 of 2005.

4. In respect of the above Civil Petition No. 97 of 2007 facts, in brief, are that Binode Behari Dutta, as plaintiff No.2, also instituted Title Suit No. 95 of 1998 in the same Court of the then 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge Dhaka for a decree for permanent injunction restraining Biswajit Dutta (Bhulu), the defendant No.1 in the above suit, from transferring the property of the deity, the plaintiff No.1, to anybody else, reaIising rents from the tenants thereunder, disturbing his functioning as the shebait of the property of the deity and also restraining the defendant No. 1 from making any construction in the building of the deity situated at 17, Shankari Bazar Road on the averments that after the death of his father Kali Pada Dutta he became the shebait of the deity and while he had been performing as such, the defendant No.1, on 15-2-98, with the help of the goondas threatened to remove the tenants from the property of the deity and when he, on 17-2-1998, requested the defendant No. 1 to refrain from such activities,' the defendant No.1 became furious. In the above suit Benode Behari Dutta also filed an application praying for an order .of temporary injunction and on 4-6-98 obtained an order of status quo. Biswajit Dutta (Bhulu), as plaintiff No. 1, also filed Title Suit No. 55 of 1993 in the same Court seeking declaration that he is the shebait of the deity the plaintiff No.2, and also praying for a decree of permanent injunction restraining Binode Behari Dutta, the defendant in the above suit, from disturbing him from functioning as the shebait of the deity and realising rents from the tenants of the property of the deity and also from obstructing him from operating the bank account of the deity. In the above suit Biswajit Dutta (Bhulu) also filed an application praying for an order of temporary injunction. Thereafter, both the petitions were heard analogously and the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) by order date 8-7-1998 rejected the prayers of both Binode Behari Dutta and Biswajit Dutta (Bhulu) for temporary injunction. As against that Bindoe Behari Dutta preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 191 of 1998 and Biswajit Dutta (Bhulu) preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 193 of 1998 and the Additional District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, who heard both the appeals analogously, considering, amongst others, that in Civil Revision No.9 of 94 in terms of the order dated 26-4-98 both the parties were added.as parties in place of their predecessor and that earlier, by order dated 9-4-96 passed in the above civil revision, the High Court Division restrained the parties from creating any obstacles to Kali Pada Dutta in operating the Bank Account No. 1057 of the deity maintained with Pubali Bank, allowed the appeals and directed both the parties to work as shebaits of the deity on the condition that pending disposal of suit no further construction be made in Holding No. 17, Shankari Bazar. As against that Bindoe Behari Dutta moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in the above Civil Revision No. 4654 of 1998.

5. Before the High Court Division, in all the Rules, common question arose as to whether the power of attorney dated 9-7-1998 executed by Binode Behari Dutta in favour of Rarnesh Chandra Barman. the petitioner, was valid and after hearing, Rules issued in Civil Revision Nos. 4243 and 4244 of 2005 as well as in Civil Revision 4654 of 1998 were discharged holding that the above power of the above attorney dated 9-7-1998 was not valid.

<u>6. The learned Counsel for the petitioner(s) submitted that Biswajlt Kumar Dutta (Bhulu) had no locus standi to institute the above Title Suit No. 227 of 1998 and the High Court Division erroneously discharged the Rules maintaining the judgment and decree passed in Title Appeal No. 104 of 2005 decreeing the suit in full and the High Court Division failed to consider that Binode Behari Dutta, at the time of executing power of attorney dated 9-7-1998, was a citizen of Bangladesh by birth as he went to India with a student visa holding a Pakistani passport and that in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Ms Ispahani 40 DLR (AD) 116 and in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Professor Golam Azam 46 DLR (AD) 192 it has been held that a citizen by birth is a citizen of the country and thus Biriode Behari Dutta, being a citizen of Bangladesh by birth, was competent to execute the above power of attorney dated 9-7-1998.</u>

7. The learned Counsel appearing for the respondent (s) submitted that Benode Behari Dutta, an Indian citizen, being not able to stay in Bangladesh and perform the functions of shebait of the deity, should have let the heirs of Janaki through his six sons and/or the devotees of the deity to choose a new shebait of the deity and he by giving power of attorney dated 9-7-1998 petitioner cannot, by dictating from India, perform the functions of the shebait of the deity.

8. As it appears the High Court Division discharged the Rules holding that in section 414 of DF Mollah’s Hindu Law (Fifteenth Edition) by ST Desai it has been written as follows:

"It was laid down by the Judicial Committee, that a shebait has not the legal ownership in, but only the title of manager of, a religious endowment."

It follows from this, that the rent of property dedicated to the services of an idol, as well as offerings made to the idol, belong to the idol, and not to the shebait. A shebait being a manager only, ceases to be shebait when he ceases to manage the property and carry on the worship of the idol."

9. The High Court Division, considering the above principle held that Binode Behari Dutta, after leaving Bangladesh for India, ceased to be the shebait or manager to look after the property of the deity and therefore, he, by executing the power of attorney dated 9-7-1998, cannot entrust Ramesh Chanda Barman, the petitioner, to perform the function of the shebait of the deity or manage the properties of the deity on his behalf.

<u>10. As it appears in the case of Bhuban Mohan Kaley vs Narendra Nath Konwar 35 CWN 478, it was held as follows:</u>

<u>"Dr Mukherji seems to proceed: on an assumption which is not justified by law that the shebaits have some sort of vested interest in the debutter property of which they cannot be divested except by some provision of the law of transfer. As is well known and the point is now undisputably settled by the decision of their Lordships of the Judicial Committee in Vidya Varvthi Thirtha vs Balusami Ayyar(1). that a shebait is a mere manager of an idol and is almost by courtesy called a trustee, though he does not occupy the position of a trustee as understood in the English law except under a specific trust. In the present case the deed of dedication is not before us, on the other hand, it is admitted by the defendants that it was only by a family arrangement that the rent was divided amongst the several co-shebaits. At p. 315 of the report their Lordships said: "Neither under the Hindue Law nor in the Mahomedan system is any property 'conveyed' to a shebait or a mutwali, in the case of a dedication. Nor is any property vested in him; whatever property he holds for the idol or the institution he holds as manager with certain beneficial interests regulated by custom and usage The curator, whether called mutwali or sajjadanashin, or by any other name, is merely, a manager. He is certainly not a 'trustee' as understood in the English system." Now, an ordinary shebait, being a manager, ceases to be a shebait when he ceases to manage the property and carry 011 the worship of the idol. He has no right of property transferable or heritable as such. The property 'belongs' to the idol which is a "jurisdiction" and the suit is brought on behalf of the idol by the persons who do its sheba and manage its property. The present suit is brought by the idol through the plaintiffs who are described as its shebaits. The finding of the Court below therefore, that the.defendant Nos. 4 and 5 have ceased to perform the sheba of the idol, is sufficient to enable the Court to hold that they have ceased to be shebaits in the absence of any rule of the trust to the contrary. The plaintiffs as managers of the idol's property are entitled to maintain the suit for rent of the idol's property.</u>

<u>11. Accordingly, in the present case, there being nothing in the record to show that there was no provision in deed of bequest to the contrary, Binode Behari Dutta, having left Bangladesh for India, ceased to be the shebait or manager to look after the property of the deity and so, on the basis of the power of attorney dated 9-7-98 given by him, Ramesh Chandra Bannan, the petitioner, cannot manage or look after the property of the deity.</u>

12. We are of the view that the High Court Division on proper consideration of the materials on record discharged the Rules and so the decision of the High Court Division does not call for any Interference.

The petitions are dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Faruque Ahmed, Advocate------ For the Petitioners. 
No one appeared------ For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Gopal Chandra Das and others------ Plaintiff- Appellant-Petitioners 
Vs. 
Nikunja Behari Sukra Das and others ------ Defendant-Respondent- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
Syed Abu Kowser Md. Dabirush-Shan, J. : This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 7-9-94 and 19-9-94 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Narayanganj, in Title Appeal No. 89 of 1986 affirming the judgment and decree dated 20-7-86 and 24-7-86 respectively passed by the Munsif, Bandar Upazila, Narayanganj, in Title Suit No. 38 of 1985 dismissing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The petitioners as plaintiff filed the Title Suit No. 34 of 1985 for declaration of title in the suit land stating, inter alia, that one Govinda Chandra Chakraborty was the superior landlord in Mirashi right in 'A' schedule land and while the same was under his management one Bhama Baishnabi was given shelter in the suit land by the said Govinda and CS record was recorded in the name of the said Bhama Baishnabi. About 60 years ago the said Bhama Baishnabi died leaving one heir and thereafter said Govinda, superior landlord of the Estate, took the 'A' schedule land in his khas possession. In the "B" schedule land said Govinda Chandra was owner in possession as Mirashi right, Govinda died leaving only two sons namely, Mukunda and Gopal. By an amicable settlement between these two brothers Mukunda got the suit land. Mukunda in exercising his sixteen annas right, title and interest in the suit properties approached to plaintifs father for taking settlement of the suit properties on payment of reasonable rent for the suit land and thereafter Mukunda gave rioyti settlement by executing an unregistered Hukum Nama with respect to the suit properties in the Bengali year 1343 BS on 17th Poush corresponding to 1936 in favour of Krishna Mohan Das, the father of the plaintiffs. Krishna Mohan Das was owner in possession of the suit properties by getting settlement and he died in the year 1956 at his own house in the suit Mouza leaving behind three sons, the plaintiffs who by inheritance became the owner and possessed the entire suit land for more than 12 years uninterruptedly and have been paying rent to the Government and that on 17-8-85 for the first time they came to know from the local Tahsilder that the suit properties have been treated as vested properties by the defendants No. 5 and 6 as the properties were earlier recorded in favour of defendant Nos. 1-4 and also Tahsilder refused to accept the rent from the plaintiffs. The defendants have no right, title and possession in the suit properties and SA Khatian has been wrongly prepared in faovur of the defendant Nos. 1-4 due to such recording in favour of the defendant No. 1-4 a cloud of doubt in the right, title and interest of the plaintiff in the suit land and to dispel such cloud and doubt plaintiffs have constrained to file the suit.

3. The defendant No. 5 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegation and contending, inter alia, that the owners of the suit properties Mukunda and Gopal Chakraborty are the sons of Govinda Chandra who are the citizens of India and they have been living in India permanently having citizenship for which the suit property have been enlisted as Vested Property. One Abdul Barek prayed for lease of the suit properties and an investigation to the effect is going on and that Gopal Chandra, Santi Chandra Das and Abdul Matin are the legal possessors in the suit properties which have already been enlisted as vested property and that the plaintiffs' right, title and interest or possession in the suit property has been enlisted as vested property, as such, the plaintiffs cannot get any relief in this suit. Hence, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. During the trial plaintiff examined 2 witnesses and the defendant examined only 1 witness Tahsilder to prove their respective cases. The learned trial Court after hearing both the parties and perusing the evidence on record document and exhibits and also the Hokum Nama came to a finding that the plaintiff failed to establish his title in the suit land by producing any document i.e. title deed. On the other hand, the defendant examined Tahsilder Md Safiuddin who stated in his evidence that the original owner of the land Mukunda, son of Govinda migrated to India and has been living in India permanently, as such, the suit property has been enlisted as vested property in the census report and the plaintiff has been illegally possessing the suit land. The learned trial Court after hearing dismissed the suit of the plaintiff by his judgment and decree dated 20-7-76 and 24-7-86 respectively.

5. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 20-7-86 and 24-7-86 passed by the learned Munsif, Bandar Upazila, Narayanganj, the plaintiff preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 89 of 1986 before the learned District Judge, Narayanganj and the appeal was ultimately heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Narayanganj who after hearing was pleased to dismiss the appeal by his judgment and decree dated 7-9-94 and 19-9- 94 respectively.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Narayanganj, the plaintiff- appellant-petitioners preferred the instant revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr Faruque Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant- petitioner submits that the lower appellate Court and also the trial Court without applying their judicial mind and without proper assessment of the evidence on record and also the legal point involved in this case came to a wrong and erroneous finding in dis- missing the suit of the plaintiff. Next, the learned Counsel submits that the plaintiff since 1343 BS corresponding to 1936 AD has been living in the suit land by erecting the houses after obtaining the Hokum Nama from the original owner Mukunda and, as such, the plaintiff have acquired a good title by way of right of adverse possession. The defendant also admitted and gave a suggestion in cross- examination to the plaintiff that he has been illegally possessing the suit land. Both the lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court also observed in their judgment that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit property illegally by way of private dhakila and Hokum Nama which has got no leg to stand in the eye of law and in this connection both the courts relied upon a decision reported in 30 DLR (SC) 41 wherein it has been clearly stated that the private document cannot be taken into notice and consideration and marked as exhibit without any formal proof unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposite party. This observation made by the courts below are not applicable and legally tenable in the context of the present suit. The learned Counsel further submits that both the courts below failed to appreciate the legal aspect of the case with regard to section 28 of the Limitation Act which reads as follows:

Extinguishment of right to property-At the determination of the period hereby limited to any person for instituting a suit for possession of any property, his right to such property shall be extinguished. In this connection, the learned Counsel referred the case of Santipada Datta being dead his heirs: Aranangsha Datta vs Salish Chandra Das reported in 7 MLR (AD) 249 = 54 DLR (AD) 173 wherein it has been held:

Section 28 Acquisition of title by adverse possession-

Transfer of Property Act, 1882-

Section 54- Transfer of immovable property by invalid document-Legal consequence thereof-

"Though the transfer by invalid document does not confer title, the transferee when continues in possession of the immovable property for more than the statutory period of 12 years uninterrupted on the basis therefof he acquired title to the said property by adverse possession notwithstanding the defect in the documents.

Thus when there is an invalid transfer in favour of a person and he holds possession of the property transferred as transferee, his possession is in his own right and adverse to the transferee. If he continues in possession of immoveable property for more than twelve years he will acquire an indefeasible title."

8. The learned Counsel submits that the plain- tiff has been possessing and living in the suit land since 1936 and the case was filed on 20-11-85 i.e. after the lapse of 49 years. Enemy Property Ordinance was promulgated in the year 1965 long after the execution of Hokum Nama by the original owner Mukunda and since then plaintiff has been living in the suit property. If, according to section 28 of the Limitation Act, the period is computed from the year 1936, then the statutory period of 12 years would expire on 1948 to extinguish the right of possession even by the original owner Mukunda. The Enemy Property Ordinance, subsequently a vested property when it was promulgated, did not give any retrospective effect, as such, the plaintiff acquired title by adverse possession after the expiry of 12 year. The learned Counsel finally submits that the lower appellate Court failed to apply his judicial mind in considering the most important legal aspect of the case occasioning failure of justice which is liable to be interfered by this Court.

9. No one appeared at the time of hearing of the case although the opposite party filed power.

10. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, exhibits, dakhilas, Hokum Nama and other connected papers and the judgment of both the Courts below it transpires that the lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court committed error in law as well as on facts. Both the courts below in their judgment observed that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land illegally and defendant also admitting that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land since long but plaintiff is possessing the suit land illegally. But prior to the institution of the title suit by the plaintiff the peaceful possession of the plaintiff was never disturbed by anybody and no notice was served by the vested property authority upon the plaintiff to the effect that the suit property has been enlisted as vested property. The Vested Property Authority could not prove any notice or paper to show that the notice was served upon the plaintiff by the Authority through DW Tahsilder. The vested property authority failed to prove any legal foundation to enlist the property in the vested property list. In this connection I like to rely on the decision in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Paresh Chandra Gharami reported in 50 DLR (AD) 70 wherein it has been stated.

"When the Government failed to prove the legal foundation for enlisting the suit property in the census report of the vested property and the plaintiffs led some evidence in support of their interest in the suit property the appellate Court decreed the suit on correct view of law."

<u>11. The lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court committed serious error of law in not considering the legal aspect of the case and long uninterrupted possession of the plaintiff which caused failure of justice. The Courts below ought to have considered the right of adverse possession acquired by the plaintiff by way of uninterrupted more than 12 years adverse possession which is liable to be interfered by this Court. In this connection I like to cite the decision in the case of Hussain Ahmed Chowdhury alias Ahmed Hussain Chowdhury vs Md Nurul Amin reported in 47 DLR (AD) 162 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"If there is misreading of evidence and non-consideration of some material evidence then it was incumbent on the revisional Court to consider the same and to arrive at a proper finding on the material evidence on record and to finally dispose of the case."</u>

12. In view of the facts and legal position of the case and also the submission of the learned Counsel for the petitioner, I find that the lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court are absolutely wrong in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff and the judgment and decree passed by both the Courts below are liable to be set aside.

13. The discussion made above and the facts and legal position of the case the impugned judgment and decree dated 7-9-94 and 19-9-94 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Narayanganj, in Title Appeal No. 89 of 1986 affirming the judgment and decree dated 20-7- 86 and 24-7-86 respectively passed by the Munsif, Bandar Upazila, Narayanganj, in Title Suit No. 38 of 1985 is hereby set aside and the Title Suit No. 89 of 1986 filed by the plaintiff is hereby decreed.

14. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to the costs.

Lower Court record be sent down at once with a copy of the judgment.

End.

parties:
Sena Kalayan Sangstha and another ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Sufi Fazal Ahmed and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 26th May, 2004 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal Nos.45 of 1993 and 86 of 1997).
full_judgment:
Md. Fazlul Karim J: The two Review Petitions are directed against the judgment and order passed by this Division in Civil Appeal No. 45 of 1993 and Civil Appeal No. 86 of 1997. Since both the Review Petitions are between the same parties involving substantially the same facts and points of law, the same were taken up for hearing together and accordingly disposed of by this single judgment.

2. Civil Appeal No. 45 of 1993 by leave arose out of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 122 of 1993, which is directed against the judgment and decree dated 1-9-1992 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Decree No. 138 of 1990 affirming those dated 31-5-1990 passed by the Subordinate Judge, First Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 124 of 1987.

3. The suit was for a decree only for khas possession in respect of the suit land together with two storied building standing thereon. The plaintiff filed Other Suit No. 131 of 1982 against the Government upon declaration that the suit property is not an abandoned property and declaration of his title to the suit property i.e. land and the residential building standing thereon, and ultimately obtained an ex parte decree to that effect which was maintained upto this Court but the defendants did not vacate the suit property and hence the plaintiff was compelled to file the instant suit for recovery of khas possession.

4. In Civil Appeal No. 86 of 1997 leave was granted in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 578 of 1997 directed against the judgment and decree dated 11-3-1997 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1714 of 1992 affirming those dated 28-5-1992 passed by the Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 321 of 1990 reversing those dated 13-5-1990 passed by the Subordinate Judge, First Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 139 of 1982.

5. The respondent No. 1 filed Other Suit No. 139 of 1982 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for declaration of title, recovery of khas possession and mesne profit.

6. Dr M Zahir, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioners, submitted that both the civil suits were barred under Articles 23 and 24 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 16 of 1972) and that this aspect was not considered in both the appeals and was also not urged at any stage of the suits leading to Civil Appeals.

7. But the plaintiff never agitated raising the issue in the suits before the Courts below and, as such, the issue would not be entertained at this stage. However, as a matter of fact, the management of the property al through was with the plaintiffs son Nazir Mohiuddin who was also the Managing Director when the land and the industry and the residential building were taken over by the Government on 31-12-1971 under the purported exercise of power under Acting President's Order No. SRO-XII-M-35/71/17 dated 26th December, 1971 published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary dated January 3, 1972.

<u>8. However, the provisions under Articles 23 and 24 of the President's Order 16 of 1972 are intended to cover only orders passed with jurisdiction and afford no protection to orders passed without jurisdiction which can always be challenged in the Court, as an order without jurisdiction having no existence in the eye of law. The Civil Courts have general jurisdiction to ascertain whether the act or authority or executive officer's order is passed with jurisdiction. No order is an order passed under any Act if it was not passed in exercise of power granted by the Act and was, therefore, without jurisdiction. The decided decision apart from the case of Secretary of State vs Mask reported in AIR 1945 (PC) 709 notable, amongst others, are Abdur Raul vs Abdul Hamid Khan, 17 DLR (SC) 515 and Md Jamil vs Improvement Trust, Rawalpindi, 17 DLR (SC) 520.</u>

9. The learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners submitted that these suits do not address the issue regarding maintainability of the suit itself against the declaration in respect of the abandoned property in view of the fact that the suits are not maintainable, as such, the impugned order in appeal is liable to be disturbed by way of review. We have perused the impugned judgment and it appears that though in the written statement in omnibus manner it was stated that the suit is not maintainable but the defendant did never agitate the issue nor cared to suggest an issue to that effect or that no issue was urged to be framed by the trial Court. The Court accordingly proceeded to hear the suit and same is the case in the appellate Court as well. No such point as urged Was ever urged in the High Court Division and before this Division. But in review the petitioner for the first time has ever urged the point as to maintainability of the suit.

10. We have perused the record of the suits and find that the Other Suit No. 124 of 1982 was for recovery of possession in respect of the two-storied building claiming title thereto and it may be mentioned that previously Other Suit No. 131 of 1982 was filed by the respondent in the 1st  Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong against the defendant Nos. 1 and 5 for declaration that the suit property was not an abandoned one and upon a decree which was set at rest in favour of the plaintiff-respondent and in that view of the matter it does not lie in the mouth of present petitioner to allege that the suit is not maintainable due to abandoned nature of the suit land. Similarly in Civil Appeal No. 86 of 1982 which arises out of Other Suit No. 139 of 1992 for declaration of title, recovery of khas possession in respect of the industry named Messrs Fasons Metal Industries at 287/288,. Baizid Bostami Industrial Area, Chittagong. The plaintiff took stand that the management of the industry was always with the plaintiff through his son Nazir Mohiuddin who was present although in Bangladesh and actively participated in the conduct, management and control as the Managing Director of the industry concerned  when the land and the industry and the residential building were taken over by the Government under the purported exercise of power under Acting President's Order No. SRO-XII-M-35/71/17 dated 26th December, 1971 published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary dated January 3, 1972. It was also decreed in favour of the plaintiff which go to show that the issue regarding the character of the property was set at rest in previous suit and, in that view of the matter, it is begging the same question again in the present review petition arising out of subsequent suit. Over and above, the petitioner or its predecessor did never asserted by forming any issue as to the abandoned character of the suit land or industry in the suits. So, it does not lie in the mouth of the present petitioner that the Court below ought to have considered the issue regarding the maintainability of the suit on alleged abandoned nature.

11. Be that as it may, we like to reproduce the submission made by the learned Counsel for the petitioner in Civil Appeal No. 86 of 1997 that Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant, submitted, that the property having been taken by a notification dated 13-121971 under Acting President's Order No. IM-35/7J-13 and on repeal of thesaid order by APO No. 1 of 1972, the property was purported to have been taken over under APO No. 1 of 1972 by virtue of Article 6(2) of the said order APO No. 1 of 1972 and therefore, the property comes within the definition of abandoned under Article 2 of PO No. XVI of 1972, which came into force on 28-2-1972."

12. The learned Counsel further submitted that in view of the plaintiffs claim that he went to Hajj in November, 1971 leaving his family in Bangladesh and was stranded there until he came back in Bangladesh in 1973 on Pakistani passport, which he surrendered and was given citizenship of Bangladesh and during his absence his son was managing the affairs of the industry when it was taken over by the Government; in that premises the Acting President's Order dated 26-12-1971 authorised the Government to take over any industry the owner and top management which are not available in Bangladesh.

13. We have considered the submissions made by the learned Counsels in both the appeals and have answered the points raised in our exhaustive judgments disposing of the appeals. This judgment has been sought to be reviewed in both the Civil Review petitions on the grounds as many as eleven in number reiterating the same arguments which the learned Counsels had advanced in the Civil Appeals and were overruled by this Court. Thereafter, the learned Counsel has raised the present issue regarding maintainability. This point was not even disclosed in the written statement and accordingly was not urged at any stage of the suit. Apart from the fact that this point was set at rest in previous Other Suit No. 131 of 1982 between the parties over the suit property but being not raised at any stage of the suit not to speak of the initial stage and no decision was arrived at by the Court below, the petitioner could not agitate the issue regarding maintainability of the suit at this stage. It may be stated here that the Courts below impliedly decided the point while deciding other issues in the suit. wereiterate the observations made with regards to review in the case of Abdul Halim Miah vs Secretary, Ministry of Establishment, 12 MLR (AD) 209, 221 that "Before we part with, this is to be remembered that 'review' under Order XXIV of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (Appellate Division) Rules, 1988 or under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure is subject to law and rules but could not be a substitute of an appeal for rehearing the impugned judgment and order passed in appeal; and for correcting the same unless there is an error apparent on the face of the record based on evidence or material on record.

14. Supreme Court of India also held the same view of the case of Sow Chandra Kante vs Sheikh Habib, (1975) 1 SCC 674. It runs as; "Once an order has been passed by the Supreme Court, a review thereof must be subject to the rules of the same and cannot be lightly entertained. A review of a judgment is a serious step and reluctant resort to it is proper only where a glaring omission or patent mistake or like grave error has crept in earlier by judicial fallibility. A mere repetition, through different Counsels of old and overruled arguments, a second trip over ineffectually covered ground or minor mistakes of inconsequential import are obviously insufficient, It is neither in fairness to the Court which decided nor awareness of the precious public time lost what with a huge backlog of dockets waiting in the queue for disposal, for Counsel to issue easy certificate for entertainment of review and fight over again the same battle, which has been fought and lost.

15. A review, by no stretch of imagination, could be termed as an appeal or rehearing of an issue directly or indirectly disposed of earlier or never agitated unless there is any error apparent on the face of the record or for any substantial reason.

16. Accordingly, for the reasons stated above, we do not find any substance in the submissions for the learned Counsel of the petitioners.

End.
