VS.
Ful Miah and another ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 25-8-2004 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria in Title Suit No. 16 of 2003 should not be set aside and or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted a suit for recovery of possession under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Nasirnager, Brahmanbaria.

3. The case of plaintiff, in short, is that, the suit land and other non suit land belonged to one Fazar Ali having 2/3 share and Khatunennese haying 1/3 share and accordingly CS khatian No. 310 was prepared in their names and thereafter by amicable partition, Fazar Ali got the suit land who died leaving behind two sons and one daughter and thereafter by amicable partition the suit land went to plaintiff Moti Miah and at the time of recent survey operation, plaintiff, being in physical possession, got the property recorded in his name in the BS khatian and thereafter took loan from Bangladesh Krishi Bank, Nasirnagar Branch, by mortgaging the suit land and was paying taxes and rent to the concerned authorities and the defendants did not possess the suit land and on several dates, they illegally dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land and hence the present suit.

4. The defendants appeared in the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and the case of the defendants is that the defendant No. 1 is the owner of the suit land by was of inheritance and purchase and accordingly, SA Khatian No. 310 was recorded in the name of defendant No. 1 in respect of the suit land and the plaintiff never possessed the suit land and defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 4, sons of defendant No. 1, on behalf of defendant No.1, were possessing the suit land and the suit is false and fabricated and is to be dismissed.

5. The trial Court dismissed the suit by the judgment and decree dated 25-8-2004 and 31-8- 2004 respectively.

6. Being aggrieved thereby, the plaintiff as petitioner filed an application under section 115(1) of the CPC before this Court and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr. Md Abul Kashem Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the trial Court passed the impugned judgment and decree on the basis of mere surmises and conjectures resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He next submits that the plaintiff has succeeded in proving the case beyond reasonable doubt by adducing and producing evidence, both oral and documentary, which the trial Court did not take into consideration illegally. He points out that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land and was ousted illegally from it by the defendants for which the present suit was filed within time and the trial Court ought to have decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff. He submits that the rent receipts being documents of possession were produced before the Court as exhibits, showing the possession of the plaintiff and subsequent dispossession from the suit property was also proved by the deposition of plaintiff witnesses.

None appears to oppose the Rule.

8. I have heard the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner and perused the revisional application along with other materials on record. It appears that the plaintiff, who is the present petitioner, filed a suit for recovery of possession under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act being Title Suit No. 16 of 2003 in the Court of Senior Assistant .Judge, Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria impleading the opposite parties as defendants. The plaintiff claims that on the death of his father Fazar Ali, he by way of amicable partition, got the suit land and BS khatian was recorded in his name after which he took loan from Bangladesh Krishi Bank and was also paying rent and taxes regularly but thereafter he was dispossessed from the suit land by the defendants illegally.

9. The defendants on the other hand claimed that the plaintiff never possessed the suit land and the sons of defendants No.1, being defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 4, were possessing the suit land.

<u>10. All that a plaintiff in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act is required to prove is his possession and dispossession within six months next before the institution of the suit. Before a person call come under section 9 he has to show that he had actual physical possession of the immovable property from which he was dispossessed without his consent by the defendant within six months prior to the institution of the suit. Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act is concerned with physical possession and not with title. It appears that the plaintiffs witnesses, though could not mention the numbers of dag and khatian, categorically mentioned the date of possession and dispossession of the plaintiff from the suit land. The trial Court observed that most of the plaintiff witnesses could not remember the birth date of their children and their marriage dates along with date of the last Eid, for which their statements regarding the date of possession and dispossession of the plaintiff from the suit land can be tutored, which they memorised and deposed before the Court. The fact that the plaintiff witnesses did not remember the important dates of their lives and only one remembers the date of possession and dispossession of the plaintiff from the suit land brought doubt on the mind of the trial Court on the credibility of the deposition of plaintiff witnesses. In a suit for recovery of possession under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such a suit, the person dispossessed without the consent or otherwise than in due course of law, can claim for recovery of the possession.</u>

11. It appears in the present case that the claim of the plaintiff regarding possession and subsequent dispossession from the suit land by the defendants was proved by the deposition of his witnesses along with other documentary evidence like rent receipts, showing possession of the plaintiff. The fact that the plaintiff witnesses could not outright disclose the dates of their marriages and the birthdays of children while being cross-examined, cannot lead to the conclusion that their statements regarding the dates of possession and dispossession of the plaintiff from .the suit land are turtord and cannot be relied upon.

12. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the view that the trial Court did not apply its judicial mind in dealing with the matter and passed the judgment on the basis of mere surmises and conjectures. The materials presented before the trial Court were not taken into consideration in its proper perspective.

13. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree dated 25-8-2004 and 31-8-2004 respectively passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria in the Title Suit No. 16 of 2003 dismissing the suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act are set aside. The trial Court is directed to take steps to restore the possession to the plaintiff in accordance with law.

Send down the lower Court records along with a copy of the judgment and order to the Court concerned.

End.

lawyer:

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated May 4, 2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1227 of 1999).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: <u>This petition for leave to appeal has been filed against the judgment of May 4,2005 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1227 of 1999 making the Rule absolute upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated March 21, 1999 of the 3rd Court of Additional District Judge, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 272 of 1982 allowing the same upon reversing the judgment and decree dated October 31, 1992 of the 3rd Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge) Dhaka in Title Suit No. 577 of 1980 decreeing the same and thereby restraining defendants permanently from entering into the 'B' schedule land or to dispossess the plaintiff therefrom or to interfere with the possession of the plaintiff in the land shown in 'B' schedule. The suit was filed seeking a decree for permanent injunction in respect of the land described in schedule ‘B' attached to the plaint.</u>

2. Plaintiff's case is that land in suit belonged to Chaitan Sheikh who died before the CS operation leaving 4 sons and a daughter, that the plaintiff has purchased 85 decimals of land from one of the sons of said Chaitan Sheikh (Naimuddin Sheikh son of Chaitan Sheikh) and possessing the same. It is the contention of the plaintiff that defendant No. 1 claiming to have purchased land from the heirs of Chaitan Sheikh having had tried to disturb his possession, he is constrained to file the suit seeking the relief of a decree for permanent injunction.

3. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement stating, inter alia, that the land in suit belonged to Chaitan Sheikh who died leaving 4 sons and a daughter, that he has purchased 1.07 acres of land from the sons (Hakim uddin and Sheikh Salim) of Chaitan Sheikh and is possessing the same and that also using a pond in the suit plot, that the plaintiff has created false document in respect of the land claimed by him but he did not get the possession, that the plaintiff has filed the suit making untrue statements and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The trial Court decreed the suit on the finding that plaintiff has proved his prima facie title in the land in suit and also has established his exclusive possession in the land in suit.

5. The contesting defendant No. 1 went on appeal. The appellate Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court on the finding that plaintiff has failed to prove his exclusive possession in the land in suit and that suit is not maintainable as both the parties have claimed title to the land in suit.

6. At one stage of the proceeding, in all probability at the appellate stage, plaintiff having had died his heirs moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained Rule. It was contended before the High Court Division that the appellate Court on misreading of the evidence of the parties decreed the suit and that finding of the appellate Court that plaintiff failed to prove his exclusive possession is based on misreading of the evidence as well as non consideration of the material evidence, that the appellate Court upon misconception of law held that the suit is not maintainable.

7. As against the aforesaid contention of the petitioners it was contended on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 that the suit as framed was not maintainable since complicated question of title was involved and, as such, appellate Court was quite correct in dismissing the suit, that in the absence of ascertainment of the respective shares of the heirs of Chaitan Sheikh and consequent thereupon in the absence of ascertainment of the share of the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 in the land purchased by them from the heirs of Chaitan Sheikh the suit for permanent injunction was not maintainable, the appellate Court has committed no error in dismissing the suit.

<u>8. The High Court Division on consideration of the materials on record, particularly the documents produced by the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1, arrived at the conclusion, "Only because the defendant has produced certain documents and claimed title to the suit land cannot disentitle the plaintiffs to a decree for permanent injunction if the plaintiffs are successful in proving prima facie title and exclusive possession, if the exclusive possession of the plaintiffs is established, suit for granting a decree for permanent injunction shall lie and a party not in possession may resort to the remedy available to him by law but that should not be a ground for dismissing a suit for permanent injunction". The High Court Division noticed that plaintiff claimed 0.85 acre of land out of 1.27 acres of land on the basis of the kabala dated May 5, 1953 and the defendant No. 1 claiming the land which belonged to Chaitan Sheikh on the basis of the kabalas which are mostly subsequent to plaintiffs kabala of 1953. The High Court Division also noticed that defendant No. 1 produced 2 kabalas which are of prior years than the kabala of the plaintiff and that by the said kabalas defendant No. 1 has purchased 0.47 acre of land out of 1.27 acres of land. The High Court Division noticed that the plaintiff in respect of his land got the record of right prepared in his name and is paying rent and the plaintiff also lead oral evidence in support of his title and possession in the land in suit. The High Court Division-on consideration of the documents filed by the plaintiff held, "The said documentary evidence therefore, proved plaintiff's prima facie title to the suit land". The High Court Division in the background of the materials on record and on consideration thereof observed that the appellate Court misread the oral evidence and misconstrued the pleading of the parties and ignored the vital piece of evidence i.e. the SA khatian prepared in the name of the plaintiff and the rent receipt showing payment of rent by the plaintiff, and thereupon held that the appellate Court, on misreading and misconstruing the evidence, made the finding that the plaintiff has not proved his exclusive possession, that upon reading of the schedule of Exhibits-K (plaintiff's document) and D (defendant's document) it is seen that the plaintiff's claim of possession is more acceptable than that of the defendant and the aforesaid 2 documents support the prima facie title of the plaintiff in the land of CS plot No. 306. The High Court Division observed that these vital documents were not considered by the appellate Court and, in the background of the aforesaid state of the matter, the High Court Division held, "It can therefore be concluded that the final court of fact arrived at the finding on possession upon misreading the oral evidence and totally ignoring the documentary evidence indicating plaintiff's exclusive possession in the suit land" and the High Court Division further held that the appellate Court "without properly assessing the evidence in the light of the pleadings of the parties and also ignoring the documentary evidence which has resulted in an error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice".</u>

9. Since the consideration of the evidence by the lower appellate Court was not a proper one or, in other words, as observed by the High Court Division there was non consideration and misreading of the evidence by the lower appellate Court, the High Court Division scrutinised the evidence of the PWs and DWs and thereupon noticed that the DWs 1,2 and 3 supported the possession of the plaintiff in the land in suit and that particularly DW 2 in his cross-examination stated that the pond in plot No. 306 is possessed by the plaintiff. The High Court Division also noticed that DW 1 admitted that no record of right was prepared in his name and that he did not pay any rent in respect of the land in suit and thereupon held that the said fact shows that "the defendants have no possession in the suit land". On the aforesaid findings the High Court Division made the Rule absolute.

<u>10. We have heard the learned Advocate-on- record. The settled principle of law is that in a suit seeking a decree for permanent injunction the plaintiff is required to establish his prima facie title in the land as regard to which he is claiming a decree for permanent injunction and exclusive possession of the land as to which the relief of permanent injunction is sought. The trial Court decreed the suit on the finding that plaintiff has prima facie title in the land in suit and he is in exclusive possession. The judgment of the trial Court is based on consideration of the documentary as well as Oral evidence of the parties. The appellate Court, as it is seen, has reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court on misreading of the evidence as well as on non consideration of the vital evidence. In that state of the matter the High Court Division instead of sending back the case to the appellate Court for disposal on consideration of the evidence on record had quite in accordance with law considered the evidence of the parties which was sufficient to dispose of the suit and thereupon held that the plaintiff has prima facie title in the land in suit and he is in exclusive possession of the land in suit. The learned Advocate on-record failed to point out that the consideration of evidence made by the High Court Division in the background of non-consideration and misreading of the evidence by the appellate Court was erroneous in any respect and the said Division was in error in arriving at the finding as to title and possession of plaintiff and thereupon in setting aside the judgment of the appellate Court.</u>

11. In that state of the matter we do not find any substance in the petition.

Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
SM Enamul Hoque Deputy Attorney-General---For the Appellant. 
SN Munir Advocate ---For the Respondent
parties:
Bangladesh ----- Appellant 
Vs.
Shamsur Rahman and ors ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Siddiqur Rahman Miah J: This appeal at the instance of the defendant No. 2 Bangladesh Government is directed against the judgment and decree dated 27-6-1979 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Khulna, in Title Suit No. 481 of 1975 decreeing the suit.

2. The respondent No. 1 as plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title to the suit land measuring 1.03 acres of land in plot Nos. 1883, 1884, 1887 and 1890 of CS Khatian Nos. 31, 33 and 144 under Mouza Maheswarpasha in the District of Khulna.

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the suit land originally belonged to proforma defendant No. 3 Nitya Nanda Munshi and defendant No. 4 Nani Gopal Munshi who while in possession of the suit land sold out the same to the plaintiff Shamsur Rahman by two registered sale deeds-on receipt of proper consideration money; that the plaintiff  for fear of creditors got those sale deeds in the benami of his close friend defendant No.1 Ahmed Reza and that the entire consideration money was paid by the plaintiff out of his own fund. It is further stated that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land in his own right since the time of purchase; that the plaintiff has paid rents in respect of the suit land to the government and got dakhilas; That on 4th June 1975 the plaintiff in order to pay tent to the Tahsil office went with all of his relevant papers of the suit land but he accidentally lost the original kabala deed and some dakhilas on his way; that the defendant No. 1 was always in agreement to effect a deed of release in favour of the plaintiff on and when necessary, that on the 25th June, 1975 one Yakub Ali, the then Manager of defendant No.1, met with the plaintiff at Maheswarpasha and claimed title of the suit land on behalf on the defendant No. 1 and under such situation the plaintiff has been compelled to file this suit for declaration of his title in the suit land.

4. Defendant No.2 namely, the Government, of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, has appeared and contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the allegations of the plaint on material points and contending, inter alia, that the plaintiff has got no cause of action to file the suit; that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner; that the suit is bad for defect of parties; that the suit is hit by the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and that the suit is barred by limitation. The further case of the plaintiff is that he never purchased the suit land in the benami of defendant No. 1 nor did he ever exercise possession over any land in suit. It is further stated that the defendant No. 1 Ahmed Reza and his brother are the residents of Calcutta and thus the suit property has been declared abandoned property; that the plaintiff has filed the suit with a malafide motive falsely claiming ownership on the land, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. At the trial, the plaintiff has examined 3 witnessed, PW 1 is Sheikh Shamsur Rahman who is the plaintiff himself, PW 2 Momin Box is contiguous land holder, PW 3, Noni Gopal Munshi is one of the executants of the sale deed. The plaintiff also filed certified copy of the Kabala deed dated 29-6-1965 executed by Nitya Nanda Munshi in favour of Ahmed Reza which is marked Exhibit-3, certified copy of the kabala deed executed by Nani Gopal Munshi in favour of Reza which is marked Exhibit- 3(a), the copies of the dakhilas marked Exhibit 19(a) to 19( c) series and also filed the certified copies of the khatians which are marked exhibits 2(a) to 2(c) of his contention.

6. The contesting defendant No. 2 Government examined no witness nor did refile any document in support of his contention. The learned Subordinate Judge, Khulna on the pleading of the parties framed following issues:

1.	Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2.     Is the suit property valued and sufficiently stamped.

3.	Is the defendant No. 1 benamder of the plaintiff?

4.	Has the plaintiff any right, title, interest and possession in the suit land?

5.	Is the suit hit by the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act?

6.	Is the plaintiff entitled to get any decree for declaration of his title as has been prayed for?

7. The learned Subordinate Judge by his judgment and decree dated 27-6-1979 decreed the suit decreeing the title of the plaintiff in the suit land.

8. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 27-6-1979, the defendant No.2 has preferred this appeal before this Court.

9. Mr SM Enamul Hoque, the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the appellant, submits that the defendant No. 1 was a real purchaser and the plaintiff has got no title and interest in the suit land. He further submits that the Court below wrongly held that the plaintiff was the purchaser of the suit land and the defendant No.1 was his benamder; that the defendant No. 1 is resident of Calcutta and the suit property has been declared as abandoned property and that the plaintiff has filed the suit with malafide intention. He further submits that the learned Subordinate Judge was not justified in passing the impugned judgment.

10. The Deputy Attorney-General refers the decision in the case of Mahmudul Hoque vs Md Golap Miah and others reported in 41 DLR 314, the case of Rupe Jahan Begum and others vs Lutfe Ali Chowdhury & others reported in 49 DLR (AD) 73, the case of Munjurur Rahman vs Naimur Rahman reported in 50 DLR 266 in support of his contention.

11. Mr SM Munir, the learned Advocate for the respondent, submits that Shamsur Rahman is a real purchaser under the sale deeds; that the defendant No.1 Ahmed Reza was his mere Benamder and that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land mutating his name and paying rent to the government. He further submits that the entire consideration money of this transaction has been paid by the plaintiffs; that the learned Subordinate Judge, Khulna, on consideration of the material evidence on record decreed the suit; that the impugned judgment and decree do not suffer from any illegality and legal infirmity which was completely justified.

12. The submissions of the learned Advocates of both the parties necessitate close scrutiny of the impugned judgment in other to ascertain whether the learned Subordinate Judge is justified in passing the impugned judgment dated 27-6-1979.

13. The main question that came up for our consideration in this suit was about the title of the suit. The plaintiff claims that he purchased the suit land from Nitya Nanda Munshi and Noni Gopal Munshi in the benami of his close friend, Ahmed Reza who is defendant No. 1 and he has been possessing the same mutating his name and paying rent to the government.

14. The appellant defendant No.1, Government, on the other hand, denying the contention of the plaintiff pleads that the plaintiff never purchased the suit land in the benami of defendant No. 1 Ahmed Reza nor did he possess the suit land. The further contention of the appellant-defendant is that defendant No. 1 Ahmed Reza and his brother were the residents of Calcutta for which their properties were declared abandoned after their departure from this country.

15. In order to ascertain the burden of proof in this case we may refer section 101 of the Evidence Act wherein the burden of proof has been explained.

Section 101 runs this:

"101: Burden of proof: Whoever desires any Court to give judgment as of facts which he asserts must prove that those facts exist.

When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person. The burden of proof lies on the party who substantially asserts the affirmative of the issue and not upon the party who denies it.

Moreover, it is but reasonable and just that the suitor who relies upon the existence of a fact, should be called upon to prove his own case.

16. The party on whom the onus of proof lies must, in order to succeed, establish a prima facie case. He cannot, on failure to do so take advantage of the weakness of his adversary's case. He must succeed by the strength of his own right and the clearness of his own proof.

17. In the instant case, the plaintiff asserts that he purchased the suit land in the benami of his close friend defendant No. 1 Ahmed Reza. On the other hand, the contesting defendant No. 2 Government asserts that Ahmed Reza and his brother were the residents of Calcutta and after their departure, the suit land has been declared abandoned property. In this case, both the plaintiff and the contesting defendant are to prove their respective part. We have to consider the submissions to arrive at a correct decision.

But the question regarding the benami transaction of a sale can arise between a party to a deed and another who is con-nominee not a party to it but puts a claim to be a beneficiary entitled to the property conveyed by the said deed. When a person asserts that particular transaction is a benami the onus in upon him to prove that the transaction is a benami one.

<u>18. The word "Benami" originates from Persia which consists of two words "be" and "nam" meaning no name that nameless which means that nominal owner is the "benamder". The inner meaning of "Benami" is that a purchaser desires to buy property but does not desire to buy in his own name but in the name of someone else. A benami transaction has been described briefly, as one in which the real owner of the property allows it to appear in the name of an ostensible owner under a sort of secret trust. This system of acquiring property is well known in our country for various reasons till 26 January, 1984 when the Land Reforms Ordinance was promulgated as the benami transaction gave rise to countless litigations which caste evil effect on the society. On coming into force of this Ordinance on 26 January, 1984 now no one is allowed to set upon his claim on the benami transaction. Since this Ordinance has no retrospective effect and as the suit was filed on 3-7- 1975 long before the pronouncement of the said Ordinance, so the suit is quite maintainable.</u>

19. In deciding the question as to whether a transaction is a benami one or not, certain ingredients in a benami transaction are required to be examined.

20. The law of benami transaction has long been settled. The judicial committee of the Privy Council in Gopeekrist Gossain vs Gungapershad Gossain (1854) 6 MIAA 53 was probably the first authority on the subject. Since then the superior Courts of this Subcontinent more or less followed the principles enunciated in the said case and certain other cases decided by the Privy Council. This Court in the case of Nurjahan Begum vs Mahmudur Rahman 34 DLR (AD) 61 traced the history of benami transaction and also the law propounded by the Privy Council for the following conclusion:

"In a benami transaction sources of purchase money is an important criteria (sic) but it is not conclusive, the initial presumption in the case of a transfer concluded by a registered deed is in favour of the person whose name appears as the transferee in the deed, but this presumption is rebuttable. Source of consideration money though an important criteria in a benami transaction but in the absence of any unambiguous ownership consideration of other relevant circumstances becomes important in a case where ownership is disputed. The disputed question of benami cannot be determined only on the consideration of source of consideration money, and it becomes incumbent for the Court to fall back upon the surrounding circumstances of the transaction, the position of the parties and the relationship to each other, the motive which could govern their actions, but their subsequent conduct including their dealings and the enjoyment of the property become relevant factors for consideration.

21. In the case of Bilas Kunwar vs Desraj Ranjit Singh (1915) LR 42 IA 202, the Privy Council while adopting the principle as laid down in Gopeekrist Gossain's case that the criterion in benami cases is the source of money with which the consideration was paid, made an important qualification, in that the source of purchase money is only to be the criterion in the absence of all other relevant circumstances. Among other circumstances, possession of the property has been held to be very important the Privy Council in Imambandi Begum vs Kumleshwari Pershad (1886) LR 13 IA 160 held as under:

"Where there are benami transactions and the question is who was the real owner, the actual possession or receipt of rents on the property is most important.

22. In the case of Ram Narain vs Mohammad Hadi (1898) LR 26 IA 38 the Privy Council laid stress on the factum of possession of the property and the collection of rents. Incidentally, it may be mentioned that in a disputed case of benami custody of the documents is relevant factor to be considered.

23. In the cited decisions we find that though the question whether a particular sale is benami or not is largely one of fact, and for determining this question, no absolute formula or acid tests uniformly applicable in all situations, can be laid, down; yet, in weighing the probabilities and for gathering the relevant indicia, the Courts are usually guided by these circumstances (1) the source from which the purchase money came; (2) the nature and possession of the property after the purchase; (3) motive, if any, for giving the transaction a benami colour, (4) the position of the parties and the relationship, if any, between the claimant and the alleged benamder, (5) the custody of the title deeds after the sale and (6) the conduct of the parties concerned in dealing with the property after the sale.

24. It is the definite case of the plaintiff that the plaintiff Shamsur Rahman purchased under those sale deeds and that defendant No. 1 was his mere benamder and that the plaintiff who has been in possession of the suit land in his own right and it is the plaintiff who paid the entire consideration money for those transactions.

25. The plaintiff in order to prove his case has filed certain papers Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 series and examined as many as 3 witnessed on his side including himself as PW 1. The papers Exhibits-1 to 1 (e) are the dakhilas granted by the government tahsilder in respect of the suit land. From those dakhilas, it appears that defendant Nos. 3 and 4 before their sale of suit land by virtue of the sale deeds Exhibits 3 and 4 paid rent to the government in respect of the suit land. Thus it appears that the rent receipts filed by the plaintiff were definitely lying with the original owners namely, defendant Nos. 3 and 4, who handed over the same to the plaintiff at the time of the impugned sale. The papers under Exhibits 2 to 2(c) are the CS and SA khatians in respect of the suit land. These Khatians are also handed over to the plaintiff by the vendors namely, defendant Nos. 3 and 4, at the time of their sale of the suit land by the sale deeds Exhibit 3 and 3(a). The plaintiff while deposing as PW 1 has made statements in unambiguous terms that he purchased the suit land from defendant Nos. 3 and 4 by the sale deeds in the benami of defendant No. 1 who happened to be his close friend. He further deposed that the motive of his benami purchase was due to fear of the creditors. The PW 1 has further asserted that it is he who paid the entire consideration money of the transaction and it is he who has been possessing the suit land in his own right. Such statement of PW I on the point of benami purchase of the suit land and possession over the same had been corroborated by PWs 2 and 3 almost in the same agreements. PW 2 Momin Box has made statements that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land for 12/13 years and that defendant No. 2 or anybody else never possessed the same. We do not find any reasons to disbelieve the evidence of PW 2. The PW 3 is Noni Gopal Munshi who is defendant No. 4 in the suit. He is also the executant of the kabala Exhibit 3(a). Thus PW 3 has made a categorical statement that the suit land belonged to him and his brother. They sold out the land to the plaintiff who paid them entire consideration money. He further deposed that he sold out his share on receipt of Taka 5,000 from the plaintiff who got the deed in the benami of defendant No. 1 Ahmed Reza who was his close friend; that his brother also sold out his share to the plaintiff for Taka 4925 by a different kabala and that the plaintiff got such kabala in the benami of defendant No.1.

26. We do not find any damaging contradiction in his statement even during his cross-examination so as to impair plaintiffs case of benami purchase in any way. Thus not getting such unequivocal assertion from the mouth of PW 3, one of the vendors, about the benami purchase we are of the opinion that the plaintiffs case of the benami purchase from the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 by virtue of the sale deeds Exhibits 3 and 3(a) has been established beyond reasonable doubt and moreover, the plaintiff's possession over the suit land is not found to have been controverted by the defence in any way.

27. The contesting appellant government has neither examined any witness nor has submitted any scrap of paper to substantiate his contention. The contesting appellant only filed the written statement and such statement without any oral or documentary evidence has not been proved. The contesting defendant has not even filed any paper regarding declaration of suit land as abandoned property. The contesting defendant pleaded in vague terms that the disputed property was owned as possessing by defendant No. 1 and his brother and that the defendant No. 1 and his brother being residents of Calcutta, their properties in Khulna town were declared as abandoned property and vested in the government but no document and oral evidence was adduced in support of his contention, in view of the facts and circumstances of the case, the defence has very shockingly failed to prove the case of acquisition of property as abandoned property and other burden reposed on him.

28. From the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record available from the plaintiffs side as has been divulged in our above discussion and observations, we without the least hesitation to hold the view that all the ingredients of benami transaction have been proved by the plaintiff as the real purchaser of the suit land under the sale deeds Exhibits 3 and 3(a) from the defendant Nos. 3 and 4; that the defendant No. 1 Ahmed Reza is his mere benamder and that the plaintiff has been in possession of the suit land in his own right as purchaser under the defendant Nos. 3 and 4. Thus, from what has been stated above we are of the view that the plaintiff has got good right, title and interest in the suit land and the burden on the plaintiff has been successfully proved. On the other hand, the contention of the contesting defendant has been hopelessly disproved.

29. The impugned judgment and decree dated 27-6-1979 passed by the trial Court are well reasoned backed by sufficient oral and documentary evidence which cannot be interfered with.

30. In view of the discussion made hereinbefore and after giving our anxious consideration to all pros and cons after taking note of catena of decisions of the Apex Court, we are of the considered view that the appeal is devoid of any substance and the same is liable to be dismissed.

31. In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 27-6-1979 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Khulna in Title Suit No. 481 of 1975 is affirmed.

Send down the LCR expeditiously.

End.
