parties:
Rezia Khatun Chowdhurani -------- Petitioners
Vs.
   Shamir Kumar Chowdhury and others  -------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
The petitioners obtained these Rules from a judgment of reversal.

The predecessor of the petitioners late Md Ishaq Ali (the plaintiff) instituted Title Suit No. 31 of 1970 on 26th March, 1970 for Specific Performance of Contract against the opposite parties (the defendant) in respect of the suit lands (the property) which on transfer was renumbered as Title Suit No. 68 of 1983.

2. Short facts of the plaint case are as follows: the suit property consisting of corrugated iron sheet- roofed two huts towards west and three huts towards the east bhiti belonged to Surendra Chandra Chowdhury. On the death of Surendra Chandra Chowdhury, his son Samir Kumar Chowdhury. (the vendor) inherited the suit property as his heir and legatee of a will. Samir Chowdhury entered into a contract with the plaintiff for sale of the suit property on 30th September, 1965 at consideration of Taka 17,000. It was provided, inter alia, in the deed of contract that out of the total consideration, Taka 6,000 would remain with the piaintiff on account of expenses for arranging a valid employment voucher in the United Kingdom for Samir Kumar Chowdhury, a passport, air ticket, etc. for UK to be procured within five months from the date of execution of the deed and the balance consideration of amount of Taka 11,000 would be paid at the time of execution of the sale deed after taking necessary income tax clearance and permission and possession the property would be delivered on that day. Samir Kumar Chowdhury put necessary signatures for obtaining income tax clearance certificate. In the meantime, the then Sub-Divisional Officer, Habigonj issued a notice for acquisition of the suit property under the Defence of Pakistan Rules and evicted the plaintiff and the opposite party No. I therefrom. Plaintiff and Samir Kumar Chowdhury filed Writ Petition No. 99 of 1966 challenging the said acquisition of the suit property. Samir Kumar Chowdhury also prosecuted Civil Revision No. 851 of 1966 in this Court in connection with the grant of probate of the will. Plaintiff could not procure the employment voucher for Samir Kumar Chowdhury and accordingly, he requested the plaintiff to adjust the expenses of the litigation out of the said amount of Taka 6,000. Plaintiff accordingly, spent Taka 1,734 towards the expenses of the Writ Petition and the Civil Revision. The Writ Petition was allowed on 9th February, 1967. The plaintiff thereupon paid Taka 11,000 by executing a promissory note on 5th Agrahayan 1372 BS and put the plaintiff into possession of a portion of the suit property. It was provided that the said amount would be adjusted towards the consideration money but if for any reason the parties decided not to execute the kabala, then Samir Kumar Chowdhury would refund the said amount of Taka 11,000. Plaintiff thereupon filed Money Suit No.10 of 1968 as the limitation of the promissory note was expiring but the suit was dismissed on technical ground. As the sale deed could not be executed within the stipulated time of 5 months, Samir Kumar Chowdhury executed a memorandum on 30th July, 1966 to the effect that the period of 5 months as disclosed in the deed of contract would start from the date of disposal of the Writ Petition and the Civil Revision. Syeda Sirajunnessa Khatun and Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, opposite parties No.2 and 3(defendants), were husband and wife and lived near the suit property who were all through aware of the contract. They influenced Samir Kumar Chowdhury who issued a notice upon the plaintiff on 15th October, 1966 alleging false and concocted allegations. Thereupon, the defendants collusively procured permission from the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet for sale of the suit property and obtained a sale deed from Samir Kumar Chowdhury.

3. Syeda Sirajunnessa Khatun (the defendant) instituted Title Suit No. 157 of 1977 for declaration of title and recovery of possession of the suit property against the plaintiff which on transfer was renumbered as Title Suit No. 93 of 1982. Her case is that Samir Kumar Chowdhury proposed to sell the suit property and upon negotiation, she agreed to purchase the same at a consideration of Taka 5,000 and on receipt of Taka 3,000 as advance Samir Kumar Chowdhury executed a deed of contract dated 23rd September, 1963 and promised to execute and register a sale deed after obtaining probate certificate. Towards January, 1966 she came to know that an acquisition proceeding was started in respect of the suit property and subsequently, the plaintiff trespassed into one room of the suit property. Samir Kumar Chowdhury told her that the plaintiff obtained a deed of contract on 30th September, 1965 upon false pretext and assured her to execute a kabala within a reasonable time. After disposal of the Writ Petition and the Civil Revision cases, Samir Kumar Chowdhury executed the kabala on 15th April, 1968 in favour of the defendant on taking necessary permission and income tax clearance certificate. He also handed over possession of the suit property except one room where the plaintiff was in illegal occupation. Thereupon, the defendant along with Samir Kumar Chowdhury filed a suit for permanent injunction against the plaintiff and obtained a decree. The plaintiff had knowledge about the defendant's deed of contract and even then he entered into the deed of contract on 30th September, 1965. The Memos dated 19th October, 1965 and 31st July, 1966 said to have been executed by Samir Kumar Chowdhury were forged and collusive. The plaintiff along with his brother Ershad Ali was influential persons and taking advantage of lawlessness after the liberation of Bangladesh forcibly entered into the suit property and evicted the tenants and the defendant.

4. The defence case of the defendant is the plaint case of the latter suit and the defence case of the latter suit is the plaint case of the earlier suit. Samir Kumar Chowdhury also contested the suit for Specific Performance of Contract jointly with the defendant. The learned subordinate Judge heard both the suits analogously and by judgment and order dated 18th September, 1986 decreed the suit for Specific performance of Contract of the plaintiff and dismissed the suit for declaration of title of the defendant. On appeal by the defendants being Title Appeals Nos. 26 and 27 of 1987 the learned Additional District Judge, Habiganj by judgment and order dated 3Ist August, 1985 dismissed the suit for Specific Performance of Contract of the plaintiff and decreed the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession of the defendants. The heirs of the plaintiff thereupon obtained these Rules.

5. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, argues that the Court of appeal below erred in law in dismissing the suit for Specific Performance of Contract on misreading Exhibits 1,2 and X which has occasioned a failure of justice. Learned Advocate further argues that the Court of appeal below erred in law in assuming that the time is the essence of the contract while dismissing the suit for specific performance. He finally submits that the Court of appeal below has committed error of law resulting an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in allowing the appeals without reversing all the findings arrived at by the trial Court and therefore, the judgment of the Court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal.

6. The learned Subordinate Judge while decreeing the suit for specific performance of contract observed that Samir Kumar Chowdhury delivered possession of the suit property to the plaintiff in pursuance of execution of the deed of contract (Exhibit 1) in September, 1965, that the deed of contract (Exhibit A) executed between the defendant and Samir Kumar Chowdhury on 23rd September, 1963 was a collusive, fraudulent and ante-dated one, that Samir Kumar Chowdhury in a deceitful manner created the deed of sale (Exhibit G) on 15th April, 1968 in favour of defendant Syeda Sirajunnessa Khatun in order to achieve his selfish gain, that the possession of the plaintiff Md Ishaq Ali has been proved satisfactorily and thus the alleged story of dispossession of the defendant by the plaintiff Md Ishaq Ali is not a believable one, that the defendant Syeda Sirajunessa Khatun collusively created Exhibit G with full knowledge of the previous con- tract in respect of the suit property with the plaintiff Md Ishaque Ali and that the suit for Specific Performance of Contract is not barred by limitation.

7. Before I meet the points argued by Mr AJ Mohammad Ali and the findings arrived at by the learned Subordinate Judge, I would like to refer the relevant portions of the deed of contract Exhibit 1, executed on 30th September, 1965. It is provided that the purchaser would procure the genuine employment voucher for UK for the vendor, his international passport and air ticket and hand over them to the vendor within 5 months from the date of execution of the deed, that if the plaintiff failed to procure employment voucher, passport, etc. within the period of five months, then the contract would automatically be void and cancelled, that the purchaser (plaintiff) after procuring necessary income tax clearance certificate and permissions from the authority at his own cost and expense would pay the balance amount of Taka 11000 and then the vendor would execute the sale deed and hand over possession of the property. These are conditions precedent for execution of a valid sale deed. The plaintiff promised to perform his part of obligation within five months for getting a sale deed in respect of the suit property. Both the parties having treated the procurement of employment voucher, passport and air ticket as an element in the contract, the contract could not be completed till the said employment 'voucher, passport and air ticket had been procured and made over to the vendor within five months of the date of contract. In the alternative, it may be said that the contract would be matured if the plaintiff performed his part of the obligation. The vendor reserved the right to repudiate the contract on failure of the plaintiff to perform his part of obligation. There is no material on record that the vendor has waived the plaintiffs part of obligation. On looking at the contract it can be inferred that the vendor never intends to bind himself to anything, till the plaintiff performs his part of obligation. The transaction between the parties cannot be equated as simple contract for sale of immovable property as is normally done by fixing a price, payment of advance and the execution of the deed at a later date on receipt of the balance consideration.

8. It would appear from Exhibit 1 that no earnest money was paid to the vendor by the plaintiff and that plaintiff had assumed all the responsibilities for getting the deed and on his failure to perform the obligations, it was clearly provided that the deed of contract would stand rescinded and that the vendor would be entitled to sell the suit property to any other person. There is no statement that on the day of execution of the contract the vendor had handed over possession of any portion of the suit property, On a plain reading of this contract, I am of the view that it may be termed as a memorandum of understanding for transfer of the suit property in the event of fulfilment of certain obligations by the plaintiff Md  Ishaq Miah within the stipulated period of 5 months. Mst  Rezia Khatun (PW 1) admitted that Md Ishaq Miah failed to procure the employment voucher for Samir Kumar Chowdhury, his international passport and air ticket and therefore, he did not spend any money out of Taka 6,000 preserved with him for the said purpose. There was no concluded contract between the plaintiff and the vendor, for which, the vendor could have been compelled to perform his part of obligation in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract. In this connection, I would like to refer section 4 of the Specific Relief Act which reads as follows:

"Savings: Except where it is herein other- wise expressly enacted, nothing in this Act shall .be deemed.

(a) to give any right to relief in respect of any agreement which is not a contract;

(b) to deprive any person of any right to relief, other than specific performance, which he may have under any contract; or

(c) to affect the operation of the (Registration Act, 1908) on documents."

9. The term "agreement" is defined in section 2(e) of the Contract Act, as every promise and every set of promises, forming the consideration for each other. A promise according to section 2(b) of the Contract Act is a proposal accepted. A proposal is said to be accepted when a person to whom it is made signifies his assent thereto, According to section 2(a) of the Contract Act, when one person signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other to such act or abstinence, he is said to make a proposal, An agreement is enforceable by law is a contract within the meaning of section, 2(h) of the Contract Act. An agreement not enforceable by law is said to be void under section 2(j) of the Contract Act. All contracts are agreement but all agreements are not a contract.

10. Under the clause (a) of section 4 of the Specific Relief Act, the provisions of the Act do not give any right to relief in respect of any agreement which is not a contract. The effect of the clause thus is to exclude from its operation of void and unlawful agreements, all imperfect obligations do not arise out of contracts, such as, moral, social and religious, and all incomplete agreements. In order to obtain specific performance there must be a concluded contract which is complete. The terms of the contract must be precise and certain and there must be no ambiguity. Voidable agreements, however, are not excluded from the operation, inasmuch as, according to the definition of voidable contract in section 2(i) of the Contract Act, such agreements are enforceable by law at the option of one or more of the parties to the contract. Sections 11-13 of the Contract Act explain the terms used in these void agreements. An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void according to section 56 of the Contract Act. Similarly, a contract to do an act afterwards becoming impossible or unlawful is void when the act becomes impossible and unlawful (section 57) where persons reciprocally promise, firstly, to do certain things which are legal, and, secondly, under specified circumstances, to certain other things which are illegal, the first set of promises is a contract but the second is a void agreement.

11. Where a party seeks to enforce specific per formance of contract, the Court must be satisfied that there is a concluded contract, in fact, that the contract so concluded is not incomplete by reason that the parties have failed to agree, expressly or by implication, on some essential matter, that the contract is precise and certain, or, in other words, that although all essential matters have been dealt with there is no such uncertainty and vagueness that exact performance cannot be ordered. Thus A offered to purchase a house on certain terms, possession to be given on or before 1st January, 2001. B agreed to the terms and said he would give possession on the 1st March, 2001. There was a variance between the terms of the proposal and those of the acceptance, and therefore, no contract arose.

<u>12. Sub-section (2) of section 6 of the Contract Act prescribes that a proposal is revoked by lapse of time prescribed in such proposal for its acceptance, or if no time is so prescribed by lapse of reasonable time, without communication of the acceptance. It is also clear that the contracts that are incomplete and not final i.e. where the proposal has not been converted into a promise by an absolute acceptance, cannot be specifically enforced. Reference in this connection is the case of Koylash Chandra Doss and others vs Tariney Charan Singhee and another, ILR 10 Calcutta, 588. A contract which is contingent upon the permission of the Court, is not a complete contract and cannot be specifically enforced. A contract is said to be completed on consideration of the subject matter, the parties to the contract, the price, and the other terms. The general rule to grant equitable relief for specific performance is that the contract must be mutual in both the senses i.e. the contract must be of such a nature that a right arises from its terms in favour of either party against the other, while the corresponding obligation rests upon each towards the other and also that either party is entitled to the equitable remedy of a specific execution of such obligation against the other party. It is not sufficient that a valid and binding agreement exists and that an action of law for damages will lie in favour of either party for a breach of other, the peculiarly distinctive feature of the equitable doctrine is, that the remedial right to a specific perfonnance must be mutual. If from the nature or  form of the contract itself, from the relations of the parties, from the personal incapacity of one of them, or from any other cause, the agreement devolves no obligation upon one of the parties, or if it cannot be specifically enforced against him, then and for that reason he is not, in general, entitled to the remedy of a specific performance against his adversary party, although otherwise there may be no obstacle arising, either from the terms of the contract or from his personal status and relation to the enforcement of the relief against the latter individually.</u>

13. The learned Subordinate Judge has treated Exhibit 1 as a concluded contract and decreed the suit for specific performance in failing to consider that admittedly the plaintiff failed to perform his part of obligation by procuring the genuine employment voucher for the vendor Samir Kumar Chowdhury, the international passport, the traveling ticket from Dhaka to London, the income tax clearance certificate and the permission for transfer of property from the authority. These obligations are pre-conditioned for registration of a sale deed in favour of the plaintiff. He was fully aware that if he failed to perform his part of obligation, the vendor reserved his right to rescind the memorandum of understanding and/or the contract for selling the suit property and, in fact, on his failure to perform his part, the vendor had exercised his right by repudiating the contract by Exhibit C.

14. The plaintiff had full knowledge that the vendor Samir Kumar Chowdhury was not willing and ready to transfer the suit property in pursuance of Exhibit 1 as he failed to procure the vendor's employment voucher for UK within the stipulated period of five months and repudiated the contract by pointing out that as he failed to perform his part of obligation by procuring the employment voucher for United Kingdom, he was not under obligation to get a sale deed. In this connection the plaintiff stated in the plaint that after receipt of the notice, he wrote a letter to the vendor refuting the allegations and thereafter, the plaintiff kept quiet for some time as he was staying in London for a long time and he was depending upon the vendor for which in spite of passing long time he did not take shelter in the Court of law for registration of the deed. Mr Mahbubey Alam argues that even fit is assumed that there was a concluded contract, the suit having not been filed within a period of 3 years from the date of cancellation of the contract, the suit for specific performance is barred by limitation. Learned Advocate pointed out that in view of the admitted position of the case, there is no scope for entering into the merit of the matter. Learned Advocate pointed out that the plaintiff instituted the suit on 26th March, 1970 even after cancellation of the deed of contract of 15th October 1969. According to article 113 of the Limitation Act a suit for specific performance of a contract, the period of limitation is three years from "the date fixed for the performance, or, if no such date is fixed, when the plaintiff has notice that the performance is refused." The plaintiff had sufficient notice from Exhibit C that the vendor had refused to perform his part of the contract and despite that, he instituted the suit after 3 years of receipt of the notice for rescinding the contract. The learned Sub- ordinate Judge observed that the vendor Samir Kumar Chowdhury with a view to frustrate the contract issued the notice without cogent reason at the instance of Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, the husband of the defendant and therefore, the suit is not barred by limitation. This observation of the learned Subordinate Judge is based on a misconception of law. The period of 3 years from the date of cancellation of the contract expired on 14th October, 1969 and the plaintiff instituted the suit on 26th March, 1970 well beyond the period of limitation. Plaintiff's suit for Specific Performance is therefore, barred by limitation and on this ground alone his suit is liable to be dismissed. I find merit in the contention of Mr Mahbubey Alam.

15. To overcome the period of limitation, the plaintiff set up two swaranlipis said to have been executed by Samir Kumar Chowdhury, on 19th October, 1965 (Exhibit 2) and on 30th July, 1966 (Exhibit X). In Exhibit 2 it was stated that despite procurement of the vendor's valid employment voucher, the latter failed to execute a sale deed and delivered possession, that the plaintiff having sustained loss in procuring the necessary documents, the vendor would be entitled to Taka 9000 out of the balance consideration of 11,000 by deducting Taka 2000 and that the plaintiff would be entitled to get the deed registered through Court on payment of Taka 9,000. The plaintiff has introduced a third case in this Swaranlipi deviating from the admitted position of the matter, inasmuch as the plaintiff has failed to procure the vendor's employment voucher within the stipulated time or at a later stage. This shows that this swaranlipi has been created for the purpose of the suit. In Exhibit X it was stated that the period of 5 months mentioned in Exhibit 1 would be counted from the date of disposal of Writ Petition No. 99 of 1966 and Civil Revision No. 851 of 1966. This is also a collusive document in that if the vendor had extended the time fixed for the completion of the transaction he would not have rescinded the contract. The Court of appeal below on consideration of these Exhibits 2 and X was of the view that after the rescission of the contract by notice dated 15th October, 1966 Exhibit C, the plaintiff created these documents on blank stamp papers, inasmuch as the recitals in Exhibit 2 were not clear, that the plaintiff or his heirs had failed to procure the vendor's employment voucher and also failed to perform other obligations as per Exhibit 1, that if he had procured the voucher, passport, he ought to have offered the balance consideration but he did not, that the presence of signature of the vendor in one deed at the bottom proved that due to shortage of sufficient space his signature was put there and that these facts proved that these deeds were created on blank stamp papers.

16. In the notice, Exhibit C the vendor Samir Kumar Chowdhury requested the plaintiff to hand over all blank papers and partially filled up papers signed by him. This notice sufficiently indicated that at the time of execution of Exhibit 1, the plaintiff obtained the signatures of Samir Kumar Chowdhury on some blank stamp papers. In his written statement also he claims as such. Moreso, after rescission of the contract on 15th October, 1966, it is not a believable story that Samir Kumar Chowdhury would execute two swaranlipis on 19th November, 1965 and 30th July, 1966. This fact proved that the recitals in Exhibits 2 and X were created by the plaintiff on blank stamp papers and that the Court of appeal below was justified in holding that these were forged documents created by the plaintiff for the purpose of the suit. These findings of the Court of appeal below were based upon proper appreciation of the documentary evidence on record.

17. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Advocate has referred the cases of Jamshed Khodaram Irani vs Burjorji Dhunjibhat, 40 ILR (PC) 289, Jamshed Khodaram Irani vs Burjorji Dhunjibhat, 20 CWN 744 and Mahadeo Pros ad Agarwala vs Narain Chandra Chakrabarti 30 CLJ 224. Mr Mohammad Ali inadvertently has referred 40 ILR 289 which is corresponding to 20 CWN 744. In the case of Mahadeo Prosad Agarwala, a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court followed the views taken by their Lordships of the Privy Council in Jamshed Khodaram Irani. In Jamshed Khodaram Irani's case, by an agreement dated 8th July 1911, the defendant agreed to sell his interest in certain lands which he had on lease from the Secretary, State of India to the plaintiff for Rs. 85,000 of which Rs. 4,000 was paid on execution of the agreement, and it was agreed that the title was to be made marketable, and that Rs. 80,500 should be paid on execution of the deed of sale which was to be prepared and received within two months from the date of agreement, and Rs. 500 on the transfer of the land after the conveyance should be registered. There was a clause to the effect that if the purchaser did not pay the amount of purchase money within fixed period he should forfeit his right to the earnest money and the vendor should be at liberty to re-sale the property. The transaction cannot be completed within the stipulated time and accordingly, the defendant refused to execute the sale deed. The trial Court decreed the suit for specific performance. On appeal, the Bombay High Court reversed the finding and dismissed the suit. The point involved in that case was whether the time should be of the essence of the contract from what has passed between the parties. The Privy Council observed as follows:

"Prima facie, equity treats the importance of such time limits as being subordinate to the main purpose of the parties, and it will enjoin specific performance notwithstanding that from the point of view of a Court of Law the contract has not been literally performed by the plaintiff as regards the time limit specified. This is merely an illustration of the general principle of disregarding the letter for the substance which Courts of equity apply, when, for instance, they decree specific performance with compensation for a non-essential deficiency in subject-matter."

<u>18. Since the case of Mahadeo Prosad Agarwala has been decided relying upon the Privy Council decision, I need not refer the said decision, I do not dispute the proposition of law stated by their Lordships of the Privy Council that mere fixing a time for completing the contract did not by itself show that the time was intended by the parties to be the essence of the contract; nor did the clause fixing a time for payment of the balance of the consideration with a provision that the advance was to be forfeited on default in payment within the time so fixed show it was the intention of the parties that time should be the essence of the contract. In this case, as observed above, there was not a concluded contract, and the plaintiff admittedly failed to per- form his part of the obligation and lastly, he sat over his right even after the rescission of the contract. Therefore, I find substance in the contention of Mr Mahbubey Alam that the suit for specific performance of contract is barred by limitation.</u>

19. Let us consider the other suit instituted by the defendant Syeda Sirajunnessa Khatun. Admittedly, in pursuance of the deed of contract dated 23rd September, 1963, Samir Kumar Chowdhury after taking necessary permission from the authority and on obtaining Income tax clearance certificate, transferred the suit property to the defendant by a registered deed dated 15th April, 1968 (Exhibit G). The learned Subordinate Judge observed that the contract Exhibit A was an ante-dated one, inasmuch as the stamp in the deed was purchased in the name of Adam Ali and that the explanation given by DW Abdur Rahman Chowdhury (DW 2) was not satisfactory" The Court of appeal below believed the said contract and observed that Samir Kumar Chowdhury wrote the said deed himself and then he put his signature at the top and the bottom of the second page and that Samir Kumar Chowdhury (DW 1) had admitted about the execution of the deed of contract. Admittedly, after cancellation of the deed of contract (Exhibit C), Samir Kumar Chowdhury executed a valid sale deed on taking prior permission from the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet and by procuring the income tax clearance certificate. Whatever right, title and interest Samir Kumar Chowdhury had in the suit property passed to the defendant Syeda Sirajunnessa Khatun after execution of the deed of sale (Exhibit G) and therefore, it is immaterial whether or not Exhibit A; is a collusive document.

20. Now let us turn to the point about the possession of the parties in the suit property. Plaintiff claimed that on 15th Agrahayan, 1372 BS he paid Taka 11,000 by executing a promissory note and that he was given possession in respect of a portion of the suit property. As regards the payment of Taka 11,000 the plaintiff failed to prove the said payment since he did not pay the said amount in cash. According to his claim, he executed a promissory note for the said amount and in view of his admitted case, the trial Court while passing the decree directed the plaintiff to deposit Taka 15,266 out of the total consideration of Taka 17,000 after deducting the amount spent in connection with the litigations. The corresponding date of delivery of possession on 15th Agrahayan, 1372 is November, 1965. It appears from the judgment in Writ Petition No. 99 of 1966 (Exhibit E(4), the then Sub-Divisional Officer took possession of the suit property under Rule 119 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 on 12th February, 1966. After the delivery of the judgment in Writ Petition No. 99 of 1966 on 9th February, 1967, the property was derequisitioned by the Sub-Divisional Officer. Samir Kumar Chowdhury claimed that on the representation of the plaintiff Md Ishaq Ali, the suit property was handed over possession to the plaintiff and Samir Kumar Chowdhury jointly and as the plaintiff Md Ishaq Ali was taking preparation for changing the nature and character of the suit lands in his possession, he along with the defendant instituted Title Suit No. 248 of 1967 for perm anent injunction against the plaintiff. The suit was decreed by judgment and order dated 4th May, 1970 (Exhibit F(2). The judgment was affirmed in Title Appeal No. 391 of 1970 (Exhibit F). The Courts below concurrently found the defendants possession in a portion of the suit property and granted permanent injunction in Title Suit No. 248 of 1967 and the possession was affirmed in Title Appeal No. 391 of 1970.

21. The defendant claimed that after execution of the sale deed, she was given possession and that the plaintiff dispossessed her after liberation of Bangladesh in 1972. The trial Court without consideration of these documents Exhibits F and F(2) held that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit property. Exhibits F and F(2) sufficiently proved that till the delivery of judgment in Title Appeal No. 391 of 1970 on 10th February, 1971, Syeda Sirajunnessa Khatun being purchaser from Samir Kumar Chowdhury was in possession in a portion of the suit property. The trial Court on a misreading of Exhibit E(4) held that Samir Kumar Chowdhury admitted the possession of Md Ishaque Miah in the High Court in Writ Petition No. 99 of 1966. After the delivery of the judgment in Writ Petition No. 99 of 1966 on 9th February, 1967, the property was handed over possession to Md Ishaque Miah and Samir Kumar Chowdhury as evident from (Exhibit F) and therefore, the learned Subordinate Judge on misreading (Exhibit E( 4) and non-consideration of Exhibit F held that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit property. Over and above, since the suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession was instituted on 1 st October, 1977 within 12 years of the date of dispossession, the defendant Syeda Sirajunnessa Khatun having acquired title in the suit property on the strength of Exhibit G is entitled to get recovery of khas possession. The Court of appeal below, in the premises, has committed no error of law in interfering with the judgment of the trial Court and decreeing Title Suit No. 93 of 1982 arising out of Title Suit No. 157 of 1977 and dismissing Title Suit No. 68 of 1983 arising out of Title Suit No. 31 of 1970. I find no infirmity or any misreading or any non-consideration of the evidence on record by the Court of appeal below in reversing the judgment of the trial Court. On the other hand, I find that the trial Court on a superficial consideration of the evidence on record and also on misreading and non-consideration of the materials on record has decreed the suit for Specific Performance of Contract. In view of the above, I find no merit in these Rules.

22. In the result, these Rules are discharged without any order as to costs.

Send down the lower Court records.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Arayesuddin J: At the time of issuance of the Rule, though the LC records were called for, but the same has not yet been arrived. During hearing of the Rule, it was felt that the LC records are not necessary to hear and dispose of the Rule. So, the Rule be treated as ready and the same be taken up for hearing.

2. Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order, dated 27-8-2005, passed by the Additional District Judge 5th Court Dhaka, in dismissing Civil Revision No. 518 of 2004 and confirming the order, dated 24-10-2004, passed by the Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 209 of 2002, should not be set aside.

3. Fact, in short, for the disposal of the Rule is that opposite party as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 in the Court of the Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, for declaration that she has no liabilities on account of Messrs Pan Asia Lines Ltd and a further declaration that she is entitled to get back her documents of properties as-described in the plaint. Further, she prayed for mandatory injunction against the present petitioner bank for giving delivery of the original documents to her. In this suit, the petitioner bank appeared and the suit came at the stage of pre-emptory hearing and deposition of the opposite party as plaintiff of Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 was recorded in part. In the meantime, petitioner bank on 6-3-2004 filed Artha Rin Suit No. 34 of 2004 in the Artha Rin Adalat, 4th Court Dhaka, against Messrs Pan Asia Carrier, SA Panama and some other foreign companies of Panama and Singapore including Messrs Pan Asia Lines Ltd. Thereafter, in. Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 this petitioner filed a petition under section 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to stay all the further proceedings of Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 till disposal of Artha Rin Suit No. 34 of 2004. The trial Court on 24-10-2004 heard the learned Advocates of both the parties and rejected the petition. Thereafter the petitioner preferred Civil Revision No. 518 of 2004 before the District Judge, Dhaka, which was heard by the Additional District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, who by his judgment and order, dated 27-8-2005, rejected the civil revision against which the present petitioner moved this Court under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule.

4. In this Rule, the main point for decision is whether Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 can be stayed or not or the order of simultaneous hearing can be passed.

5. On behalf of the petitioner, the learned Advocate Mr Sayyid Shahid Hussain, submitted that the matter in issue in Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 and that of Artha Rin Suit No. 34 of 2004 are the same and if those suits are tried by two different Courts, there is every apprehension for conflicting decisions. So, he submitted that to avoid conflicting decision it is desirable that both the suits be tried by the same Court. He submitted that since the Artha Rin Suit cannot be transferred to any other Court, the Court of the Artha Rin Adalat being the Joint District Judge, Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 can be transferred to the Court of the Artha Rin Adalat with a direction to try the suit as Joint District Judge simultaneously with Artha Rin Suit No. 34 of 2004 pending in his Court. He has further submitted that though in section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure it has been mentioned that the later suit should be stayed, but for the sake of administering justice the former suit can be stayed, if circumstances demand so. He has further submitted that when the trial Court has rejected the petition filed by the petitioner under section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, he could have given that relief under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure by staying Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 pending in his Court, but he has not done so. As in both the Courts two suits over the same cause of action are pending, there is every likelihood for conflicting decision. Therefore he submitted for simultaneous trial of both the suits. To that effect, he has relied on the case of PP Gupta vs East Asiatic Co. in Civil Revision No. 218 of 1957 reported in AIR 1960 (Allahabad, 184; the case of Mahangu Prasad Sah and another vs Pravag Sah and others in Civil Revision No. 364 of 1971 reported in AIR 1972 (Gauhati), 40 and also the case of Smt. Naurati and others vs Mehma Singh in Civil Revision No. 364 of 1971 reported in AIR 1972 (Punjab & Haryana), 421. In those Civil revisions their Lordships have discussed the provision of section 10 along with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and examined two suits pending in two civil Courts, but in the present case, one suit is pending before the Civil Court and another in the Artha Rin Adalat. So, the learned Advocate submitted that if Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 be withdrawn and placed under the jurisdiction of the Joint District Judge who is working as Artha Rin Adalat, Court No.4, Dhaka, directing him to try both the suits simultaneously, there would be no chance of conflicting decisions. Referring section 18 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain the learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that in that section analogous hearing has been barred and the Artha Rin Suit cannot be transferred to any other Court for hearing with any other suit and also it cannot be stayed. Therefore, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted for withdrawing Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 from the Court of the Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, and to transfer the same to the Court of the Artha Rin Adalat who is also a Joint District Judge and to try the same simultaneously for avoidance of conflicting decision.

6. On behalf of the opposite party, the learned Senior Advocate Mr Rafiq-ul-Huq submitted that provision of section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure is distinct and clear. As per provision of section 10 of the aforesaid Code subsequent suit is to be stayed. He submitted that opposite party instituted the suit long before two years in 2002, but the petitioner bank filed Artha Rin Suit No. 34 of 2004 long after two years. Therefore, he submitted that as per the provision of section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Artha Rin suit ought to have been stayed. Since there is bar in section 18 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, he submitted that there is no bar to proceed both the suits. To this effect, he submitted that Title suit No. 209 of 2002 is at the peremptory stage and the evidence of opposite party No. 1 has been recorded in part. At this stage, by obtaining the Rule, the petitioner has stayed the further proceeding of Title suit No. 209 of 2002, otherwise this suit would have been disposed of. So, he submitted that there is no bar to continue the two suits. He further submitted that opposite party has filed Title suit No. 209 of 2002 for getting back the documents of his properties alleging that she is not liable for payment of the loan money. So, he submitted that this suit has no nexus with the realisation of loan money and the Artha Rin suit has scope to proceed to realise the loan money. He has further submitted that Artha Rin Adalat is not a Civil Court. It is a Civil Court of limited jurisdiction only to realise the loan money, It has got no jurisdiction to decide any other matter. So, he submitted that there is no bar to continue both the suits as usual. By referring the judgment of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 738 of 2004 which has been disposed of on 5-7-2004, he submitted that respondent No.1 filed Title suit No. 208 of 2007 which was renumbered as Title Suit No. 197 of 2001 against this petitioner for declaration that the plaintiff had no liability to the petitioner bank for any loan amount and the so called memo of deposit of title dead dated 17-3-1988 was forged, concocted and illegal and the plaintiff is entitled to get back the title deed along with other supporting documents lying in the bank and prayed for a decree of Taka 75,00,000 as compensation against the petitioner bank. The trial Court decreed the suit in part without any order as to costs against which there was appeal. The appeal was dismissed and this petitioner bank was directed to return the scheduled documents. He submitted that the Appellate Court by its judgment and decree, dated 12-4-2004, affirmed the judgment of the learned Joint District Judge which has been reported in 56 DLR 588. The Appellate Court held that "jurisdiction of the Artha Rin Adalat has been created with a particular object for recovery of the loan and to that effect it is deemed to be a Civil Court, but it has not all the powers of the civil Court. "In the civil petition for leave to appeal the matter has been dealt with elaborately and the leave petition filed by the petitioner has been rejected. So, the learned Advocate for the opposite party submitted that by filing a subsequent suit in the Artha Rin Adalat, the bank wants to delay the matter. In such circumstances, he forcefully submit- ted that under no circumstance Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 can either be stayed or any order of simultaneous hearing be passed. Therefore, he submitted for discharging the Rule with costs.

<u>7. We have perused the impugned order, dated 27-8-2005, passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, in Civil Revision No. 518 of 2004 and that of the order, dated 24-10-2004, passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Title suit No. 209 of 2002 .and the citations referred by both the parties. As per section 18 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, no case filed in the Artha Rin Adalat can be transferred to any other Court for analogous hearing or any other suit can be brought to this Court for analogous hearing with the suit filed in the Artha Rin Adalat and it is settled law that Artha Rin Adalat is not a fulfledged Civil Court. It has been created by special enactment only for recovery of the defaulted loan. So, it has got no power to adjudicate on any other matters. The suit filed by the opposite party in the Court of the Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, relates to his entitlement to return back the documents of her properties together with declaration that she is not liable for the loan money to the bank as described in the plaint together with mandatory injunction directing the bank to give delivery of the original documents with compensation which is purely under the jurisdiction of the Civil Court and this point was also agitated in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 738 of 2004 before the Hon'ble Appellate Division and their Lordships upheld the decision of the High Court Division and that of the trial Court. Therefore, we are unable to agree with the learned Advocate for the petitioner for invoking jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to transfer Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 to the Artha Rin Adalat and to try it simultaneously with Artha Rin Suit No. 34 of 2004 as Joint District Judge. In such circumstances, we find that the learned Joint District Judge and the learned Additional District Judge committed no error in rejecting the petition of the petitioner bank filed under sections 10/151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In view of that we find no merit in the Rule.</u>

Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. Since in Title Suit No. 209 of 2002 plaintiff has been examined as PW 1 in part, the trial Court is directed to dispose of the suit within three months from date of receipt of the Judgment.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Awlad Ali J : This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why sections 6 and 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 insofar as they provide for payment of 50% of the decretal amount when it was sought by the defendant petitioner to either have the ex parte decree set aside under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure or for preferring an appeal against the ex parte preliminary decree dated 12-9- 02 in Mortgage Suit No. 26 of 2001 being unconstitutional as it is violative of Articles 27, 31 and 44 of the Constitution and why the ex parte decree dated 12-6-02 passed in Mortgage Suit No. 26 of 2001 (Annexure-F to the petition) should not be declared to have been passed or made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. The facts as stated in the petition briefly, are that the petitioner is the proprietor of Messrs Jamil Trading Company. The respondent No. 2 being plaintiff filed Mortgage Suit No. 26 of 2001 on May, 2001 against the petitioner and his two guarantors for realisation of Taka 42,96,879 as on 30th April, 2001. The petitioner in course of his business at one time fell short of cash flow and applied to the respondent bank by a letter dated 23-2-95 to sanction revolving LTR (Loan Against Trust Receipt) for an amount of Taka 50 lac in a bid to release some goods covered by the letter of credit opened by the petitioner in the respondent bank. The respondent bank failed to sanction the said sum although the L/C was secured by the documents of title of the imported goods and there was also full security for the proposed revolving LTR. As a result the petitioners imported goods were auctioned by the authorities which made the petitioner to incur a huge loss for failure and negligence by the respondent bank. The L/C good were hypothecated in favour of the bank. The respondent bank failed to provide the revolving LTR and therefore was unable to obtain possession of the L/C goods and in the process failed to stop the auction process and avoid the loss to the petitioner. After long four months of the petitioner's application on 25th June, 1995 for revolving LTR, the respondent bank sanctioned the revolving LTR for a sum of Taka 40 lac against further security to cover the forced loan created in respect of the goods auctioned earlier. The petitioner had already repaid the respondent bank the sums due under the letter of credit opened earlier. Although the forced loan was ultimately of no use to the petitioner as he had already incurred loss due to late sanction by the respondent bank, nevertheless the petitioner had already paid almost 75% of the principal amount of the loan. Despite regular repayments made by the petitioner the respondent bank filed Mortgage Suit No. 26 of 200 1 against the petitioner-the Firm Messrs Jamil Trading Company and the two guarantors. In the suit the respondent bank did not serve summons upon the petitioner personally and the petitioner had no way to know that a suit was filed against him. On 29th July, 2001 the respondent No. 1 the Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Chittagong by Order No.5 ordered publication of notice to the petitioner in two newspapers as per section 5(Ka) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990. Pursuant to the said order notices were published on 2nd August, 2001 in two Bangla newspapers, namely, the Daily Azker Chattagram and the Daily Azker Kagoj. The said order and publications were contrary to the requirements of section 5(Ka) and that no publication was made in an English newspaper as provided under the said section. The petitioner has come to know of the suit and the preliminary decree very recently and the petitioner felt aggrieved that he was not given an opportunity to contest the suit. The summons that was published was defective and therefore the decree passed was an irregular decree and illegal one. It is contended that the impugned preliminary decree is an irregular decree liable to be set aside and sections 6 and 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 are contrary to the petitioner's fundamental right to justice as guaranteed under the Constitution. Even if sections 6 and 7 are found to be valid that should not apply in case of an irregular decree which was passed in breach of procedural rules set down in the Ain or in the Code of Civil Procedure.

3. The respondent No. 2 has filed an affidavit-in-opposition. Denying the material allegations the respondent bank has stated that despite repeated written and verbal reminders the petitioner did not come forward to adjust its liabilities in LTR facility to the respondent Bank. The respondent bank served a legal notice upon the petitioner through its lawyer on 13-2-2000 and requested the petitioner to adjust his outstanding dues with up to date interest. After receiving the notice although the petitioner promised to pay his outstanding dues by his letter dated 13-6-2000 but ultimately, did not take any step to adjust the liability and then the respondent bank filed the Mortgage Suit No. 26 of 2001. The summons in the mortgage suit was issued several times at the address of the petitioner. Finally, the summons were published in the daily newspaper as per provisions of the Ain, 1990 and it is not true that he was totally unaware of the suit filed against him and his firm. As soon as the summons were published in the newspapers as per order of the Adalat under section 5(Ka) of the Ain it would be deemed that the notices have been duly served. Since the petitioner did not appear in the suit despite publication of summons in the national dailies the suit was decreed ex parte against the petitioner and the other defendants. Upon publication of the summons in the newspaper the defendant No.4 Mst. Golbahar Begum wife of Haji Saru Miah Sowdagar appeared in the suit on 27-9-01 and prayed for time for filing written statement. Defendant No.3 (Ka) to 3 (Ta) also appeared in the suit on 1-4-2002. It has been contended that sections 6(2) and 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 provided remedy against an ex parte decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat on depositing 50% of the decretal amount. Instead of complying with the provision of law the petitioner has filed the writ petition which is not maintainable. In the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition it has been stated that before publication of the summons under section 5(Ka) of the Ain the summons was issued on 12-6-01 by usual process and by registered post with AD which is evident from the order-sheet.

4. Mr Azmalul Hossain, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, has contended, pointing out the provision of section 5(Ka) of the Ain that the summons had not been duly served upon the defendant petitioner and the summons under order of the Adalat had not been published in accordance with the provision of section 5(Ka) of the A in as no summons was published in the English daily newspaper and therefore, the petitioner had no knowledge about the proceeding of the suit and the ex parte decree obtained by the respondent bank and consequently, the ex parte judgment and decree is an irregular judgment which has to be set aside on the ground of non-service of summons upon the petitioner. He has further contended that the provision for preferring appeal as laid down under section 7 and also the provision for setting aside the ex parte decree under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure on depositing 50% of the decretal dues is not equally efficacious remedy as in that case the petitioner has to deposit a substantial amount to apply to set aside a decree which is irregular. It is his contention that the provision for deposition 50% of the decretal amount for setting aside the irregular decree is a denial to have access to justice and such provision is contrary to the provision of Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution. He has further contended that sections 6 and 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 even if found valid law insofar as the provision for setting aside the ex parte decree under Order IX, rule 13 CPC or for an appeal against an ex parte decree upon depositing 50% of the decretal amount does not apply on its true construction of irregular judgment and decree as the judgment and decree has been passed on breach of the Rules of Procedure as provided in the Ain as well as in the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his submission and on the proposition that the decree is an irregular decree in breach of the Rules of Procedure he has cited some decisions of our jurisdiction as well as of English jurisdiction. Reference may firstly be made to the case of Md Abdur Rashid and another vs Abdul Barik and another, reported in 1984 BLD (AD) 83 where it has been observed that the provision of Order IX, rule 13 CPC clearly lays down that once it has been found that summons were not duly served, that by itself is sufficient for setting aside the ex parte decree. In paragraph 10 it has been stated-

"Under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code, if summons is not duly served on the defendant, that is a good ground for setting aside an ex parte decree. On a perusal of the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure it would be apparent, that due service of summons is an essential condition, which must be satisfied before the Court can proceed to give a judgment and under Order IX, rule 13 if a party satisfies a Court that summons were not duly served upon him, the Court is bound to set aside an ex parte decree."

Chandpur Jute Suppliers owned by Sekander Khan (since dead), Chandpur and others vs Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Chandpur and others, reported in 2 BLC 49 as cited by Mr Azmalul Hossain on question of validity of sections 6 and 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 having regard to the provision of Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution will not be of any assistance to the petitioner.

5. Among the cases of English jurisdiction reliance has been placed in the case of Regina vs County of London Quarter Sessions Appeals Committee, reported in, The Law Reports (1956), Queen s Bench Division, 682 where it has been stated that it is to be remembered that it is a fundamental principle of our law that no one is to be found guilty or made liable by an order of any tribunal unless he has been given fair notice of the proceedings before it makes any order against him. The next case is White vs Weston, reported in All England Law Reports (1968)2 All ER 842 and the relevant proposition (per Russell, LJ) as stated in page 846 is to the following effect:

"There has in the past been much discussion whether a judgment is a nullity or a mere irregularity, and for the cases on the subject I may perhaps refer to re Pritchard (Decd.) (2) where they were discussed. Upjohn, LJ., in that case expressly stated (3) to be a nullity proceedings which ought to have been served, but have never come to the notice of the defendant at all, excluding, of course, cases of substituted service, service by filing in default, or cases where service has properly been dispensed with. Danckwerts, LJ., adopted that judgment. I do not myself attach importance to the question whether it is proper to label a judgment obtained in circumstances such as this as "irregular" or "a nullity". The defect is, in my judgment, so fundamental as to entitle the defendant as of right, ex debito justitiae to have the judgment avoided and set aside."

In Anlaby and others vs Praetor ius, reported in Volume xx. Queen's Bench Division 764 the principle has been enunciated by Fry, LJ in the following language:

"There is a strong distinction between setting aside a judgment for irregularity, in which case the Court has no discretion to refuse to set it aside, and setting it aside where the judgment, though regular, has been obtained through some slip or error on the part of the defendant, in which case the Court has a discretion to impose terms as a condition of granting the defendant relief."

Relying on the aforesaid principle the learned Counsel has contended that for ex debito justitiae this Court on the ground of non-service of summons upon the defendant in breach of the procedural rules can set aside the ex parte decree which is not valid in the eye of law and that is the fundamental and constitutional right of the defendant to challenge the decree on the ground of breach of the Rules of Procedure. He has referred to us portion of the order-sheet and pointed out that summons upon the present petitioner was not duly served and the summons was not published in the newspaper complying with the provision of section 5(Ka) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990. He has concluded his submission by referring the provision of the Constitution that the petitioner has not been treated in accordance with law as provided under Article 31 of the Constitution and for imposing the condition that to set aside the ex parte decree requiring the petitioner to deposit 50% of the amount decreed, the petitioner has been denied the access to justice.

6. Mr Morshed Ahmed Khan, the learned Advocate, on the other hand, has contended that sections 6 and 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 had already been repealed and there is no legal necessity of declaring the two sections as invalid and unconstitutional. He has, placing the supplementary affidavit and also the relevant order of the Court, argued that the summons was issued by the Adalat both by registered post and in usual course by process server and as the petitioner did not appear, subsequently the summons was published in the newspaper in accordance with the provision of section 5(Ka) of the Ain and there has been due service of summons upon the defendant-petitioner. He has argued that the other defendants in the suit appeared before the Court and prayed for time for filing written statement but they did not appear at the time of hearing and consequently the ex parte decree was passed. His further contention is that there is a specific provision under section 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain to prefer an appeal for setting aside the decree and also provision for setting aside the ex parte decree under Order IX, rule 13 CPC after fulfilling the requirement of that Ain ie by depositing 50% of the decretal amount. Having not availed of that opportunity as the alternative remedy the writ petitioner has come up before this Court to have the decree set aside on the ground of non-service of summons and, as such, the writ petition is not maintainable. Mr Khan has placed his reliance in the case of Zahirul Islam vs National Bank Ltd. and others, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 191 where the contention had been raised to the effect that to make a deposit of half of the decretal dues is no efficacious remedy for the petitioner and that submission was made relying on the case of Nagina Silk Mill, Lyallpur vs Income Tax Officer, Lyallpur, 15 DLR (SC) 181 and the Appellate Division held that the submission is misconceived and stated that

"Nagina Silk Mills Ltd. was a case, under the Income Tax Act. In the present case a regular suit has been filed and a decree has been given against the petitioner. If he has to deposit half of the decretal dues at the time of the filing of the appeal, that is a condition of appeal in a regular suit with which Income Tax appeals and Customs appeals cannot be equated."

In the case of Gazi M Towfic vs Agrani Bank and others as cited by Mr Morshed Khan reported in 54 DLR (AD) 6 it has been observed that

"The law is now settled that since special provision for appeal has been made against the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat no application under Article 102 lies against such judgment and decree.

7. The main contention raised by Mr Azmalul Hossain in this case is that the judgment is an irregular judgment for non-service of summons upon the petitioner who was one of the defendants in the suit and that condition to deposit 50% of the decretal dues is the curtailment of the petitioner's fundamental right to go to the Court to set aside the irregular decree.

8. In Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 under section 6(2) it has been provided that

উপধারা (১) এ যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, কোন অর্থ ঋণ আদালত কর্তৃক বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে প্রদত্ত কোন একতরফা ডিক্রি রদ করার জন্য বিবাদী Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908) এর Order IX এর rule 13 বিধান মোতাবেক আদালতে দরখাস্ত করিতে চাহিলে তাহাকে তাহার বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রিকৃত অর্থের অন্তত অর্ধেক অর্থ বা উহার সমপরিমাণ অর্থের ব্যাংক জামানত দরখাস্তের সহিত আদালতে জমা করিতে হইবে, এবং উক্তরুপ জমা না হইলে তাহার দরখাস্ত গ্রহণযোগ্য হইবে না।”

In the foregoing provisions no limitation has been provided for filing an application under Order IX, rule 13 CPC to have an ex parte decree set aside on the ground of non-service of summons. Therefore, in that case the petitioner could have preferred an application under Order IX, rule 13 CPC for setting aside the ex parte decree within 30 days from the date of knowledge under the Code of Civil Procedure, for, the Artha Rin Adalat was exercising its power as a civil Court. The alternative recourse that was opened to the petitioner was to prefer an appeal according to the provision of section 7 within 30 days from the date of decree which he could not however, avail of because the petitioner had no knowledge about the proceeding of the suit and the ex parte decree. Therefore, the alternative and efficacious remedy that was available to the petitioner is by filing an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Irregular decree in common parlance seems to be that due service of summons upon the defendant was not effected before the decree was passed or that the defendant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing before the Court when the suit was called on for hearing. If either of these conditions is satisfied the Court is bound to set aside the ex parte decree.

<u>9. Because of the default culture of the loan receiver who received the loan from the financial institution and the bank the legislature had taken a stringent measure and enacted the special law providing the special procedure for realisation of the loan speedily and thus the enactment, namely, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 was enacted. By subsequent amendment the provision was introduced in the Ain for setting aside the ex parte decree according to the provision of Order IX, rule 13 CPC on the ground of non-service of summons or on any other grounds sufficient to satisfy the Court to have the decree set aside. The special law provided for the special provision for depositing the 50% of the decretal amount in having the ex parte decree set aside on the grounds which would seem to be sufficient to the Court. Now the question that has been urged, whether 50% deposit is a curtailment of the right to have access to justice, namely, to file an application under Order IX, rule 13 CPC or to prefer an appeal. Under the Ain one cannot simply go to the Court and obtain a decree on the claim laid without having produced sufficient materials before the Court to justify the claim and in case of realisation of money by the bank or by any financial institution the claim has to be proved by documentary evidence and even in case of ex parte decree the Court has to be satisfied on the materials submitted before it in awarding a money decree or decree for realisation of money. The legislature, for realisation of money from the defaulter and keeping in view the conduct of the defaulting parties, enacted this provision for depositing 50% of the decretal amount both in preferring the appeal and in preferring an application under Order IX, rule 13 which cannot be said to be unreasonable restriction on the defaulting borrower to go to the Court to set aside the ex parte decree on sufficient ground. The principle as enunciated in English jurisdiction as regards setting aside ex parte judgment and decree and the principle that has been settled in our jurisdiction are almost the same. Furthermore, the question that summons was duly served upon the defendants including the present petitioner is a question of fact which cannot be decided in writ jurisdiction and that question can appropriately be decided by the Court which passed the ex-part decree or by the appellate Court if any appeal under the law is preferred, taking the ground of non-service of summons. Therefore, the alternative and efficacious remedy was available to the writ-petitioner under sections 6 and 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 and the writ petition is thus in our view, not maintainable.</u>

The Rule is accordingly, discharged with cost. The order of stay granted by this Court earlier stands vacated.

End.
