full_judgment:
Md Tafazzul Islam J : The above Civil Petition Nos. 1498 of 2007 and 1333 of 2007 are directed against the Judgment and Order dated 9-11-2006 of the High Court Division passed in Civil Revision No. 3257 of 2003 making the Rules absolute and the above Civil Petition No. 1499 of 2007 is directed against the judgment and Order dated 9-11-2006 of the High Court Division passed in Civil Revision No. 3747 of 2002 making the Rule absolute. Since the facts of the above cases are more or less similar the question of law involved are also same and both the petitioners are heard together and disposed of by this judgment.

2. Facts of Civil Revision No. 3257 of 2003 as placed before the High Court Division, are that Dr. Ashequr Rahman, the Respondent No. 1 in Civil Petition No. 1498 of 2007 and the petitioner in Civil Petition No. 1333 of 2008, instituted Preemption Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 1998 against Maha Maya Rani Saha, the petitioners both in Civil Petition Nos. 1498 and 1499 of 2007 and respondent No. 1 in Civil Petition No. 1333 of 2008, On the averments that in CS Dag No. 3123 Altabuddin owned 05-decimal of viti l and in Khatian No. 1590, Kafiluddin owned 05-decimals of land in CS Khatian No. 1591, Ukiluddin owned 05 decimal land in CS Khatian Nos. 1592, Lektunnessa and Badrunnessa owned 04 decimals of viti land in Khatian No. 1593, Shorforaj Uddin Kazi owned 05 decimal land in Khatian No. 1594 and in the said CS Dag No. 3123, out of 53 decimals land, 27 decimals were recorded in the names of the above persons and the remaining 26 decimals were recorded in the names of Shatish Chandra and Roshik Chandra, two brothers, in khatian No. 1588 who possessed their lands in ejmali; Lektonnessa was survived with husband Shakhawat Chowdhury, brothers Kafiluddin Kazi and Shorforaj Uddin Kazi, sister Badrunnessa and mother Ayesha Khatoon and that Shakhawat Chowdhury gifted his share in the above land inherited from his wife to other successors; Kazi Shamsul Huda and Ajimunnessa, respectively the son and wife of Altabuddin, and Jamordonnessa Sakinabad and Omdatunnessa, three daughters of Altabuddin, by registered patta dated 19-8-1924, by purchasing 22 decimals of lands from Khatian Nos. 1591, 1592, 1593, 1594 and 1595 became the absolute owners of 27 decimals of land and possessed the said land in ejmali along with the co-owners of the remaining 26 decimals of lands CS Dag No. 3123 and also the co- owners of CS Dag Nos. 3134 and 4223, subsequently by amicable settlement Kazi Shamsul Huda and others owned and possessed the entire 16 annals land in Dag No. 3123 and Jotish Chandra Rabri got the land in Dag No. 4123; Kazi Shamsul Huda, in the year 1348 BS, settled his entire 27 decimals land to his wife Jibonnessa, Dr Ashiqur Rahman, Anwara Khatoon and Shahjadi Begum and they having been possessing the said land by paying rent their names were recorded in SA Khatian No. 1090 in respect of the lands of Dag Nos. 3123, 360 and 4011 and the balance 26 decimal land of Dag No. 3123 was recorded in the Khas Khatian of the Government; SA recorded owner Shahjadi Begum sold her land to Dr Ashequr Rahman in the year 1980; in the year 1977, Kazi Shamsul Huda, by paying arrear rents of 22 years of the remaining 26 decimals of land of Dag No. 3123 which was recorded in Khas Khatian, also took lease of the same in the name of his wife Jibonnessa and planted trees therein, after the death of Kazi Shamsul Huda, his wife Jibonnessa, formed Kazi Shamsul Huda Trust vide registered deed No. 20169 dated 6-12-1982 and included 63 decimals of viti land of Dag No. 3123 in the above trust deed and appointed the Dr Ataur Rahman Khan, the pro- forma respondent No.2, as the Managing Trustee of the above trust; then Dr Ashequr Rahman, with the consent of Jebonnessa, used to possess the said land as a co-sharer and he is still in possession of the same and his name has been recorded in last SA Khatian No. 1090 and thereby he became co-sharer of the case land and it is only on 12-1-1998 he, for the first time, came to know that the respondent No. 1, on 16-4-1998, purchased the case land from the proforma respondent No.4 and that the respondent No.1, by filling Title Suit No.7 of 1990 also obtained decree therein in her favour in respect of the above khas khatian land; then on 22-1-1998, he on obtaining the certified copy of the said judgment and decree of the above said suit then on 16-4-1998, he after obtaining the certified copy of the deed of sale dated 23-9-1981 which was subsequently amended vide deed No. 3828 dated 31-7-1991, came to know about the sale of the case land; before selling the case land, the proforma respondent No.4 never informed him (Dr Ashequr Rahman) or other co-sharer about the sale and further neither the proforma respondent No. 4 nor the respondent No. 1 was ever in possession -of the case land and that the respondent No. 1 also did not make him (Dr Ashe- qur Rahman) a party in the above Title Suit No.7 of 1990. The respondent No. 1 contested the above miscellaneous case by filing written objection denying the material allegations made therein and con- tending that the total land in Dag No-3223 is 53 decimals out of which 26 decimals belonged to Roshik Chandra and Satish Chandra and the rest 27 decimals land were divided into 6 Khatians being numbers 1591-1595 in the names of Altabuddin and others; subsequently Roshik Chandra died leaving behind son Jogesh Chandra and Shatish Chandra died leaving being son Haripada; mistakenly the heirs of Jogesh Chandra got the land of Dag No. 3123 and subsequently Haripada died leaving only the cousin Jogesh and Jogesh died leaving behind wife Shovarani, the proforma respondent No.4, and another daughter; while in possession of the suit land, the proforma respondent No.4 sold her entire property including the 26 decimals of land, the suit land, to the respondent No.1 and she is the owner and possessor of the land; since the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Sreenagar threatened to lease out the suit land to others, she had file Title Suit No. 7 of 1990 and she obtained decree therein and the Government did not prefer Appeal against it and then she took steps for mutation of the case land on payment of rent, which is pending before the Additional Commissioner (Revenue); the" pre-emptor Dr Ashequr Rahman was never in possession of the case land and the Government also never possessed the case land. The learned Assistant Judge, after hearing by judgment and Order dated 31-5- 2000 dismissed the miscellaneous case. On Appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 38 with 41 of 2000, the learned District Judge, after hearing by judgment and Order dated 15-4-2003 also dismissed the Appeal. The pre-emptor then moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 3257 of 2003 and after hearing, the High Court Division, by the impugned Order made the Rule absolute.

3. Facts of Civil Revision No. 3747 of 2002, as placed before the High Court Division, are that the above Mahamaya Rani Saha, instituted Title Suit No.7 of 1990 seeking declaration of her title and also permanent injunction in respect of the case land which was recorded in khas Khatian as vested property, on the averments that out of CS Dag No. 2313, eight anna land in Khatian No. 1588 was recorded in the name of Satish Chandra and Roshik Chandra and the balance eight anna land in Khatian No. 1590 to 1595, was recorded in the name of Altabuddin and others and that as per amicable partition Satish Chandra and Roshik Chandra got the northern part of the above CS Dag No. 3123, while Altabuddin and others got the southern part in equal share; Ka schedule suit land was recorded in the name of Jibonnessa and others in SA Khatian No. 1090 but Kha schedule land measuring 26 decimals instead of being recorded in the name of Jogesh, was wrongly recorded in the name of the Government in SA Khas Khatian No.1; as per mutual partition between Jogesh and Haripada, Jogesh took Kha schedule land and was possessing the same and that Jogesh transferred the said suit land to proforma respondent No.4 vide Heba Deed No. 2313 dated 28-3-1978 and then she sold the same to her vide registered deed No. 2313 dated 23-9-1981 and that by mistake in the said deed the number of Khatian was wrongly written as Khatian No. 1589 and the said mistake was subsequently corrected on 31-7-1991 and that she had been possessing the suit land over twelve years while the government as well as the defendants, had no title and possession over the same and the suit land was wrongly recorded in the khas khatian. The defendants contested the above suit by filing written statement denying the material allegation and contending, inter alia, that 27 decimals of land of CS Dag No. 3123 was rightly recorded in the name of Jibonnessa in SA Parched and the owner of the rest 26 decimals of land having left the country before partition and the said land was never sold and accordingly the same was rightly recorded in the Khas Khatian No. 1 and nobody raised any objection thereto and that Mahamaya Rani Saha and/or her predecessor never possessed the said land and the so called documents of settlement of the suit land in favour of the defendant Nos. 6-7 Shorforaz Uddin and Momtaz Begum on 20-2-1989 vide Case No. 39/ 88-89 with effect from 1977 is of no effect and Mahamaya Rani also never paid any rent in respect of the suit land. The trial Court, after hearing, by judgment and decree dated 29-4-1993 dis- missed the suit. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Munshiganj and others, the defendants in the above suit, preferred Title Appeal having No. 163 of 2000 and the learned Joint District Judge, after hearing, by judgment and decree dated 24-4-2002 dismissed the Appeal. The Government then moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 3747 of 2002 and after hearing the High Court Division made the Rule absolute.

4. We have heard the learned counsel and perused the impugned judgments and Orders of the High Court Division and other connected papers.

<u>5. As it appears, in respect of Civil Petition No. 1498 of 2007 and Civil Petition No. 1333 of 2008, the learned Assistant Judge dismissed the Pre-emption Case No. 17 of 1998 on the ground of limitation only. On Appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 38 of 2000 the learned District Judge also dismissed the same on ground of limitation. The High Court Division however disposed of the Rule issued in Civil Revision No. 3257 of 2003 holding that none can file any pre-emption miscellaneous case against any vested property or land recorded in the khas Khatian of the Government and that the case land is vested property as the original owners left this country before 1965 and that the Government rightly prepared Census List in Pursuance of Notification No. 6199 dated 3-12-1965 issued under the Defence of Pakistan Rules published in the Dhaka Gazette dated 4-12-19.65 and then the SA and RS records were rightly prepared in the name of the government in khas khatian.</u>

6. In respect of Civil Petition No. 1499 of 2007, it appears that High Court Division disposed of the Rule issued in Civil Revision No. 3747 of 2002 holding that the trial Court without considering the documents filed by both the parties erroneously decreed the suit and the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Munshiganj, who heard the Appeal, also erroneously dismissed the Appeal and that the suit property was recorded in Khas Khatian of the Government long before the filing of the suit and the suit was barred by limitation and the original owners of the suit property having left this country before 1965, the suit property became a vested property and the concerned authority duly prepared census list by the Government and the case . land being and enemy property vested in the Deputy Custodian of Enemy property (Land and Building) in pursuance of Government notification No. 6199- Gen dated 3-12-1965 issued under the Defense of Pakistan Rule published by the Dhaka Gazette dated 4-12-1965.

7. We are of the view that the High Court Division on proper consideration of the materials on record arrived at a correct decision in both the Rules and there is no illegality or infirmity in the above decision so as to call for any interference.

8. All the petitions are dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Abdul Hamid ------- For the Petitioner.
No one ------- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Rajendra Shirali and others  ------- Petitioners. 
Vs. 
Mahadev Shirali  ------- Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya J.- This Rule arises out of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against an order of rejection of an application filed by the petitioners under section 151 read with section 148 of the Code of the Civil procedure praying for vacating an order of dismissal of a suit for specific performance of contract. The petitioners filed a suit against the opposite parties for specific performance of contract for sale of certain land and the suit was decreed ex parte on 3-4-67. The operative portion of the order is to the following effect:-

“That the suit be decreed ex parte with costs. Defendants are directed to execute and register a Kabala in favor of the plaintiffs within 30 days, in default, there will be a Kabala through court. Plaintiffs to deposit Rs. 75/- to the credit of defendants within 15 days, in default, the suit stands dismissed.”

2. It appears that no deposit was made by the plaintiffs as directed in the said order in consequence whereof the default order became operative. The following order was then passed by the court on 19-4-67:-

“Balance of consideration money of Rs. 75/- not deposited within the prescribed time. Hence the suit is dismissed as per order dated 3-4-67. There will be no cost to any Party.”

3. On 5th August. 1967 the Plaintiffs filed an application purporting to be under section 151 read with section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoring the suit to the original file on vacating the order of dismissal and for extending time for deposit of the sum of Rs. 75/-. It was stated in the said application that two of the three plaintiffs had been away from the country in connection with their business and the plaintiff No. 2 was in charge of the conduct of the said suit, that the said plaintiff No. 2 having been laid down with fever and dysentery was confined to bed and unable to move and that as such he could not deposit the money on the date fixed by the court.

4. The learned Munsif by his order dated 15-8-67 rejected the said application on the view that the suit having been dismissed as per order dated 19-4-67 in terms of the judgment dated 3-4-67 there was nothing for that court to do.

5. The present petition of revision is directed against the said order and Mr. Abdur Hamid, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners contends that the learned Munsif failed to exercise jurisdiction in not granting extension of time under section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure or in the alternative, in exercise of his inherent powers under section 151 of the Code for doing justice to the Party. The learned Advocate also contends that in any view or the matter, the learned Munsif should have treated the application as one for review and granted relief on the said basis.

This Rule is not opposed, there being no appearance on behalf of the opposite parties.

6. The learned Advocate has strenuously argued that the court below had ample powers to extend the time, if not under the specific provision of the Code, in exercise of its inherent powers.

7. There is a specific provision in the Code in section 148 for extension of time, where any time is granted by the court for doing any act prescribed or allowed by the Code. This provision has obviously no application to a case where time is fixed by the court in a decree for performing an obligation which arises out of a contract between the parties. Moreover, if we consider that the power under the aforesaid provision can be invoked even in a case where time is fixed by the court in its final Order, there is no question of exercise of such power in this case in view of the fact that the conditional order has become operative, and the court has become functus officio.

8. This case appears to be clearly governed by the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Shah Wali Vs. Ghulam Dim as reported in 19 DLR, S.C. 143. In that case the Supreme Court of Pakistan had to deal with the question of deposit of a certain amount of pre-emption money after the expiry of the date fixed by a decree in a pre-emption suit. The trial court directed the plaintiff to deposit a sum of Rs. 3000/- on account of the pre-emption money on or before 21st March, 1961 and it was further directed that in default of deposit by that date, the suit would be dismissed with costs. On an appeal against said decree the appellate court enhanced the amount of pre-emption money to Rs. 8000/- which was directed to be deposited within 1 month of the appellate decree dated the 30th March, 1962 in default whereof the suit would be treated as dismissed. A second appeal was filed to the High Court of West Pakistan but this appeal being treated as revision under an amendment of the relevant law was dismissed on the 9th of October, 1962. The pre-emption money as directed by the court was supposed to have been deposited by the plaintiff but it subsequently appeared that through a mistake in calculation the deposit made was short by a small amount. The question arose whether the court had any jurisdiction to extend the period of time after the suit had been dismissed owing to the operation of the default order. It has been held by the Supreme Court that when for the plaintiffs default in making payment of the correct amount within the time fixed by the appellate decree the suit had been dismissed, there is no question of extension of time involved either by the original court or by the appellate court thereafter, although in an appeal from the decree itself which has prescribed the time limit, such an extension can be granted by the appellate court hearing the said appeal Hamudoor Rahman, J (as he then was) in a separate judgment elaborated the reasons in support of the decision of the Supreme Court in the following words:-

“Section 148 of the Civil Procedure Code gives the Court powers to extend time previously fixed or granted by it for the doing of any act prescribed or allowed by the Code of Civil Procedure and this they can do even after the period originally fixed or granted has expired. But this section, it is now well settled, does not apply where the period is fixed by a decree in a suit unless the decree is in the nature of a preliminary decree and the court still retains seisin over the action. The principle upon which it has been so held is that since a decree normally puts an end to a suit the power of the court to pass any other order with respect to that particular suit thereafter also comes to an end and the court becomes functus officio with regard thereto. The exception made in the case of a preliminary decree is also on the same basis that in the case of such a decree the court does not become functus officio but still retains control over the action and therefore, has full power to make necessary orders therein including an order for the extension of time. This distinction is not without importance, for, even orders contained in decrees, which are not strictly speaking preliminary decrees, may not always be such as are intended to operate automatically without any further intervention by the court. The real test, in my view, is whether the decree has been made in such terms as to indicate that the court has finally disposed of all matters so that it is to operate automatically or whether the court has still retains some control over the litigation. An examination, therefore, has to be made of the precise terms used in the decree. In the present case, the decree of the trial court used the words that in the event of default, the suit "will be dismissed". These are not: the words of automatic operation, for, they contemplate a further order dismissing the suit. but the District Judge in the appellate decree made good this defect by stating that in the event of default, the suit "will be treated as dismissed." These words were capable; in my view, of operating automatically without any further order of the court."

<u>9. In the instant case the words used in the operative part of the decree dated 3. 4. 67 are "in default, the suit stands dismissed" and, therefore, in accordance with the principle laid down in the said decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan the court became functus officio in this case after, expiry of 15 days from the date of the decree and, therefore, had no jurisdiction to make any alteration of that order by extending the time limit as prescribed therein.</u>

10. Mr. Abdul Hamid, the learned Advocate has next submitted that if the court feels that a grave injustice has been caused to a party for which he is not to be blamed, the court can certainly invoke its inherent powers for doing justice to the party. Although the inherent power of a court to do justice as will appear from the language used in section 151 of the Code, does not contemplate any restriction on its exercise but judicial authorities have laid down certain norms and conditions under which the said powers should be exercised by a court. The question of the exercise of the inherent power of a court came up for consideration before a Division Bench of this court in the case of S.M. Yousuf and another Vs. Khandker Hafizur Rahman and others, in Civil Revision case No. 326 of 1962 decided on the 16th August, 1972 by Sayem, J and Bhattacharya, J. It is pertinent to refer here to the following observation made in the said case:-

“These powers, as contemplated in the said section are intended to supplement the other provisions of the Code, as a Legislature cannot foresee and provide for every eventuality which may occur, but they are not for the purpose of evading or ignoring the express provisions of the law or for inventing a new procedure according to the individual inclination of a particular Judge. Under the cover of these powers, a court cannot over-ride the express provisions of the law applicable to a particular case. These powers cannot be invoked in a case which is fully covered by a specific provision In the Code, or, where there is a positive prohibition regarding a particular act or order or where there is an alternative remedy.”

<u>11. It will appear that if there is specific provision in the Code which covers a particular case or if there is a positive prohibition against an act, the said powers are not to be invoke of course as was pointed out in the said decision there is an important exception to this general rule. Where a mistake of a court or court's officer causes some injustice to a particular party, as has been held in the said case, the power under section 151 of the Code can be exercised in a particular case for the purpose of giving necessary relief, even though such an act is prohibited under the general law or there is any alternative remedy for doing the same.</u>

12. Mr. Abdul Hamid cited the case of Azizul Hoque and others Vs. Shuasini Ghose, reported in 21 DLR (Dacca) 334. In that case the High Court in a Civil Revision case directed the payment of deficit court fee by ascertain date and it was further directed in the said costs. When the case records went back to the trial court the plaintiff paid deficit court fees as directed by the trial court but it appears that there having been a mistake in calculation the amount mentioned in the court's order and paid by the party fell short of the requisite amount. The relief, however, was granted by the High Court, in a suo Motu rule issued, by extending time on the ground that the Party was prevented from putting in the required amount because of the mistake committed by the court. This case fails in the line with the exception mentioned in the case of S. M. Yusuf and another and the view of the learned Judges has been clearly expressed in the following observation:-

“From the above discussion it will appear that sections 149 and 151 Civil Procedure Code read with section 28 of the Court Fees Act granted adequate power to this court to grant extension of time in pulling in proper court fee even though the period for depositing such court fee has expired provided that the delay is due to the mistake of the court which prevented the Party in question informing its duty.”

13. Another distinguishing feature of that case from the present one is that the dead line together with the default clause was set down by a procedural and interlocutory order for the payment of court fees, whereas in the present case the time limit was imposed by the decree itself containing a decision on merits. This case therefore does not help the learned advocate.

14. I may refer in this connection to the case of Bhutnath Das and others Vs. Sahadeb Chandra Panja reported in AIR 1962 Cal. 485, the facts of which are similar to those in the present case. The suit was decreed in the said case for Specific Performance on the basis of the alternative prayer and the relevant terms of the decree are as follows :-

“Ordered that the suit be decreed on contest with costs. Plaintiff's alternative prayer for reconveyance of the property is allowed. Plaintiffs shall deposit the sum of Rs. 1425/- in favor of the defendant within a fortnight from today in court. If the plaintiffs fail to make the deposit within the specified time, then the suit shall stand dismissed on contest with costs.”

15. Before the expiry of the date, the Plaintiffs filed an application purporting to be under section 148 and 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure Praying for extension of time for making the deposit by three months. The learned Subordinate Judge having rejected the said application, the correctness of the said order of rejection was challenged in the Revisional Jurisdiction of Calcutta High Court which held that such an extension could not be granted under section 148 of the C.P.C. nor under section 151 of the C.P.C and K.C. Das Gupta, J (as he then was) expressed the view of the Bench in the following manner:-

"If the deposit of money that was ordered in this case could be considered to be an act prescribed or allowed by the Code there would be no doubt, in by opinion, that the court had jurisdiction under section. 148 C.P.C. to extend the time. I cannot see, however, how this deposit of money for the performance of the contract can be considered to be an act either prescribed or allowed by the Code. I have no hesitation, therefore, in holding that section 148 C.P.C. has no application."

<u>16. The question whether section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives the court jurisdiction to extend the time is more difficult. In the first place, we have to remember that if the court has lost seisin of the case all-together, there is no scope for the application of section 151 C.P.C. It is only if the court has retained jurisdiction in the litigation that the question of making any order in inherent jurisdiction arises. If jurisdiction had already ceased to exist the scope of making order in the inherent jurisdiction of the court totally disappears. The real question, therefore, is whether in a case like this, where an order has been made for the payment of certain money within a certain time for the purpose of getting specific performance and at the same time an order has also been made that if the money is not paid the suit will stand dismissed, the court retains jurisdiction. Through not without hesitation, I have reached the conclusion that in such a case it will be unrealistic and unjust to say that the court retains jurisdiction. Whether the court has retained jurisdiction or not will in my view, depend very much on the substance of the directions given. In granting a decree for a specific performance, the court makes it conditional on the payment being made within a certain time and it appears that the time specified was intended by the court to be the essence of the order, it would be unreasonable, in my opinion, to hold that the court has still retained jurisdiction. Where a decree for specific performance is made and at the same time a direction is given to the plaintiff to put in the money within ascertain time and there is no indication that time is the essence of the order, it might be possible and ordinarily reasonable to say that though a time has been specified for the performance of the act, the court has not finally dealt with the matter and retains jurisdiction to pass such other orders as may appear to it to be reasonable. Where, however, the court makes also an order that if the amount is not deposited within the lime specified the suit will stand dismissed, I find it difficult to agree that the court retains any jurisdiction whatsoever".</u>

17. It may be noted that in that case the application for extension of time was filed even before the default order became operative. I respectfully agree with the ultimate decision in the above case but want to add my own comments about the reasoning given by the learned Judge of the Calcutta High Court in support of the decision of the Bench so far as the application under section 151 C.P.C. was concerned. If I may say with respect the said reasoning is generally correct in view of the provision of Order 20 Rule 3 of the Code which prohibits any alteration in or addition to a judgment after it has been signed, except under section 152 or in review. This, expect of the case has been considered in the above mentioned case of S. M. Yusuf and another Vs. Khandker Hafizur Rahman and others of this court. I therefore, hold that section 151 C.P.C. cannot be invoked in the present case in view of the fact that any alteration of the operative part of the decree containing the time limit is prohibited under Order 20, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and there was an alternative remedy by way of appeal in which the necessary relief might have been granted.

18. Mr. Abdul Hamid, the learned advocate for the petitioner, last of alt, submits that in any view of the matter this application under Section 151 C.P.C. might have been regarded as an application for review, and proper relief could have been granted by the learned Munsif under it. But I do not sec how can a ground as made out in the said application may be regarded as a ground for review. It may be pointed out that the case as made out in the present application under section 115 of the C.P.C. is entirely different from the case which was sought to be made out in the said application under section 151 of the C.P.C. before the learned Munsif. In the present application want of knowledge about the order by which the time limit was fixed by the court has been taken as a ground for failure to deposit the money whereas illness of the petitioner No. 2 was stated to be the cause of failure in the said application under 151 C.P.C. Code. Such a ground as has been taken in the application under 151 C.P.C. Code can never be a ground within the meaning of order 47 Rule 1 of the Code. The extension of time could have been granted by the appellate Court if the decree itself was challenged in the appeal.

19. It is necessary to take notice here of a decision of a single Judge of the Dacca High Court in the case of Ashaf Ali Vs. Bayla Hadsa and others, reported in 17 D.L.R. (Dacca; 593, in which Ali J has, disagreed with the view expressed in Sheikh Ayezuddin Vs. Priya Sankar Choudhury reported in 6 D.L.R. 595 and has made certain observations with which, I may say with respect, 1 have been unable to agree. The facts of that case are, of course, distinguishable from those of the instant case and no exception can be taken to the ultimate decision taken therein, as the learned Judge was dealing with the case in second appeal arising from the decree itself, containing the default clause.

20. The default clause similar to that in the present case, which was to the effect (hat in case the Plaintiffs failed to make the deposit by 15.5.60 the suit should stand dismissed. The 15th May, 1960, was a Sunday; on the 16th May, a petition was filed for extension of time for making the deposit and the same was rejected. The decree was affirmed in appeal by the court of the District Judge and then there was a Second appeal to the Dacca High Court, challenging the correctness of the decree of dismissal of the suit.

<u>21. Relying upon a Bench decision of the Madras High Court, namely, Abdul Shakerb Saheb Vs. Abdul Rahman Sahib, reported in I.L.R 46 Madras 148, same case AIR 1923 Mad. 284 and a Single Judge decision of Nagpur High Court, namely, Gokul Prosad Vs. Fattalal, reported in AIR 1946 Nag. 29, Mr. Justice Ali held:</u>

<u>“It is thus clear that the decree in an action for specific performance of contract, no matter whatever may be the form in which it may be drawn up, is, in the eye of law, a preliminary decree, and as such, even when a default clause is attached thereto is not dead, but pending, though in a condition. Necessarily, the Court retains control over the action and has therefore jurisdiction to enlarge time regardless of the said default clause.”</u>

22. In laying down the proposition quoted above. Mr. Justice Ali did not notice that there was no default clause in the decree dealt in the Madras case, of the same nature as in the case dealt by him. It was clearly indicated by the terms of the decree before him that there could be automatic dismissal of the suit without any further intervention of the Court, an failure to comply with the direction for deposit by a particular date, and so far as this part of the decree is concerned, it cannot be said that it was in the nature of a preliminary decree. It is true that a decree for specific performance of a contract for sale, ordinarily, has been regarded to be in the nature of a preliminary decree and the practice of making such a decree in the final form has been disapproved in a number of cases, unless time is of essence of the contract in a particular case, because in case of a default in payment of the balance of the consideration it is open to the other side to apply for rescission of the contract under Section 35 or the Specific Relief Act. The nature of such a decree as did not contain a default clause in terms of finality came up for consideration before a Division Bench of this Court, to which I was a Party, in the case of Chowdhury Md. Sarwar Vs. Shahadat Hossain Khan and others (F.M.A. 16 of 1970), decided on 25. I. 73 and it has been held in the said case that it is in the nature of a preliminary decree. But the introduction of default clause of the nature referred to above, whether it is done rightly or wrongly, undoubtedly transforms the character of the decree, and it becomes final, so far as that particular part of the decree is concerned, and the Court passing the decree docs not retain any jurisdiction to grant any extension of time, either under section 148 of the Code or under any other Provision, unless mistake of the Court or Court's Officer leading to some injustice is involved. It is however perfectly within the powers of the Court of appeal to grant any extension of time in super-session of the default clause, when it is seized of the entire case on an appeal from the decree itself.

23. So far as the Nagpur case is concerned, the learned Judge of the Dacca High Court did not notice that in that case there were an appeal at the instance of the Plaintiff against the decree itself as well as a Revision case at the instance of the defendant against the order of the Trial Court granting extension of time for making the deposit, notwithstanding the default clause in terms of finality. Although the learned Single Judge of the Nagpur High Court Niyogi J., made some observations in the nature of obiter dicta on which Ali J. relied, he exorcised his powers in the appeal by granting an extended period for making the deposit by modifying the decree itself and held that the argument that the Lower Court had no jurisdiction to extend the time fixed by the decree did not call for any consideration in view of the modification or the lower Court's decree in the appeal.

<u>24. The above mentioned two cases of Madras and Nagpur High Courts were distinguished by a Division Bench of the Patna High Court in the case of Ramdhani Ram Vs. Sital Prasad Ram reported in AIR 1959 Patna 181 and it was held in the said case that the court had no jurisdiction to extend the time fixed by it in a decree for specific performance of contract containing a default clause in terms of finality.</u>

25. It is interesting to motive here that the Allahabad High Court in the case of Someshwar Dayal and others Vs. Widow of Lalmon Shah and others, reported in AIR 1958. All 488 took the view that the fixation of a date for making the deposit to the balance or the consideration incorporated in a decree for specific performance of a contract (in a case where there was no default clause in terms of finality) was not a decree or a part of a decree within the meaning of Section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure as fixation of such a time was no part of the controversy between the parties nor did it determine any-rights of the parties in the suit and therefore an alteration of such a date by the court was not fit by Order 20 Rule 3 of the Code.

26. It may be noted here that there have been certain clauses of eases in which Courts have exercised jurisdiction, notwithstanding default clauses in terms of finality, to modify orders fixing a dead line for the performance of an act and grant an extended period for the performance of the said act, although the time fixed already expired and the default clause became operative. These are mainly interlocutory orders dealing with procedural matters. In such a case, the Court does not lose jurisdiction over the said or proceeding in which such an order may be passed, because the suit or preceeding does not terminate but remains pending.

27. One of such cases, viz. Jyotish Chandar Sen Vs. Rukmini Ballav Sen and others, reported in 62 CWN 588 same case  AIR 1959 Cal. 35 was referred to in the judgment of Ali J., mentioned above. In that case, a prayer for acceptance of additional written statement was allowed on condition of payment of certain costs by a certain date in default whereof, it was directed, the written statement would stand rejected. It was holds in the said case that the court had jurisdiction to enlarge time under Sec. 148 C.P.C. in such a case, Similar view was taken in the cases of, Bhupendra Nath Vs. Prabhat Kumar, reported in 63 CWN. 460 same case AIR 1960 Cal. 75, Printing and Industrial Machinery Ltd. Vs. Swastika Press Ltd. reported in 90 Cal. L.J. 105 and Bokaro and Ramgarh Ltd. Vs. State of Bihar, reported in AIR 1965 Cal. 308. It has been pointed out in these eases, that the Court retains seisin over the principal action, even though the interlocutory proceeding has come to an end and has jurisdiction, in such cases to give an extension of time.

28. There is another line of cases in which it has been held that when a default clause, though incorporated in a decree, is merely procedural in nature, the Court retains powers to modify such a procedural order in order to grant relief in an appropriate case. A judgment of Supreme Court of India may be referred to in this connection. In the case of Mahanth Ram Das Vs. Ganga Das, reported in AIR 1961 S. C. 882, Hidayetulla J. (as he then was) in delivering the judgment of the Bench made the following observation:

"..........These orders turn out often enough to be inexpedient. Such procedural orders though peremptory (conditional decrees apart) are, in essence, in terrorem, so that dilatory litigants might put themselves in order and avoid delay. They do not however, completely estop a Court from taking note of events and circumstances which happen within the time fixed.......Such orders are not like the law of the Meco and the Persians. Cases are known in which the Courts have moulded their practice to meet a situation such as this and to have restored a suit or proceeding though a final order has been passed," The present case does not come under any of these categories."

I therefore, do not find any substance in this Rule. The rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.
